entities/john-lambert.title: John Lambert
entities/john-lambert.content:
John Lambert (d. 1538), otherwise Nicholson, was burned at Smithfield in 1538 after a disputation before the king at Greenwich — condemned in a session Foxe calls bloody, with judgment reserved to the Lord against that day when princes and subjects shall be judged.
Disputation and Condemnation
Lambert answered forty-five articles on the sacrament. Foxe prints his treatise addressed to the king and his apology. Entrapped by craft and subtlety of the bishops, he was judged and condemned to death.
Cromwell and Execution
On the day appointed, Lambert was brought at eight in the morning from prison to Lord Cromwell’s inward chamber; Cromwell desired forgiveness for what he had done. Admonished that his hour was at hand, Lambert was greatly comforted; he saluted gentlemen in the hall and sat down to breakfast showing no sadness or fear.
Carried to Smithfield, he offered himself a sacrifice of sweet savour. Foxe notes that of all burned at Smithfield none was so cruelly handled: after his legs were consumed to the stumps and tormentors withdrew the fire so that but small coals remained, two with halberts pitched him upon their pikes as far as the chain would reach; he lifted up flaming fingers and cried, “None but Christ, none but Christ,” then fell into the fire and gave up his life.

entities/john-philpot.title: John Philpot
entities/john-philpot.content:
John Philpot (1516–1555), archdeacon of Winchester, is one of the most fully documented Marian martyrs in Foxe — thirteen examinations and open judgment before Bonner.
Examinations
The process and history of John Philpot, examined, condemned, and martyred in defence of the gospel (vol7):

First through thirteenth examinations
Manner of calling before the Bishop of London
Two private conferences with Bonner; another in the coal-house
Examinations in open judgment by Bonner in the consistory at Paul’s, 13 and 14 December
Bonner’s exhortation to John Philpot
Letters to Lady Vane; godly letter of reproof of a certain gospeller to Bonner
Harpsfield’s letter to Bonner on Thomas — Robert Johnson the registrar to Bonner
Letter to Bonner by the queen’s council

Philpot was brought before Winchester as chancellor with others; Winchester and Bonner thirsted after blood in several cases narrated nearby.

entities/john-rogers.title: John Rogers
entities/john-rogers.content:
John Rogers (c. 1500–1555), preacher and associate of Tyndale’s Bible work, was the first of the Marian martyrs burned at Smithfield in Foxe’s chronology.
Life and Examination
The story, life, and martyrdom of Master John Rogers (vol6) includes his examination and answer, second confession, sentence condemnatory, and other godly matter penned by Rogers including his legacy.
Rogers was committed the same day as other prisoners in the opening of Mary’s persecution narrative (1553 sequence).
Martyrdom at Smithfield
Sheriff Woodroofe asked Rogers whether he would revoke his doctrine and opinion of the sacrament of the altar. Rogers answered: “That which I have preached I will seal with my blood.” Woodroofe called him a heretic; Rogers replied that should be known at the day of judgment.
On Monday the 4th of February 1555 he was brought from Newgate toward Smithfield, saying the psalm Miserere by the way; the people rejoiced at his constancy. Before master Rochester, comptroller of the queen’s household, sir Richard Southwell, both sheriffs, and a great multitude, the fire was put to him. When it had taken hold on his legs and shoulders he washed his hands in the flame as though in cold water, lifted his hands to heaven, and mildly yielded his spirit. A pardon was offered if he would recant; he utterly refused.
Foxe calls him the first proto-martyr of all the blessed company that suffered in Queen Mary’s time — the first adventure upon the fire. His wife and eleven children (ten able to go, one sucking at her breast) met him by the way; the sight did not move him from constant and cheerful death.

entities/lady-jane-grey.title: Lady Jane Grey
entities/lady-jane-grey.content:
Lady Jane Grey (1537–1554), called by Foxe a virtuous lady and queen, was beheaded on Tower Green 12 February 1554 — nine days after Northumberland’s attempt to place her on the throne, and two days before Master Fecknam was sent to reduce her from Christ’s doctrine to Mary’s religion.
Fecknam and the Sacrament
Fecknam told Jane he lamented her heavy case; she answered she accounted it a manifest declaration of God’s favour rather than cause for lamentation. On faith alone justifying, two sacraments (baptism and the Lord’s supper), and the bread and wine as remembrance — not the natural body on the cross — she held the evangelical position against Fecknam’s seven sacraments and corporal presence.
Foxe prints her letter to her father, letter to Master Harding (late chaplain, now relapsed), prayer before death, and verses written with a pin: “Do never think it strange, / Though now I have misfortune.”
The Scaffold
Mounting the scaffold, Jane told the people she came to die by law; the fact against the queen was unlawful and she consented thereto, but she washed her hands in innocency before God concerning procurement or desire of the crown. She died a true christian woman, looking to be saved only by mercy through Christ’s blood — confessing she had neglected God’s word, loved herself and the world, and therefore this punishment was worthily happened; yet God had given her time to repent.
She said the psalm Miserere in English, gave her book to Fecknam, laid her head on the block saying “Lord, into thy hands I commend my spirit,” and finished her life 12 February 1554. Lord Guilford Dudley, her husband, was beheaded the same day — two innocents, Foxe writes, compared to those who devised and proclaimed the scheme.
Judge Morgan, who condemned her, shortly fell mad, crying to have Lady Jane taken away from him. On 23 February Henry Duke of Suffolk, her father, was beheaded at Tower Hill.

entities/laurence-saunders.title: Laurence Saunders
entities/laurence-saunders.content:
Laurence Saunders (c. 1519–1555), parson of Allhallows in Bread-street and of Church-Langton, was burned at Coventry 8 February 1555 — among the early Marian martyrs after Rogers and Hooper in Foxe’s chronology.
Life and Ministry
Of worshipful parentage, Saunders was scholar of Eton and King’s College Cambridge, then briefly apprentice to Sir William Chester (later sheriff of London the year Saunders burned). His master, finding his mind bent to Scripture, released him; he returned to Cambridge, proceeded MA, and under Edward VI preached at Fotheringay, Lichfield minster, and Church-Langton before taking Bread-street.
Married and unblamable, he was diligent in study and prayer; companions found his spiritual exercises singularly comforting. When Mary inhibited preaching, he continued privately as pastor to his flocks, refusing counsel to flee the realm.
Apprehension and Examination
On 14 October 1554 Sir John Mordant overtook him entering London; Saunders offered to preach next day in Bread-street and confirm all he had taught. Mordant warned Bonner; Saunders was imprisoned. Foxe prints examinations, letters to his wife, to Cranmer, to Bradford, Philpot, and Taylor, and communications with Dr Pendleton.
On 4 February 1555 Bonner disgraded him; Saunders said, “I thank God, I am none of your church.” Carried to Coventry, he slept little the night before execution, spending it in prayer and instructing fellow prisoners. A shoemaker of Coventry whom he had served said, “O my good master! God strengthen and comfort you.” Saunders answered he was the unmeetest man appointed to this office, “but my gracious God and dear Father is able to make me strong enough.”
Martyrdom at Coventry
8 February 1555, barefoot in an old gown and shirt, he fell flat praying as he went to the park without the city. Offered pardon if he would revoke, he answered it was Bonner and such as he who marred the queen’s realm and resisted God’s word; he held the blessed gospel, not heresy. He kissed the stake, saying, “Welcome the cross of Christ! welcome everlasting life!” and slept in the Lord when fire was put to him.

entities/mary-i.title: Mary I
entities/mary-i.content:
Mary I (1516–1558), daughter of Henry VIII and Catherine of Aragon, reigned from 1553 to 1558. Foxe’s Acts and Monuments treats her accession as the reversal of Edward VI’s reformation and the opening of a period in which many were put to death for refusal of the Mass and the sacrament of the altar.
Lady Mary under Henry and Edward
Foxe preserves a letter of the Lady Mary to Henry VIII with her protestation to certain lords sent by him. Under Edward VI, letters passed between the Lady Mary and the king and council; the council sent answers and instructions. Mary resisted the Edwardian changes — Ridley, after dining where God’s word had been refused, said he had done amiss to drink in that place and ought to have shaken off the dust of his shoes for a testimony against the house.
Foxe notes Mary’s nature and disposition before she came to the crown, preparing the reader for the troubles of Book X.
Accession and Alteration of Religion
Book X begins with the reign of Queen Mary. Foxe describes the first entering of Mary to the crown, with the alteration of religion and perturbations in the realm. Mary wrote to the lords of the council; they answered. An inhibition forbade preaching and printing. The whole canon of the Mass after Salisbury use was set out in English translation in the narrative.
Jane Grey’s brief claim appears in the same transition: see lady-jane-grey — her letter in Greek to Lady Katherine, communication with Fecknam, words on the scaffold, verses and epitaphs. Mary’s oration at the Guildhall (1 February 1554) is recorded.
Religion and Persecution
Foxe’s preface to Book X states that many were put to death in Mary’s time especially for the cause of the Mass and the sacrament of the altar; he prefixes a declaration on the origin and abuse of the popish mass so the reader may judge of those who gave their lives for the word of truth.
Articles from the queen went to Bonner and other bishops for execution in every diocese. A copy of the queen’s proclamation drove strangers and foreigners out of the realm. Convocation was summoned; disputations were held. Cranmer, Ridley, and Latimer were sent to Oxford. Commissions from philip-ii-of-spain and Mary to persecute the poor members of Christ appear in Book XII; Cardinal Pole’s articles touching clergy and lay-people are transcribed.
Foxe records Mary’s words touching abbey lands, communication with her council on religion, and (in the closing books) the expected child, prayers for Queen Mary, and the alteration of style in letters to Bonner.
Death and Succession
Foxe relates burnings continuing into November 1558, shortly before Mary’s death — including Alice Driver and Alexander Gouch at Ipswich (4 November 1558) and three burned at Bury. The narrative then turns to the Lady Elizabeth: her miraculous preservation, and John Hales’s oration to the noble Queen Elizabeth.

entities/mary-queen-of-scots.title: Mary Queen of Scots
entities/mary-queen-of-scots.content:
Mary Stuart (1542–1587) was Queen of Scotland from infancy and a Catholic claimant to the English throne through her grandmother Margaret Tudor (sister of Henry VIII). Forced to abdicate in 1567 following her disastrous marriage to Lord Bothwell and a Protestant rising against her, she fled to England in 1568 and threw herself on Elizabeth’s mercy — beginning 19 years of comfortable but permanent captivity. Every Catholic conspiracy against Elizabeth’s life eventually circled back to Mary, since she was the obvious Catholic successor. Francis Walsingham used the Babington Plot (1586) to produce her own written endorsement of Elizabeth’s assassination, and she was beheaded at Fotheringhay Castle on February 8, 1587.
Scotland and the Three Marriages
Mary was born December 8, 1542 — six days before her father James V died, leaving her queen of an infant. She was sent to France in 1548 and married Francis, Dauphin of France (later Francis II) in 1558; he died in 1560 and she returned to Scotland in 1561 as a Catholic queen returning to a country that had just completed a Protestant reformation under John Knox.
She married her cousin Henry Stuart, Lord Darnley, in 1565 — a politically disastrous choice. Darnley proved to be vain, jealous, and unstable; he murdered David Rizzio (Mary’s Italian-born secretary and court musician) in March 1566 in a scene of deliberate political theatre, stabbing him in Mary’s presence while she was heavily pregnant. The murder was intended as a public humiliation and warning. Mary was approximately six months pregnant at the time; she gave birth to the future James VI three months later.
Darnley was himself found dead — strangled, in an explosion — at Kirk o’ Field outside Edinburgh in February 1567. Suspicion fell immediately on Mary and her new lover, James Hepburn, Earl of Bothwell — whether Bothwell acted on her knowledge or independently has never been established. Mary married Bothwell in May 1567 (a Protestant who had obtained a rapid Protestant divorce from his wife to make the marriage possible), triggering a Protestant rising. The marriage destroyed her support even among those who had previously defended her. She abdicated in July 1567 and fled to England in May 1568. ^[source: hume_history_tudor_vol2_raw.txt]
English Captivity (1568–87)
Elizabeth refused to meet Mary but also refused to return her to Scotland where she would certainly be executed. This created a permanent strategic problem: Mary was the most dangerous person in England — simultaneously a Catholic queen, a plausible heir to the English throne, and an obvious rallying point for every Catholic conspiracy against Elizabeth.
She was kept under house arrest at a succession of locations under the guardianship of various Protestant nobles, most notably the Earl of Shrewsbury (who kept her at Sheffield and Tutbury for years). She maintained a court in miniature and continued to correspond with foreign powers — with the French court, the Spanish ambassador, and the Catholic exile community — though her correspondence was monitored with increasing effectiveness as Walsingham’s postal interception operation improved. Philip II included her cause in his justifications for the Armada, naming her his preferred candidate for the English throne over Elizabeth’s Protestant Protestant successor.
The Ridolfi Plot (1571) and the Throckmorton Plot (1583) were earlier conspiracies that involved Mary’s name before the Babington Plot trapped her in writing. Each plot increased parliamentary pressure for Mary’s execution; Elizabeth consistently resisted, unable to bring herself to execute an anointed queen. ^[source: walsingham_raw.txt, hume_history_tudor_vol2_raw.txt]
The Babington Plot and Walsingham’s Trap
The Babington Plot (1586) was Walsingham’s masterwork of entrapment. Anthony Babington, a young Catholic gentleman who had served as a page to the Earl of Shrewsbury and had therefore had direct contact with Mary’s captivity world, was the nominal head of a conspiracy to assassinate Elizabeth and free Mary. Walsingham recruited Gilbert Gifford (trained at the seminary at Rheims) as a double agent and established a postal channel — concealed in beer barrels delivered to Mary’s household at Chartley — through which every letter was intercepted, decoded by Thomas Phelippes, copied, and re-forwarded. Mary wrote letters to Babington explicitly approving Elizabeth’s assassination, describing it as “the dispatch of the usurping Competitor.”
A postscript was added to Mary’s July 17 letter requesting the names of the six men designated to carry out the assassination — an addition whose authenticity historians dispute (it may have been Walsingham’s forgery or Mary’s own supplementary request). Either way the main body of the letter was sufficient. Phelippes decoded it and drew a gallows on the outside. Mary was tried at Fotheringhay in October 1586 and convicted of treason. ^[source: walsingham_raw.txt]
Execution (February 8, 1587)
Elizabeth signed the death warrant but then, characteristically, attempted to delay its dispatch — and reportedly suggested to Sir Amyas Paulet (Mary’s keeper) that Mary might be dispatched by private means, saving Elizabeth the public responsibility. Paulet refused: “my conscience and my honour” would not permit private assassination. William Davison, a Secretary of State, sent the warrant without waiting for further instruction; Elizabeth subsequently imprisoned him in the Tower.
Mary was executed at Fotheringhay Castle on the morning of February 8, 1587. She wore red under her black outer gown — the colour of Catholic martyrdom — which was removed on the scaffold. The beheading required two or three blows of the axe. When the executioner lifted her head by what he thought was her hair, her red wig detached and the head fell; her small dog was found hiding beneath her skirts. ^[source: walsingham_raw.txt, hume_history_tudor_vol2_raw.txt]
Dynastic Significance
Mary’s execution provoked a formal protest from her son James VI of Scotland — but James calculated carefully. His succession to the English throne depended on maintaining Elizabeth’s goodwill; he protested without breaking with England. Philip II used the execution as additional justification for the Armada, adding the cause of avenging Mary (who had named him her heir) to his existing religious and strategic grounds.
Mary’s son James VI succeeded Elizabeth as James I of England in 1603 — fulfilling in Protestant form the Catholic dynastic claim his mother had been executed for asserting. The Elizabethan resolution of the succession crisis was to produce a Protestant male heir from a Catholic female claimant: the irony is structural, not accidental. ^[source: hume_history_tudor_vol2_raw.txt]

entities/nicholas-ridley.title: Nicholas Ridley
entities/nicholas-ridley.content:
Nicholas Ridley (c. 1500–1555), Bishop of London under Edward VI, appears in Foxe from Edwardian liturgical reform through Oxford disputations to martyrdom with Latimer.
Edward VI
Edward’s letter to Bishop Ridley gave reasons why the Lord’s board should be a table rather than an altar (vol6). Gardiner objected to Ridley’s court sermon. Ridley wrote to the Lady Mary; after dining where the word was refused, he judged he ought to have shaken off the dust of his shoes.
Oxford and Disputation
Cranmer, Ridley, and Latimer were sent to Oxford to dispute (vol6). Disputation between Dr Smith and colleagues and Bishop Ridley; Latimer’s disputation 18 April 1554. Ridley wrote to the prolocutor, to Cranmer, and a report on the misordered disputation. Tables of arguments against Cranmer and resolutions follow.
Ridley conferred with Latimer in prison and wrote letters to prison-fellows, Bradford, Grindal, and Bernher (vol7).
Last Acts
Before death Ridley sued to a lord for poor men whose leases the new bishop of London would not allow — troubled in conscience for grants made while he occupied the see.
Martyrdom
16 October 1555, Oxford. After Latimer’s words at the stake, Ridley cried loudly, “In manus tuas, Domine, commendo spiritum meum,” repeating “Lord, Lord, receive my spirit” in English. By reason of the evil making of the fire (wooden faggots laid about the gorse and over-high), Ridley’s suffering was prolonged compared with Latimer’s.

entities/philip-ii-of-spain.title: Philip II of Spain
entities/philip-ii-of-spain.content:
Philip II of Spain (1527–1598), King of England jure uxoris during his marriage to Mary I (1554–1558), appears in Foxe chiefly as co-author of the Marian persecution apparatus and as a shadow at the Tudor succession crisis.
Bloody Commission (1557)
Foxe transcribes a commission given by “Philip and Mary, by the grace of God king and queen of England, defenders of the faith,” to Edmund Bonner, Thomas Thirlby Bishop of Ely, Lord Windsor, Lord North, and many councillors — authorizing inquiry by oaths, witnesses, and all politic means into heresies, heretical books, lollardies, false rumours, and seditious words against the sovereigns.
Commissioners might search printers’ houses, seize heretical and seditious writings, punish refusers of the sacrament of the altar and mass, and commit obstinate persons to their ordinaries. Foxe titles this a terrible proclamation against the poor members of Christ. Similar commissions and papal letters to Philip and Mary appear in the closing Marian books (vol4).
Marriage and Elizabeth
After Mary’s accession, Foxe’s narrative tracks Philip’s entry into English affairs alongside the alteration of religion. When Lady Elizabeth was examined by Mary, Foxe records few comfortable words from the queen in English — but what she said in Spanish, God knoweth; it is thought King Philip was behind a cloth, not seen, and showed himself a very friend to Elizabeth in that matter.
Foxe links the decay of Somerset and the Marian restoration to broader providential preservation of Elizabeth and the realm — Philip’s reign as consort coinciding with the intensification of burnings recorded in Books X–XII.

entities/reginald-pole.title: Reginald Pole
entities/reginald-pole.content:
Reginald Pole (1500–1558), cardinal and legate, appears in Foxe as papal legate under Mary — visitor at Cambridge, author of articles for clergy and laity, and figure in the posthumous condemnation of Bucer and Phagius.
Henrician Background
Tonstal and Stokesley wrote to Cardinal Pole proving the bishop of Rome to have no special superiority over other bishops (vol5-pratt). Foxe notes Henry’s practices with Cardinal Pole to stir other nations against England.
Legate under Mary
Book XII (vol4) opens January 1557, fifth year of Queen Mary. Cardinal Pole, three years after his return into England, having established the Romish religion, began the Cambridge visitation.
The order and manner of the cardinal’s visitation at Cambridge, with condemning, taking up, and burning the bones and books of Martin Bucer and Paulus Phagius, anno 1557, January 9, occupies a major set-piece. Master Stokes’s oration to the queen’s visitors; Scot bishop of Chester’s answer; oration before condemnation; sentence; sermons of Perne and Watson; oration of Acworth at the restitution of Bucer and Phagius; Pilkington’s sermon; Redman’s epitaph on Bucer.
Cardinal Pole’s articles touching the clergy and lay-people follow. A bloody commission of King Philip and Queen Mary to persecute the poor members of Christ is transcribed. Pole sent dispensation for the lives of some condemned (e.g. William Adams, Thomas Freeman — noted in appendix).
Pole was appointed to come into England with the legatine commission; Foxe traces his role in restoring papal religion.

entities/richard-field.title: Richard Field
entities/richard-field.content:
Richard Field (1561–1624) was a London printer and senior Stationers’ Company member — and, crucially, William Shakespeare’s schoolfellow from Stratford-upon-Avon. Field published Shakespeare’s first printed works: Venus and Adonis (1593) and The Rape of Lucrece (1594). He trained under Thomas Vautrollier, the Huguenot refugee printer, and married Vautrollier’s widow on his master’s death in 1587, inheriting the press and trade connections that made him one of the most accomplished printers of Elizabethan London. Ames/Herbert’s Typographical Antiquities documents Field’s career and press; Greenblatt’s Will in the World analyses the significance of the Field-Shakespeare connection for Shakespeare’s literary formation.
Origins and Apprenticeship
Field was born in Stratford-upon-Avon in 1561, the son of Henry Field, a tanner — roughly two years older than Shakespeare, and a schoolfellow at the King’s New School. He was apprenticed to George Bishop (a senior Stationer) at Michaelmas 1579 and subsequently turned over to Thomas Vautrollier, completing his apprenticeship in February 1586–7. Working under Vautrollier in the Blackfriars press, Field learned to produce books of exceptional typographic quality — Vautrollier’s press specialized in high-quality literary, classical, and theological printing, and Field absorbed both the craft standards and the network of scholarly and literary clients. ^[source: typographical_antiquities_ames_raw.txt, greenblatt_will_in_the_world_raw.txt]
Inheriting the Vautrollier Press
Thomas Vautrollier died before 4 March 1587–8. Field married his widow, Jacqueline Vautrollier, and took over the business. He set up at the sign of the White Greyhound in St Paul’s Churchyard — the centre of the London book trade — and quickly established himself as a printer of the first rank. In 1589 he received a fine from the Stationers’ Company for printing contrary to an order — an early regulatory collision that did not impede his subsequent career. He was admitted to the Livery of the Stationers’ Company on July 1, 1598, and served as Upper Warden in his 67th year (1622–23). ^[source: typographical_antiquities_ames_raw.txt]
The Shakespeare Publications
Field published Shakespeare’s two narrative poems:

Venus and Adonis (1593): The first appearance of Shakespeare’s name in print. The poem is dedicated to Henry Wriothesley, 3rd Earl of Southampton, in carefully elegant prose that reveals Shakespeare’s ambitions as a literary rather than merely theatrical author. Field’s printing is clean and careful — this was a prestige publication, intended to establish Shakespeare as a serious poet in the classical genre tradition.
The Rape of Lucrece (1594): The second poem, again dedicated to Southampton, with a warmer and more familiar dedicatory letter than the first — suggesting the patronage relationship had deepened.

Greenblatt argues that Field’s press was Shakespeare’s point of entry into the world of professional literary publication: Field had access to the classical texts (North’s Plutarch, Ovid) that Shakespeare read and plundered, and the Blackfriars/St Paul’s Churchyard location connected Shakespeare to the sophisticated London book world. The Field connection illustrates how personal networks from Stratford persisted and mattered in London professional life. ^[source: typographical_antiquities_ames_raw.txt, greenblatt_will_in_the_world_raw.txt, stationers_registers_arber_vol2_raw.txt]
Field and the 1599 Bishops’ Order
Richard Field was among the fourteen named printers who received the Bishops’ Order of June 4, 1599 — the Archbishop of Canterbury and Bishop of London’s censorship directive that ordered specific books burned (Marston’s Pygmalion, Davies’s Epigrams, Nashe and Harvey’s works), prohibited printing further plays or satires without special authority, and restricted English history books to Privy Council approval. Being named in the Order placed Field explicitly within the censorship apparatus’s view — simultaneously an acknowledgement of his importance as a printer and a constraint on his press. ^[source: stationers_registers_arber_vol3_raw.txt]
Other Notable Publications
Field’s press produced texts of significance beyond the Shakespeare connection:

Thomas North’s translation of Plutarch’s Lives of the Noble Grecians and Romans (continuing from Vautrollier): the source text Shakespeare used for Julius Caesar, Antony and Cleopatra, Coriolanus, and Timon of Athens
Philip Sidney’s Apology for Poetry (posthumously printed)
Ariosto’s Orlando Furioso in Harington’s translation (1591)

The press’s specialisation in classical and literary works made it the appropriate venue for a poet attempting to establish himself in the classical genre tradition. Through Vautrollier’s inheritance, Field controlled one of the key conduits through which Continental humanist scholarship reached English literary culture. ^[source: typographical_antiquities_ames_raw.txt]

entities/richard-hun.title: Richard Hun
entities/richard-hun.content:
Richard Hun (d. 1514), merchant-tailor and freeman of London, was imprisoned in the Lollards’ Tower at St Paul’s, murdered in custody, and his corpse burned at Smithfield for heresy — an early Henrician persecution case Foxe treats at length, with a defence against Sir Thomas More and Alanus Copus.
The Mortuary Dispute
In 1514 Hun had a child at nurse in Middlesex (St. Mary Matfilon); the child died aged five weeks. Parson Thomas Dryfield sued Hun in the spiritual court for a bearing-sheet as mortuary; Hun answered the child had no propriety in the sheet. Dryfield ascited him to the spiritual court; Hun pursued a writ of præmunire against Dryfield and his adherents.
The priestly order, disdaining that a layman should enterprise such a matter and fearing precedent, sought means to accuse Hun of heresy before Bishop Fitzjames of London. Hun was committed to the Lollards’ Tower so none of his friends might visit him.
Murder and Posthumous Condemnation
Examined at Fulham 2 December 1514 upon articles (denying tithes were ordained save by priests’ covetousness; calling bishops and priests the Scribes and Pharisees; keeping English books of Scripture), Hun was sent back to the tower. Chancellor Dr. Horsey, by suborned ministers, accomplished his murder within two nights; the next morning the bell-ringer Spalding left keys so the sumner’s boy might find Hun hanged toward the wall — to make it appear suicide. The coroner and inquest found otherwise.
Fitzjames, with bishops of Durham and Lincoln, sat in judgment 16 December against Hun being dead; none appearing to defend his opinions, the bishop condemned the carcase of heresy and delivered it to be burned at Smithfield 20 December — sixteen days after the murder, to the great grief and disdain of the people.
King Henry VII’s letter in Hun’s behalf and depositions of witnesses are printed in Foxe.

entities/robert-barnes.title: Robert Barnes
entities/robert-barnes.content:
Robert Barnes (c. 1495–1540), doctor of divinity and prior of the Augustines at Cambridge, was burned at Smithfield in July 1540 with Thomas Garret and William Jerome — within two days after Thomas Cromwell’s execution, when Stephen Gardiner had, Foxe writes, his full swing to exercise cruelty.
Cambridge and Early Persecution
After Louvain, Barnes came to Cambridge as prior of the Augustines. He read Terence, Plautus, and Cicero; with Thomas Parnell he caused the house to flourish with good letters. He read Paul’s Epistles openly and put by Duns and Dorbel, making divers good divines. Mentioned among those Wolsey caused to abjure (vol3), Barnes later returned to evangelical preaching.
Final Apprehension and Martyrdom
Gardiner’s first assault after Cromwell’s fall fell upon Barnes, Garret, and Jerome. Jerome had preached at Paul’s Cross on Hagar and Sarah from Galatians; Gardiner picked a quarrel that St. Paul himself would have been apprehended at Paul’s cross for heresy had he preached the same words in English.
The three were drawn into Smithfield and constantly endured martyrdom in the fire A.D. 1540. The same day and place three papists — Powel, Fetherstone, and Abel — were executed for denying the king’s supremacy; a stranger present said, “Good God! how do these people live here? Here papists are hanged, there antipapists are burned.”
Foxe prints Barnes’s protestation at the stake and Winchester’s articles against him.

entities/rowland-taylor.title: Rowland Taylor
entities/rowland-taylor.content:
Dr Rowland Taylor (d. 1555), doctor in civil and canon law, was parson of Hadley and burned there 9 February 1555 — the town Foxe calls one of the first in England to receive the word at Thomas Bilney’s preaching.
Pastor at Hadley
Taylor left Cranmer’s household to dwell personally among his flock at Hadley — preaching every Sunday and holy-day, living as an example of holiness, rebuking sin plainly, and caring for the poor as a father. His wife and children were well nurtured; the parish knew Scripture so well that women and men had read the whole Bible and could recite great portions of Paul’s epistles — the town seemed a university rather than a cloth-making village.
Persecution under Mary
After Edward VI’s death the papists openly overthrew the reformation. Foster the lawyer and John Clerk conspired to restore the Mass at Hadley; Taylor retained Edward’s service and preached against popish corruptions. Examined before Gardiner, he defended priests’ marriage (nine children in lawful matrimony), refused the parson of Aldham to say Mass in his cure, and held the communion a memorial sacrifice of thanksgiving — not a repeated propitiatory offering. Gardiner called him blasphemous heretic and sent him to the King’s Bench.
Imprisoned with John Bradford, Taylor was merry and cheerful before and after condemnation; awaked at three in the morning for his burning, he cried against those who “rob God of his honour.”
Martyrdom (9 February 1555)
At the stake in Hadley, Warwick cast a faggot that broke Taylor’s face; he said, “O friend, I have harm enough; what needed that?” Sir John Shelton struck him on the lips for saying Miserere in English. When fire was set, Taylor held up both hands: “Merciful Father of heaven, for Jesus Christ my Saviour’s sake, receive my soul into thy hands.” He stood without crying until Soyce with a halbert struck him on the head. Foxe prints his will, letters to his wife and to Hadley after popish preaching returned, and his examination before Winchester.

entities/smithfield.title: Smithfield
entities/smithfield.content:
Smithfield, north-west of the City of London, was the principal place of burning for heresy convictions delivered to the secular power under Mary I in Foxe’s London narrative.
Marian Burnings
John Rogers — first proto-martyr under Mary; Newgate to Smithfield, Monday 4 February 1555; fire before Rochester, Southwell, and the sheriffs (vol6).
Thomas Tomkins — weaver of Shoreditch; burned Smithfield 16 March 1555; Bonner had kept him at Fulham half a year and beat him about the face (vol6).
John Bradford and John Leaf — behaviour at Smithfield narrated with verses to their memory (vol7).
William Tyms and others — death and martyrdom at London; examination before bishop of London (vol4).
Three women — Katherine Hut, Elizabeth Thackvel, Joan, burned same time in Smithfield (vol4).
Colchester and Essex martyrs — several parties brought to Smithfield bound to the stake (vol4).
Processions were made in Smithfield after the manner of Catholic ceremony (vol6).
Henrician and Other References
Tables of abjured persons under Stokesley and London persecutions (vol5-pratt, vol3) tie Smithfield and London diocese to earlier burnings. Lollards’ Tower and Newgate fed prisoners brought out to Smithfield.

entities/stationers-company.title: Stationers' Company
entities/stationers-company.content:
The Stationers’ Company was the London guild that governed the English book trade from its royal charter of 1557 through the lapse of the Licensing Act in 1695. Every printer, bookseller, and bookbinder in England was expected to be free of the Company, and every title intended for sale was expected to be entered in the Company’s Register before printing — a requirement that served simultaneously as a commercial record, a property right, and a censorship mechanism. The Company was the institutional centre of English printing across the century that produced the Elizabethan literary renaissance, the King James Bible, and the Shakespeare First Folio.
Origins
The name “Stationer” derives from the “stations” — fixed market points at the Cheapside crosses — at which medieval book-dealers stood. By 1379 the Corporation of London was leasing a set of stations to eleven named women. The Fraternity’s pre-charter history begins with the Corporation Ordinance of 1403, which appointed two Wardens for “the Writers of Text-Letter, Limners, and others, who bind and sell books.” The Ordinance also covered Scriveners, reflecting the overlap between manuscript copying, binding, and selling that characterized the trade before print displaced the manuscript economy. The custom of registering copies before printing is believed by Hazlitt to have already been in use at the time of the 1403 Ordinance — making the Register a practice that predated the charter, which the charter then codified and enforced. Pynson and Wynkyn de Worde were probably members of the pre-incorporation Fraternity; Wynkyn de Worde is specifically cited by Hazlitt as having a relationship with the pre-charter body. ^[source: hazlitt_livery_companies_raw.txt]
The 1557 Charter
Philip and Mary granted the royal charter on 4 May 1557. The preamble — quoted in full by Hazlitt — identifies censorship of “seditious and heretical books, rhymes, and treatises” as the explicit motive: the Company was chartered as an instrument of press control. Total cost to the grantees was just over £20, including 9s. for a rejected first draft. Thomas Dockwray was named first Master; John Cawood (royal printer) and Henry Cooke were first Wardens — though Hazlitt notes that other sources name the first Wardens as Cawood, Tottel, and Wight, and the discrepancy in the sources has not been resolved. Elizabeth I confirmed the charter on 10 November 1559. Patterson’s legal analysis argues that the charter was essentially a bargain: the Crown received an efficient censorship mechanism, and the stationers received a legally enforceable monopoly over the English book trade. The apparatus built to suppress Protestants under Mary was immediately redeployed against Catholics under Elizabeth — the same charter, the same enforcement mechanism, the same Wardens’ search powers, now oriented against the other side. ^[source: hazlitt_livery_companies_raw.txt, copyright_patterson_raw.txt]
Governance
The Company followed the standard livery company structure: a Master and Wardens elected annually; a Court of Assistants as governing board; the Livery (senior freemen eligible for governance); the Yeomanry (general freemen). The Stationers — noted by Hazlitt alongside the Apothecaries and Brewers — admitted only members of the vocation, making it a true Craft Gild throughout the Elizabethan period, enforced through apprenticeship. In 1882 the Company had 312 on the Livery and 445 Freemen; approximately 100 apprentices were annually bound at the Hall. James I confirmed the charter in 1603 and granted an enlargement of privileges in 1616. ^[source: hazlitt_livery_companies_raw.txt]
The Register of Copies
Entry in the Register at Stationers’ Hall created what Patterson calls “stationer’s copyright” — an exclusive right, enforceable within the Company’s jurisdiction, to print a specific title. The right belonged to the stationer who entered the title, not to the author; the author had no legal interest in the copy once the manuscript was sold. The Register survives in full from 1557; Arber’s five-volume Transcript (1875–94) contains every entry through 1640. There is, however, a known gap in Arber’s transcript for the years 1571–76, associated with a register kept by a clerk named Wapull that was subsequently lost — creating a documentary lacuna for those years that affects copyright history for works entered in that period.
Notable entries include: the first Hamlet (26 July 1602, James Roberts, 6d); Shakespeare’s Sonnets (20 May 1609, Thomas Thorpe, 6d); the Shakespeare First Folio (8 November 1623, Blount and Jaggard — 7 shillings for the Comedies, 6d per History and Tragedy, listing 16 previously unregistered plays by name). Specific transferred copies — books that passed through multiple assignments — illustrate how the stationer’s right was treated as a commercial asset; T. East’s books, for instance, passed through several assignments across the period documented in Arber. ^[source: stationers_registers_arber_vol2_raw.txt, stationers_registers_arber_vol3_raw.txt, stationers_registers_arber_vol4_raw.txt, copyright_patterson_raw.txt]
Power of Search and Censorship
The 1557 charter conferred on the Company a power of search throughout England: the right to enter premises and seize books printed without licence or in violation of the charter. This was the operational mechanism of Tudor press censorship. The Arber Registers record specific suppressions: French books burned by the Primate (1595); Raleigh’s History of the World ordered suppressed by the Archbishop of Canterbury (1614); Lithgow’s Travels erased from the Register (1616); Prynne’s Histriomastix erased and the author fined £5,000, ears cropped, and imprisoned for life (1634); the MS and whole impression of Buchanan’s History of Scotland seized. The Star Chamber Decrees of 1586 and 1637 both channelled all enforcement through the Company’s search power. ^[source: hazlitt_livery_companies_raw.txt, stationers_registers_arber_vol3_raw.txt, stationers_registers_arber_vol4_raw.txt, copyright_patterson_raw.txt]
The Patent Controversy and the John Wolfe Rebellion (1582–83)
The 1560s and 1570s saw an explosion of printing patents — grants of exclusive rights to print specific categories of text (law books, almanacs, ABC-books, psalters). These patents were separate from the stationer’s copyright and created bitter divisions within the trade: small printers and journeymen found that the most commercially valuable titles were locked up by patent-holders, many of whom farmed out the work to others rather than printing it themselves.
Christopher Barker, appointed Queen’s Printer in 1577 (through Walsingham’s patronage), produced a detailed Report in 1582 — submitted to Walsingham — describing the state of the trade, the specific grievances of general stationers against the patent-holders, and the inequity of a system in which a few privileged printers controlled the most profitable texts while the rest of the trade scrambled for the remainder. The Report is an important documentary source for understanding how the patent system was experienced from inside the trade.
In 1582–83, John Wolfe — a printer who had worked in Florence and returned with Continental ideas about printing freedom — led an open rebellion against the monopoly patents, arguing they were legally void and that any stationer had the right to print any book. He and a group of journeymen began printing books in defiance of the existing patents. The Company arrested and fined several of the rebels. The controversy was ultimately defused not by prosecution but by incorporating Wolfe into the system: he was made a member of the Company and eventually appointed Beadle, and the more legitimate grievances of general stationers were addressed through the creation of shared investments in printing rights. ^[source: stationers_registers_arber_vol2_raw.txt, copyright_patterson_raw.txt, hazlitt_livery_companies_raw.txt]
Common Stock and English Stock
The Company operated collective investment funds: the Latin Stock (scholarly books), the Irish Stock (printing rights in Ireland), the ballad stock, and the Bible stock. These arrangements developed through the 1570s and 1580s partly in response to the patent controversy — giving more Company members a financial stake in the privileged printing rights rather than concentrating all benefit in individual patent-holders. About 1601 a Crown grant consolidated these into the English Stock — a joint enterprise giving Company members a proportional share of revenue from the most commercially valuable printing rights (ABC/catechism, almanacs, psalms). The English Stock represented the institutional resolution of the Wolfe rebellion’s legitimate grievances: widened participation in profits without abandoning the monopoly structure. In 1882 the English Stock still had capital of £41,000–42,000 among 306 members, distributing £400 annually to Company poor. ^[source: hazlitt_livery_companies_raw.txt, copyright_patterson_raw.txt]
George Wither and the Challenge to Stationer’s Copyright (1623–25)
The most sustained direct challenge to the stationer’s copyright from an author’s perspective came from the poet George Wither. Wither obtained a royal patent requiring his Hymns and Songs of the Church (1623) to be bound with every copy of the Company’s metrical psalter — a requirement that would have compelled the Company to distribute his work whether they wished to or not. The Company resisted vigorously, seeking to suppress the patent. Wither responded by writing The Schollers Purgatory (c.1625), a detailed polemic attacking the Company’s monopolistic practices, arguing that the stationer’s system subordinated authors’ interests entirely to those of booksellers and printers. Patterson cites the Wither dispute as the clearest Jacobean articulation of a counter-theory of authorial rights — a theory the law did not yet recognize. ^[source: copyright_patterson_raw.txt, hazlitt_livery_companies_raw.txt]
Journeymen Disputes and the 1637 Decree
By the 1630s, tensions within the trade had shifted from patent-holders versus general stationers to masters versus journeymen. Journeymen printers — wage employees without a share in copyright or patents — complained that impression sizes (the number of copies printed from a single setting of type) were being increased to maximize masters’ profits at the cost of journeymen’s employment. The Star Chamber Decree of 1637 addressed this directly by specifying maximum impression sizes tied to type size: Nonpareil (very small type) was limited to 5,000 impressions; Brevier (small text type) to 3,000. These limits were designed to ensure that type was re-set more frequently, generating more compositing work for journeymen rather than allowing masters to run off unlimited copies from a single composition. ^[source: stationers_registers_arber_vol4_raw.txt, copyright_patterson_raw.txt]
Hall History
The Company occupied five successive halls: (1) Clement Court, Milk Street, Cheapside (probably mid-15th century); (2) Peter College at the south-west angle of St Paul’s churchyard, c.1550 — formerly converted to a printing office by William Seres after the Dissolution; (3) the frontage of Peter College, let to Edward Kynaston (vintner) in 1606, who made it the Feathers Tavern; (4) Abergavenny House, acquired 1611; (5) the rebuilt Hall, completed 1674 after the 1666 Great Fire, with wainscoting contracted with Stephen College, the “Protestant Joiner,” for £300. The Great Fire of 1666 reduced the Hall “to a wreck, with the contents and even the common seal, the registers excepted.” The registers survived because they were with the Clerk at his house in Clerkenwell Green. ^[source: hazlitt_livery_companies_raw.txt]
Quo Warranto Proceedings
The Company faced Quo Warranto proceedings in 1663 and 1684. The 1663 writ arose from “a belief that the Company was not sufficiently vigilant and strict in its capacity as a curb on the press, and connived at the publication of inflammatory or scurrilous literature” — an extraordinary inversion in which the censorship body was attacked for insufficient censorship. The charter was restored by Act of 2 William and Mary (1690). ^[source: hazlitt_livery_companies_raw.txt]
Notable Members
Thomas Berthelet (king’s printer, first-year Master); Reginald Wolfe (four times Master); John Cawood (royal printer, first Warden); Richard Jugge; Richard Tottell (law printer, patent-holder through three reigns for law books); the Harrisons; the Days; the Nortons; the Barkers; the Rivingtons; Christopher Barker (queen’s printer from 1577, patron-appointed through Walsingham); Richard Field (publisher of Shakespeare’s Venus and Adonis). Later: Samuel Richardson (Master 1754); Jacob Tonson; Henry Sampson Woodfall (printer of the Letters of Junius, Master 1797). ^[source: hazlitt_livery_companies_raw.txt, typographical_antiquities_ames_raw.txt]
The Stationers’ Commonwealth: Knowledge and Credibility (Johns)
Adrian Johns’s The Nature of the Book (1998) reframes the Stationers’ Company not as a trade guild that happened to enforce censorship but as an epistemic community — a “Stationers’ commonwealth” — that set the conditions under which all printed knowledge was produced, circulated, and judged in early modern England. “In early modern England, knowledge had to be made, articulated, communicated, and defended in a Stationers’ commonwealth.” This commonwealth was “distinctive not only socially, but epistemologically.”
Credibility as a social achievement. The central problem of print in Johns’s account was that it provided no automatic guarantee of credibility. “Credit was fragile and ephemeral to an extraordinary degree. The conditions in which knowledge must be constructed, maintained, and defended were riven by private deals, intrigue and distrust.” Any printed book could be pirated — reprinted without authorization, falsely attributed, or corrupted by compositors. Authors who wanted their works credited had to actively navigate the Stationers’ practices: visiting the printing house, supervising composition, using the trade’s social mechanisms to vouch for their texts. The Quakers appointed individual booksellers to oversee the press precisely for this reason; the Royal Society developed its own conventions for the same purpose. The Stationers’ Company was “the most authoritative and effective” of such disciplining efforts.
The concept of “copy” as an epistemic tool. The Company’s principle of “copy” — recognizing another stationer’s prior claim to print a work in which they had invested time, skill, capital, and credit — was not merely a commercial mechanism. It was “the most vivid representation” of the uncertainty pervading the book trade, and the primary institutional response to it. Holding the “copy” of a text was a claim about credit and investment, contested by piracy and “countering” (unauthorized reprinting). The conventions of propriety embedded in the copy system were, in Johns’s formulation, “a way of looking at the world, as well as a means of sharing it.”
Stationers’ Hall as architectural authority. Johns argues that the physical architecture of Stationers’ Hall itself embodied the Company’s disciplinary hierarchy. The Hall’s spatial organization — with its graduated zones of access, from the outer spaces open to the general trade to the restricted chambers where the Court of Assistants met — mirrored the hierarchy of trust and authority within the Company. Stationers’ customs, not statute law, were the primary mechanism of discipline; the Company’s conventions of propriety gave print its credibility in Tudor and Stuart England. ^[source: nature_of_the_book_raw.txt]

entities/stephen-gardiner.title: Stephen Gardiner
entities/stephen-gardiner.content:
Stephen Gardiner (c. 1483–1555), Bishop of Winchester, appears throughout Foxe’s Henrician, Edwardian, and Marian books — as oath-taker for the royal supremacy, author of De Vera Obedientia, chief antagonist in Edward VI’s reign, and chancellor under Mary.
Henrician Supremacy
Foxe’s Book VIII (vol5-pratt) records Gardiner among those who took oaths to the king against the pope’s usurped power (1534). His book De Vera Obedientia, with his reasons against the pope’s supremacy, is summarised; Bonner prefixed a preface as archdeacon of Leicester. Bonner also sent letters to Cromwell describing Gardiner’s evil behaviour and causes why he misliked him — and Gardiner’s letters complaining of Bonner.
Edward VI: Trial and Deprivation
Book IX (vol6) gives the history of Gardiner’s doings and attempts: letters, nineteen articles objected to Winchester, copies of writs, the king’s and council’s letters, sequestration, and Gardiner’s sermon before the king. Sessions ran from the first through the fourteenth against him; he proposed long justificatory matter and answered articles. Somerset and commissioners wrote touching points he should treat in his sermon.
Ridley had objected to Gardiner’s sermon at court. The Edwardian book closes with Gardiner still the leading conservative voice before Mary’s accession.
Marian Chancellor
Under Mary, Gardiner as Bishop of Winchester and lord chancellor appears in examinations (vol7): letters to Bonner on celebrating mass; preaching; conferences with prisoners; talk with those brought before him as chancellor. Foxe also records matters wherein Gardiner varied from other papists on the sacrament, and matters wherein he varied from himself.
Death
The Death and End of Stephen Gardiner, Bishop of Winchester, the Enemy of God’s Word, is narrated in vol7 (1555). Foxe juxtaposes this with Gardiner’s earlier books impugning the pope’s supremacy.

entities/thomas-bilney.title: Thomas Bilney
entities/thomas-bilney.content:
Thomas Bilney (c. 1495–1531), called by Hugh Latimer “little Bilney, that blessed martyr of God,” was burned at Norwich in 1531 — a Cambridge scholar whose conversion of others, including Latimer, Foxe treats as a root from which the university later flourished.
Cambridge and First Abjuration
Brought up at Cambridge from a child, Bilney profited in liberal sciences unto both laws; the Holy Spirit endued his heart with knowledge of better things and he converted his study to godliness. He inflamed many fellows, including Thomas Arthur and Hugh Latimer (then cross-keeper at Cambridge).
Persecuted by Cardinal Wolsey, Bishop Nixe of Norwich, friars of Ipswich, Sir Thomas More, and others, Bilney abjured about 1529. He thereafter fell into such repentance and sorrow that he was near utter despair — Latimer testified that his friends feared to leave him alone; comfortable places of Scripture ran him through the heart like a sword. Revived, he took his death patiently against the tyrannical see of Rome.
Return to Norwich and Martyrdom
Bilney voluntarily set his face toward Jerusalem, resigning himself to fall into the hands of the Scribes and Pharisees for the gospel’s sake. At the stake in Norwich (Lollards’ pit) he stood upon the ledge in hose and shirt; Dr. Warner came to bid farewell weeping — Bilney smiled and said, “Feed your flock, feed your flock; that when the Lord cometh, he may find you so doing.”
Friars asked him to declare they were not authors of his death lest the people withdraw alms; he cried with a loud voice: “I pray you, good people! be never the worse to these men for my sake, as though they should be the authors of my death; it was not they.” Reeds and faggots were set; crying “Jesus!” and “Credo!” he gave up the ghost A.D. 1531. Foxe, citing witnesses present, affirms he never recanted and never had bill or scroll in hand to read, contrary to More’s account.

entities/thomas-cranmer.title: Thomas Cranmer
entities/thomas-cranmer.content:
Thomas Cranmer (1489–1556) was Archbishop of Canterbury from 1533 to 1555 — the ecclesiastical architect of the English Reformation. He provided Henry VIII with the canonical mechanism for the divorce from Catherine of Aragon, presided over the liturgical reformation under Edward VI that produced the foundational texts of Anglican worship, and was burned at the stake under Mary I for heresy. His two recantations — signing documents withdrawing his Protestant beliefs under pressure, then publicly withdrawing the recantations at the stake — define both his human weakness and his final courage. He is the chief ecclesiastical figure in the backdrop of Mantel’s Cromwell trilogy and a subject of sustained analysis in Hume’s first Tudor volume.
Rise and the Divorce
Cranmer was born in 1489 at Aslockton, Nottinghamshire, and educated at Jesus College, Cambridge. He came to Henry VIII’s attention in 1529 when he suggested that the king seek opinions from European universities on the canonical validity of his marriage to Catherine of Aragon — a diplomatic-theological strategy rather than a direct papal appeal. Henry sent him on embassies to Rome and to the Emperor. During his Continental service, Cranmer secretly married the niece of a German Lutheran cleric — a marriage he later had to conceal and eventually deny under the Six Articles (1539), reportedly hiding his wife in a trunk during travel. He was consecrated Archbishop of Canterbury on March 30, 1533 — making him technically the head of the English Church at the moment Henry was about to break with Rome. On May 23, 1533, he pronounced Henry’s marriage to Catherine void; on June 1 he crowned Anne Boleyn. He thus performed both acts that made the break with Rome structurally necessary. ^[source: hume_history_tudor_vol1_raw.txt, wolf_hall_raw.txt]
The Boleyn Affair and the Letter to Henry
When Anne Boleyn’s destruction was underway in May 1536, Cranmer wrote a remarkable letter to Henry VIII that survives as one of the most diplomatically difficult documents of the reign. In it he expressed that “he never had better opinion in woman” than in Anne, while simultaneously acknowledging that if the charges were true she deserved punishment. The letter navigated the impossible position of a man who had crowned Anne, annulled Catherine’s marriage to make her queen, and now found himself required to annul Anne’s marriage in turn. He pronounced Anne’s marriage to Henry void on May 17, 1536 — two days before her execution — meaning Elizabeth was technically illegitimate at the moment her mother was condemned. Cranmer survived Henry’s entire reign through doctrinal flexibility and political discretion: he maintained Henry’s personal affection. Henry reportedly told his councillors on his deathbed that Cranmer was the one man he trusted completely. ^[source: hume_history_tudor_vol1_raw.txt, wolf_hall_raw.txt]
The Prayer Books and the Edwardian Reformation
Under the boy-king Edward VI (1547–53), Cranmer implemented the Protestant reformation he had deferred throughout Henry’s reign. His two great achievements were:

The First Prayer Book (1549): The first English-language order of service, replacing the Latin Mass with vernacular worship. Its language was deliberately ambiguous — acceptable to traditionalists and reformers alike. The Western Rising (Prayer Book Rebellion) protested it as too Protestant; Continental reformers complained it was too Catholic.
The Second Prayer Book (1552): A more explicitly Protestant revision, removing the last ambiguities about the nature of the Eucharist. The “black rubric” explicitly denied the doctrine of real presence in the communion elements.
The 42 Articles (1553): The doctrinal foundation of Anglicanism, drafted by Cranmer and issued in the final months of Edward’s reign — later revised as the 39 Articles under Elizabeth.

Cranmer also oversaw the first English-language Bible in church services and the dissolution of chantries. As a prose stylist, his contribution to the Prayer Books gave the English language some of its most enduring rhythms — the collect form, the marriage service, the burial office. ^[source: hume_history_tudor_vol1_raw.txt]
The Six Articles and the Hidden Wife
The Act of Six Articles (1539) reaffirmed Catholic doctrines including clerical celibacy — making Cranmer’s secret German wife suddenly and dangerously illegal. He sent her back to Germany for the duration. The episode illustrates both the doctrinal uncertainty of the Henrician Reformation and the personal cost that uncertainty imposed on those who navigated it: Cranmer was a convinced Protestant doing the work of a king whose Protestantism was jurisdictional rather than doctrinal. ^[source: hume_history_tudor_vol1_raw.txt]
Mary I, Recantation, and the Stake
When Mary I succeeded Edward in 1553 and began restoring Catholicism, Cranmer was arrested on charges of heresy and treason. He was tried and condemned; under sustained pressure — including the psychological and physical conditions of prolonged imprisonment — he signed multiple recantations of his Protestant beliefs. These recantations shamed his supporters deeply; a man who had done so much to establish Protestant England appeared to have abandoned it at the last moment.
On March 21, 1556, at the burning place in Oxford (Broad Street), he was brought to make a final public recantation before the assembled crowd. Instead, he withdrew all his recantations. When the fire was lit, he thrust his right hand — the hand that had signed the recantations — into the flames first, saying “this hand hath offended.” He died holding it in the fire. His was the most famous death among the nearly 300 Protestants burned under Mary — the final public theatre of a career that had always been conducted in the proximity of great danger. ^[source: hume_history_tudor_vol1_raw.txt]
Foxe’s Account of Cranmer at Oxford
Foxe’s Book XI–XII (foxe-acts-monuments-vol4.txt) gives the fullest narrative in this knowledge base. The life, state, and story of Thomas Cranmer, Archbishop of Canterbury, martyr, opens the Marian section for 1556. Orations of Dr Brooks (bishop of Gloucester) and Dr Martin to Cranmer at St Mary’s Church, Oxford; Cranmer’s faith and profession before the commissioners; Dr Story’s oration; talk between Martin and the archbishop; Cranmer’s fuller answer to Brooks; letters to Queen Mary; papal commission with sentence definitive; appeal to the next general council; form of degrading an archbishop; copy of Cranmer’s recantation sent abroad by the papists; sum of Dr Cole’s sermon at Oxford; Cranmer’s prayer; further letters to the queen, to Mrs Wilkinson, and to a lawyer.
Foxe applied to Archbishop Parker (c. 1562) for the certified copy of the Oxford disputation of Cranmer, Ridley, and Latimer exhibited in Convocation 1° Mariæ — probably the document used in the 1563 edition. Cranmer was sent down to Oxford with Ridley and Latimer; the order and manner of the disputation and condemnation are set out in Book X (vol6).
See burning-of-cranmer-1556, oxford-disputations-1554, marian-persecutions.
Hume’s Assessment
Hume acknowledges Cranmer’s intellectual contribution to the Reformation (the Prayer Books as literary and theological achievements) while condemning what he calls his “tergiversations” — the willingness to serve successive monarchs’ doctrinal positions without visible personal conviction, and the recantations under Mary before the final reversal. The recantations followed by the recantation of the recantation make Cranmer a difficult figure for any historian: was the final courage the real man, or a last calculation that dying Protestant was strategically better than living Catholic? Hume leaves the question open. Mantel, working at a longer distance, finds the question similarly unresolvable — Cranmer appears in the trilogy as a man of genuine faith and genuine pliability, which is to say a man rather than a saint. ^[source: hume_history_tudor_vol1_raw.txt]

entities/thomas-cromwell.title: Thomas Cromwell
entities/thomas-cromwell.content:
Thomas Cromwell (c.1485–1540) was Henry VIII’s principal minister from approximately 1532 to 1540 — the most powerful subject in England during those years, and the executive intelligence behind the legislative Reformation that made England permanently Protestant. He drafted the statutes severing England from Rome, managed the dissolution of the monasteries, directed the Crown’s intelligence networks, and oversaw the legal proceedings that brought more than one queen to the scaffold. His fall in June 1540 was sudden and complete; he was executed on Tower Hill on July 28, 1540, the charges largely fabricated by his enemies. He is the narrator’s point of view in Hilary Mantel’s Cromwell trilogy, the most sustained fictional reckoning with an English administrator’s inner life.
Origins
Born c.1485 in Putney, the son of a blacksmith and brewer named Walter Cromwell — the fact of this origin his enemies never let him forget. Mantel’s trilogy opens with a childhood scene in the Putney yard, Walter beating him; his sister Kat and brother-in-law Morgan Williams taking him in afterward. He had no formal legal education and no university background; he educated himself in law, languages, and commerce through practical experience. He may have fought as a soldier at the Battle of Garigliano in Italy in 1503; he traded silk in Italy; he worked as a merchant and agent in the Netherlands. On the Continent he acquired a Lutheran book from Germany — a possession that marked him from the outset as a man of the new European intellectual world. He survived what Mantel describes as an assassination attempt in Italy, involving an estoc (a thin Italian knife) pushed up under the ribs: the near-miss left a lasting impression. ^[source: wolf_hall_raw.txt]
Household at Austin Friars
By the late 1520s Cromwell maintained a substantial household at Austin Friars in London — a multilingual establishment of clerks, merchants, and legal practitioners flowing through its rooms. His wife Liz had recently died (by 1529 in Wolf Hall’s timeline); his daughters Grace and Anne had died before her. His son Gregory was at Cambridge. Into the household Cromwell took Helen Barre — a destitute woman with two small children whom he provided for out of what Mantel presents as characteristic practical charity. His dog Bella was a constant companion. Mantel uses this domestic texture to establish Cromwell’s interiority before his public career begins. ^[source: wolf_hall_raw.txt]
Memory and Method
Mantel introduces early in Wolf Hall the Simonides story — the technique of the memory palace, by which information is stored through spatial positioning. Cromwell identifies himself with the method: in a moment of crisis (the collapse of a banqueting hall, identification of the dead by their seating positions), he recognises how memory and spatial intelligence work together. The technique becomes a figure for Cromwell’s entire working method: holding vast quantities of information in ordered mental space, accessible on demand. ^[source: wolf_hall_raw.txt]
Service under Wolsey
Cromwell administered Wolsey’s household, his building projects (including Cardinal’s College, Oxford, now Christ Church), and his extensive land and legal transactions. When Wolsey fell in 1529, Cromwell entered Parliament through a Taunton seat arranged by the Duke of Norfolk — Norfolk believed Wolsey had buried treasure and that Cromwell knew where. He made himself useful to the king rather than fleeing with his disgraced patron. Wolsey died at Leicester Abbey on November 29, 1530, on his way south to face charges. Cromwell had already transferred his primary loyalty; the transition is the central narrative arc of Wolf Hall.
Cromwell’s encounter with Wolsey at Esher after the fall captures the personal bond: Wolsey paced and asked Cavendish every hour when Cromwell would arrive; George Cavendish (Wolsey’s gentleman usher and later biographer) found Cromwell apparently weeping at the humiliation. Wolsey’s household goods had been stripped room by room by Norfolk and Suffolk — the gold plate, vestments, tapestries, books, the Solomon and Sheba tapestries rolled up, the hunting scenes taken down. “You shall price me by the yard,” Wolsey said. ^[source: wolf_hall_raw.txt]
Chief Minister: The Legislative Reformation (1532–36)
From approximately 1532, Cromwell was Henry’s principal executive instrument. He read and presented to Henry the forty-two propositions of Marsiglio of Padua’s Defensor Pacis (1324) — the medieval text arguing that Christ had not granted the Pope power over princes — and Henry’s response was delight: “I never remember the cardinal spoke of this.” Cromwell also drew on the aged jurist Christopher St German’s confirmation that “if the church cannot reform itself, Parliament may do so.”
He drafted and drove through Parliament the foundational Reformation statutes:

Act in Restraint of Appeals (1533): Declared England an empire subject to no external jurisdiction — the legal foundation for the break with Rome.
Act of Supremacy (1534): Made Henry Supreme Head of the Church of England.
Treasons Act (1534): Made denial of the Royal Supremacy a capital offence.

He managed the proceedings against John Fisher and Thomas More, who were executed in the summer of 1535 for refusing the oath of supremacy. More’s imprisonment in the Tower presented Cromwell with a legal problem: More’s silence — his refusal to give a reason for refusing the oath — was technically not treason until legislation made it so. Rich’s subsequent perjury (claiming More had denied the supremacy in private conversation) solved the problem. ^[source: wolf_hall_raw.txt, hume_history_tudor_vol1_raw.txt]
Dissolution of the Monasteries (1536–40)
Cromwell directed the dissolution through two waves: the lesser monasteries under the Act of 1536, the greater under the Act of 1539. He commissioned the Valor Ecclesiasticus (1535) — a systematic survey conducted by commissioners who visited each house, recorded revenues, and documented mismanagement. The survey served simultaneously as pretext and strategic map: it told Cromwell exactly which houses were most valuable and in what order to proceed. The Court of Augmentations received the dissolved lands and revenues; the sales were rapid and the prices generally below market value, since Cromwell needed cash quickly.
The Pilgrimage of Grace (autumn 1536) — a northern rising in defence of the monasteries — was suppressed through negotiation followed by bad-faith reprisal: Henry promised a pardon, then used further disturbances as pretext to execute over 200 leaders, including Robert Aske, hanging abbots at their own monastery gates. Mantel’s The Mirror and the Light renders this destruction at the level of individual experience — buildings stripped of lead, stone quarried, monks dispersed — while showing Cromwell’s dim awareness “that he is participating in something that cannot be undone.” ^[source: the_mirror_and_the_light_raw.txt, hume_history_tudor_vol1_raw.txt]
The Fall of Anne Boleyn (1536)
In spring 1536, Cromwell constructed the case that brought Queen Anne Boleyn to trial and execution. Mantel’s Bring Up the Bodies presents the investigation’s mechanics in detail: Lady Worcester, pregnant and vulnerable, is brought into a small room with cakes and a cushion, where Cromwell listens while she unburdens herself about Anne being “free with her body,” certain gentlemen being overfamiliar, Mark Smeaton being in the queen’s chambers when he should not be. Cromwell writes nothing down and asks her to come again. Lady Rochford hints at nocturnal visitors to Anne’s chamber. Smeaton is interrogated at his Stepney house through Cromwell’s silence, patience, and darkness — Mantel is explicit that no rack is used, only psychological pressure. Smeaton confesses.
The charges: adultery with Henry Norris, Francis Weston, William Brereton, and Smeaton; incest with George Boleyn; conspiracy to murder the king. At the trial, Lord Percy (Anne’s first love) fainted and was carried out. The Duke of Norfolk — Anne’s own uncle — pronounced the sentence with a steady voice. Cranmer pronounced Anne’s marriage to Henry void two days before her execution. Anne was beheaded on Tower Green on May 19, 1536, by a Calais swordsman using a sword rather than an axe (requiring her to kneel upright and unsupported, without a block); the swordsman cleaned his Toledo steel blade lovingly afterward. The narrow corpse was fitted into an arrow chest used as a coffin. Henry was betrothed to Jane Seymour the following day.
Cromwell later examined his own motives: the Boleyns had destroyed Wolsey; he had wanted them destroyed in part for that reason. He asks himself whether what he had done was justice or revenge — and finds he cannot answer. ^[source: wolf_hall_bring_up_the_bodies_raw.txt, hume_history_tudor_vol1_raw.txt]
The Holbein Portrait
Mantel includes a scene in which Cromwell examines Holbein’s portrait of himself section by section: the hand, the smooth skin, the Pacioli book, the turquoise ring that was Wolsey’s. He cannot read his own face. His son Gregory says: “Did you not know?” The scene encapsulates the trilogy’s central preoccupation — Cromwell as a man who understands everyone around him but cannot see himself clearly. ^[source: wolf_hall_raw.txt]
The Unnamed Daughter
In The Mirror and the Light, a young woman arrives at Austin Friars from Antwerp with no letter, only a message — claiming to be the child of Anselma, a woman Cromwell had known thirty years before in the Netherlands. He cannot verify her claim but recognises something of himself in her face. The episode, which has no historical documentation, gives Mantel a device to explore Cromwell’s continental past and his emotional inaccessibility. ^[source: the_mirror_and_the_light_raw.txt]
The Tower and the Cleves Marriage
Cromwell fell because he recommended the marriage to Anne of Cleves based on Holbein’s flattering portrait; Henry found Anne repellent in person at Rochester (“She is nothing as fair as she hath been reported”), returned to Greenwich in cold fury, and asked Cromwell repeatedly “Is there none other remedy?” His enemies — the Duke of Norfolk and Bishop Gardiner — seized the moment. Cromwell was arrested on June 10, 1540, attainted by Parliament without trial, and sent to the Tower. In the Tower he was confined to the queen’s apartments — the rooms he himself had rebuilt for Anne Boleyn’s coronation and later redecorated for Jane Seymour (he had changed the goddesses on the walls from brown eyes to blue when Jane came in). He was aware of the mirrors-for-princes tradition — books counseling the great man to live each day as his last — and alternated between imagining reprieve and accepting the end. He was executed on Tower Hill on July 28, 1540, the same day Henry married Catherine Howard. At the moment of death, Mantel describes the flint of the Tower sparkling like sunlight on the sea. ^[source: the_mirror_and_the_light_raw.txt, hume_history_tudor_vol1_raw.txt]
Hume’s Assessment
Hume characterises Cromwell as an “artful and dextrous” minister who “manipulated the king’s passions and enriched himself through the dissolution.” He dwells on the fabricated charges against Anne Boleyn and on Cromwell’s willingness to destroy More and Fisher as evidence of moral bankruptcy. The assessment serves as a counterpoint to Mantel’s sympathetic intimacy — but both Hume and Mantel agree on the fundamental dynamic: Cromwell was the indispensable instrument of a despotic king, and instruments are discarded when they break. ^[source: hume_history_tudor_vol1_raw.txt]
Foxe: Lambert, Fall, and Barnes
On the morning John Lambert was to burn (1538), Cromwell had him brought to his inward chamber and desired forgiveness for what he had done; Lambert breakfasted cheerfully in Cromwell’s hall before going to Smithfield.
Foxe’s account of Cromwell’s own end (July 28, 1540) presents him attainted by Parliament yet guiltless in conscience: he called for breakfast and ate cheerfully, met Lord Hungerford going to execution on the hill within the Tower, and comforted him — “there is for you mercy enough with the Lord.” They went together to Tower Hill and took their death patiently. Within two days Gardiner caused Robert Barnes, Thomas Garret, and William Jerome to be burned at Smithfield.

entities/thomas-more.title: Thomas More
entities/thomas-more.content:
Sir Thomas More (1478–1535), lord chancellor, was beheaded on Tower Hill 6 July 1535 for refusing the royal supremacy. Foxe presents him chiefly as a persecutor of evangelical men and a defender of Rome — executed, ironically, by the same supremacy he upheld against Lutherans.
Persecutor of Evangelical Men
Foxe names More with Bishop Fisher as men by whom John Frith, Thomas Hitten, Bayfield, Tewkesbury, and divers other saints were brought to death. More’s books slanderously and contumeliously writ against Luther, Zuinglius, Tyndale, Frith, Barnes, Bainham, and Tewkesbury — falsely belying their articles, Foxe asserts, with sufficient matter to prove against him.
More delivered Philip to Bishop Stokesley; he and Fisher caused one to be burned a year and a half before Rochester’s own execution. Foxe’s extended defence of Richard Hun and of Thomas Bilney rebuts More’s accounts of their supposed recantations — “per licentiam poeticam,” poetical licence.
Execution and Manner of Death
More refused the oath of supremacy and brought the scaffold of Tower Hill upon his own neck. Edward Hall, cited by Foxe, doubted whether to call him a foolish wise man or a wise foolish man — mingling great wit with taunting and mocking.
At the Tower gate a poor woman asked him to declare evidences of hers he held in office; he answered she should have patience, for the king would within half an hour discharge him of all businesses and help her himself. Going up the scaffold he asked a sheriff’s officer for his hand, saying when he came down again he would shift for himself. To the hangman who knelt for forgiveness he said he forgave him but promised he should never have honesty of striking off his head — his neck was so short. Laying his grey beard over the block lest it be cut, he ended with a mock.
Fisher was executed 22 June 1535; the pope had sent a cardinal’s hat as far as Calais, but Fisher’s head was at London Bridge ere it arrived.
