entities/thomas-smith.title: Sir Thomas Smith
entities/thomas-smith.content:
Sir Thomas Smith (1513–1577) was one of the most accomplished Tudor statesman-scholars: Cambridge regius professor of civil law, Secretary of State twice, privy councillor, ambassador, and author of De Republica Anglorum — the foundational contemporary description of Elizabethan governance. F. W. Maitland called the work essential for any understanding of the Tudor constitution. Smith occupied exactly the intersection of humanist learning and practical administration that characterised the generation Cromwell had shaped in the 1530s and that Elizabethan government depended upon.
Career
Smith was born in 1513 at Saffron Walden, Essex, the son of a grazier. He was educated at Queens’ College, Cambridge, where he became a fellow and eventually Provost, and at Padua (civil law). In 1540 he was appointed the first Regius Professor of Civil Law at Cambridge — a chair created by Henry VIII as part of the humanist reform of the universities. At Cambridge he was the principal advocate of the Erasmian reformation of Greek pronunciation (against the traditional medieval pronunciation), a controversy that also involved John Cheke and Roger Ascham, the intellectual circle that would later staff Edward VI’s and Elizabeth’s governments.
Under Edward VI he served twice as one of the two Principal Secretaries (1548–49 and 1550–52), the central administrative position in the Tudor government. He lost office under Mary (being a Protestant and a supporter of Lady Jane Grey) but was restored under Elizabeth. He served as ambassador to France three times, most importantly 1562–66, during which he wrote De Republica Anglorum. He was again Principal Secretary under Elizabeth from 1571 to 1576 — serving alongside Francis Walsingham, who took up the secretaryship in 1573 — and was a privy councillor throughout the 1570s until his death in 1577. ^[source: de_republica_anglorum_raw.txt]
De Republica Anglorum
De Republica Anglorum (“A Discourse on the Commonwealth of England”) was written in France between 1562 and 1565 and published posthumously in 1583. It is the only sustained contemporary Elizabethan account of how the English state actually functioned — written not as a theoretical treatise but as a descriptive account of existing institutions by a man who had operated at their centre.
Parliament. Smith’s central constitutional claim: “The most high and absolute power of the realme of Englande, consisteth in the Parliament.” Parliament can abrogate old laws, make new ones, legitimate bastards, establish forms of religion, give forms of succession to the crown, and restore attainted persons — “all that ever the people of Rome might do either in Centuriatis comitijs or tributis, the same may be doone by the parliament of Englande, which representeth and hath the power of the whole realme both the head and the bodie… And the consent of the Parliament is taken to be everie mans consent.” This parliamentary sovereignty argument was not a constitutional innovation but a description of what Cromwell’s legislative programme of the 1530s had established and what the Elizabethan settlement had confirmed.
Social hierarchy. Book I describes the four orders: Nobilitas major (titled nobility), Nobilitas minor (knights, esquires, gentlemen), citizens and burgesses, and yeomen — plus “the fourth sort of men which do not rule” (labourers, servants, copyholders). This taxonomy describes exactly the social world the Tudor state governed and the distinctions that determined access to political life, jury service, and military obligation.
Criminal justice. Smith devotes Book II to English legal procedure and is explicitly proud of its differences from continental practice. His account of torture is the most cited passage in the book: “torment or question which is used by the order of the civill lawe and custome of other countreis to put a malefactor to excessive paine, to make him confesse of him selfe, or of his felowes or complices, is not used in England, it is taken for servile.” He argues this on both moral and practical grounds — torture-extracted confessions were epistemically worthless since “the nature of English men is to neglect death, to abide no torment” and a man would confess to anything rather than endure it — and England still achieved “as few murthers committed as any where.” The jury formula — “by God and the Countrie” — is described in meticulous procedural detail, including the finality of the jury verdict, unreviewable by any judge.
Benefit of clergy. Smith describes the literacy privilege by which a convicted felon who could read (“legit ut clericus”) received a brand on the hand rather than hanging — creating a formal legal distinction between literate and illiterate criminals that gave concrete legal significance to literacy in Tudor England. ^[source: de_republica_anglorum_raw.txt]
Significance
De Republica Anglorum is the single most important primary source for understanding how Elizabethan governance actually worked from the inside. It supplies what all the secondary sources (Hume, Read, Corbett) can only reconstruct: a contemporary participant’s account of Parliament’s procedure, the social structure of the commonwealth, and the criminal justice system. Its description of Parliament as sovereign — exercising power that no external authority could override — is the constitutional foundation on which all the events of Tudor history, from the Reformation statutes to the execution of Mary Queen of Scots, rested.
Smith’s career also illustrates the Tudor administrative class. He was a product of the humanist university reform of the 1540s, a product of the European civil law tradition, a Secretary who worked under Protector Somerset, a diplomat who negotiated with Catherine de Medici, and a privy councillor who overlapped with Walsingham. He was not a great man of the first order — not Cromwell or Burghley — but the Tudor state could not have functioned without men of exactly his type. ^[source: de_republica_anglorum_raw.txt, walsingham_raw.txt]

entities/thomas-vautrollier.title: Thomas Vautrollier
entities/thomas-vautrollier.content:
Thomas Vautrollier (d. before 4 March 1587–8) was a Huguenot refugee printer who established one of the finest presses in Elizabethan London — operating from the liberty of Blackfriars outside the strict jurisdiction of the City — and who ran a secondary press in Edinburgh, producing theological and literary texts of exceptional quality. He was Richard Field’s master; Field married his widow and inherited the press on Vautrollier’s death. Ames/Herbert’s Typographical Antiquities documents Vautrollier’s career, his typography, and the books he produced.
Origins and Admission to the Stationers’ Company
Vautrollier was a French Protestant — probably from the Paris or Troyes region. He was admitted to the Stationers’ Company as a “stranger” (foreign printer) on October 2, 1564 — under the specific arrangements that allowed alien craftsmen to work in London’s liberties. He established his press in Blackfriars — a former Dominican friary dissolved under Henry VIII and now a liberty (an enclave not subject to normal City jurisdiction), which made it a natural home for printers operating under the Company’s regulatory reach while enjoying some insulation from it. His device was an anchor with the motto Anchora Spei (“Anchor of Hope”) — an emblem that linked him to the Continental humanist printing tradition and signalled the aspirations of his press. ^[source: typographical_antiquities_ames_raw.txt, stationers_registers_arber_vol1_raw.txt]
The Blackfriars Press and Continental Network
Vautrollier’s press specialised in high-quality literary, classical, and theological printing that required sophisticated typographic skill: Greek and Latin texts, scholarly publications in the Continental humanist tradition, Reformed theological works. His Huguenot background gave him direct connections to the Continental Reformed publishing world — French, Swiss, and Low Countries printers who were producing the intellectual output of the Protestant Reformation. From 1570 onwards, from July 1581, he appears to have been frequently absent from London, possibly maintaining connections with Continental publishing centres and managing the Edinburgh operation. ^[source: typographical_antiquities_ames_raw.txt]
The Edinburgh Press
Vautrollier operated a press in Edinburgh — a significant undertaking connecting the London and Scottish book trades. In Edinburgh he printed primarily theological and Reformed texts, serving the Scottish Protestant readership in the aftermath of John Knox’s reformation. The Edinburgh operation illustrates how skilled printers of the period operated across national jurisdictions: Vautrollier moved between London and Edinburgh as his commissions and regulatory circumstances required. The episode of Giordano Bruno’s works is connected to this period: Vautrollier printed two of Bruno’s works in London in 1584, and the diplomatic and religious controversy this generated contributed to his subsequent need to operate in Edinburgh, where the London regulatory apparatus had less reach. ^[source: typographical_antiquities_ames_raw.txt]
Major Publications
Vautrollier’s press produced works of lasting significance:

Thomas North’s Plutarch’s Lives (1579): The translation of Plutarch that Shakespeare used as the source for his Roman plays (Julius Caesar, Antony and Cleopatra, Coriolanus). The connection between Vautrollier’s press and Shakespeare’s dramaturgy runs through this text — continued by Field when he inherited the press.
Byrd and Tallis’s Cantiones Sacrae (1575): Music printing under the monopoly patent granted to William Byrd and Thomas Tallis — one of the few Elizabethan music printing patents; Vautrollier produced it under license.
Giordano Bruno’s works (1584): Two of the Italian philosopher’s texts, printed during Bruno’s London stay and his period of residence at the French embassy. The association with Bruno — whose cosmological and philosophical heterodoxy would eventually cost him his life in Rome — illustrates both the reach of Vautrollier’s intellectual networks and the risks that came with it.
Theological works in Latin: Calvin, Beza, and other Reformed authors.
Classical texts in Latin and Greek, in the humanist tradition of high-quality scholarly printing.

The quality of Vautrollier’s typography — noted by Ames/Herbert — placed his press among the leading London printers of the 1570s and 1580s. ^[source: typographical_antiquities_ames_raw.txt, stationers_registers_arber_vol1_raw.txt]
Death and Succession
Vautrollier died before 4 March 1587–8 — the exact date uncertain, but bounded by that record. His widow Jacqueline could not legally continue operating the press herself: the Stationers’ Company’s regulations, like those of other livery companies, made it extremely difficult for a widow to maintain a business independently without a male freeman as head. She married Richard Field, Vautrollier’s former apprentice, who then took over the press and its London operation. This pattern — widow marrying a trained journeyman to maintain the enterprise and satisfy Company requirements — was typical of the Elizabethan book trade, and the Company’s regulations were designed partly to facilitate such transfers. Through Field, Vautrollier’s press became the vehicle for Shakespeare’s first publications. ^[source: typographical_antiquities_ames_raw.txt]

entities/tower-of-london.title: Tower of London
entities/tower-of-london.content:
The Tower of London was the primary instrument of royal coercive power in Tudor England — fortress, palace, state prison, treasury, armory, and place of execution. It is where Tudor monarchs sent those they could not simply dismiss: the Constable of the Tower was a high office; imprisonment in the Tower signified that the Crown took the prisoner seriously as a political threat. Under Henry VIII alone, among those imprisoned or executed at the Tower were Thomas More, John Fisher, Anne Boleyn, Thomas Cromwell, Catherine Howard, and Lady Jane Grey. The Tower functions as the terminal point in Mantel’s Cromwell trilogy — the place toward which the narrative moves — and appears throughout the sources as the space where political destruction takes its final form.
Function and History
The Tower was built by William the Conqueror after 1066 as a fortress to dominate London; by the Tudor period it had accumulated centuries of royal use as residence, treasury (the Crown Jewels were housed there), armory, Royal Mint (until 1810), royal menagerie, and state prison. Prisoners of the highest rank — including kings, queens, and great ministers — were held in the Royal Apartments or the Beauchamp Tower, while those of lesser but still significant status occupied the Bell Tower and other accommodation. Execution within the walls — on Tower Green — was reserved for those of sufficiently high rank that a public execution on Tower Hill would be inappropriate; those executed on Tower Hill outside the walls included figures of slightly lower social standing. The distinction between dying within and without the walls was itself a statement of rank. ^[source: hume_history_tudor_vol1_raw.txt]
Thomas More and John Fisher (1535): The Legal Problem of Silence
More and Fisher were imprisoned in the Tower for refusing the oath of supremacy. More’s case presented Cromwell with an unusual legal problem: More’s silence — his refusal to give a reason for refusing the oath — was technically not treason under the existing legislation. A man could not be convicted of treason for silence alone. The solution came from Richard Rich, who subsequently testified at More’s trial that More had denied the supremacy in a private conversation during a Tower visit. Rich’s perjury — widely believed to be fabricated — provided the legally necessary spoken denial. Cromwell used the occasion. More was executed on Tower Hill on July 6, 1535; Fisher had been executed there on June 22. Their deaths were the foundational act of Henrician state coercion — the demonstration that the Supremacy was enforced at the cost of life, not merely conscience. ^[source: wolf_hall_raw.txt, hume_history_tudor_vol1_raw.txt]
Anne Boleyn (1536): The Arrow-Chest Coffin
Anne Boleyn was imprisoned in the Tower in May 1536 on charges of adultery, incest, and conspiracy to murder the king. She was held in the Tower’s Royal Apartments — the same rooms that had been prepared for her coronation. Executed on Tower Green on May 19, 1536, by a Calais swordsman rather than an English axeman, she was buried in the Chapel of St Peter ad Vincula within the Tower. Her body was placed in a narrow arrow-chest that served as a coffin; no proper funeral preparation had been made. Her brother George Boleyn and the other accused men were executed on Tower Hill two days earlier. ^[source: wolf_hall_bring_up_the_bodies_raw.txt, hume_history_tudor_vol1_raw.txt]
Thomas Cromwell (1540): Confined to the Rooms He Rebuilt
Cromwell was arrested and sent to the Tower on June 10, 1540. He was confined in the queen’s apartments — the rooms he himself had rebuilt and redecorated for Anne Boleyn’s coronation, and later redecorated again for Jane Seymour (changing the goddesses painted on the walls from brown eyes to blue when Jane came into the king’s favour). The spatial irony — that the man who had managed Henry’s queens was imprisoned in the rooms he had decorated for them — was not lost on Mantel. Cromwell was attainted by Parliament without trial; executed on Tower Hill on July 28, 1540. The Mirror and the Light closes with Cromwell’s weeks in the Tower and the morning of his execution — the flint of the Tower sparkling like sunlight on the sea at the moment of death. ^[source: the_mirror_and_the_light_raw.txt, hume_history_tudor_vol1_raw.txt]
William Davison (1587)
The Secretary of State William Davison was imprisoned briefly in the Tower by Elizabeth after he dispatched the death warrant of Mary Queen of Scots — held as a face-saving exercise that allowed Elizabeth to claim the warrant had been sent without her final approval. Davison was eventually released but never returned to royal service; Elizabeth paid him a pension, which was her way of acknowledging he had done what was required while refusing to admit she had required it. ^[source: walsingham_raw.txt, hume_history_tudor_vol2_raw.txt]
The Tower in Mantel’s Trilogy
The Tower functions in the Cromwell trilogy as the space where political power manifests its final logic. Mantel uses the Tower’s physical geography precisely — the Beauchamp Tower, the Lieutenant’s lodgings, Tower Green, Tower Hill — to locate her characters in the institutional reality of Tudor power. In Wolf Hall, More’s imprisonment is a warning about what refusal costs; in Bring Up the Bodies, the Tower is where Anne and the accused men are held while Cromwell builds the case against them; in The Mirror and the Light, Cromwell himself is imprisoned there in the book’s final movement, confined to the rooms he furnished, waiting for the same outcome he once administered to others. The spatial memory of the building — what it has held, who has died there, what it is — is present in every scene Mantel sets within its walls. ^[source: wolf_hall_raw.txt, wolf_hall_bring_up_the_bodies_raw.txt, the_mirror_and_the_light_raw.txt]
Foxe: Lollards’ Tower and the Rack
Richard Hun was committed to the Lollards’ Tower at St Paul’s (1514) so none of his friends might visit; he was murdered there before posthumous burning at Smithfield (vol3).
Anne Askew was sent to the Tower in 1546 when she would not name ladies of her sect; Wriothesley and Rich put her on the rack with their own hands till she was nigh dead, then reasoned with her on the bare floor (vol5-pratt).

entities/william-cecil-burghley.title: William Cecil, Lord Burghley
entities/william-cecil-burghley.content:
William Cecil, 1st Baron Burghley (1520–1598) was Elizabeth I’s Principal Secretary from 1558 to 1572 and Lord Treasurer from 1572 until his death on August 4, 1598 — the dominant figure at the Elizabethan court for forty years and the longest-serving of all Elizabethan ministers. Where Walsingham sought confrontation with Catholic powers and advocated aggressive Protestant intervention, Cecil preferred diplomatic caution, fiscal prudence, and the management of threats through intelligence and negotiation rather than military action. The two men represented the fundamental strategic debate of the Elizabethan reign: whether England could survive through cautious diplomacy or required active Protestant militancy. Hume’s assessment is that Cecil was the essential “ballast” that prevented Elizabethan foreign policy from running aground on either Catholic aggression or Protestant adventurism.
Early Career and Edwardian Service
Cecil was born in 1520 at Bourne in Lincolnshire and educated at St John’s College, Cambridge, and Gray’s Inn. He served as Secretary of State under Edward VI from 1550 to 1553. Under Mary I he was cautious, conformed outwardly to Catholicism, and survived. When Elizabeth acceded in November 1558, her very first appointment was Cecil as Principal Secretary — a confidence placed in him before any other minister was in position. ^[source: hume_history_tudor_vol2_raw.txt]
Secretary and Lord Treasurer
Cecil served as Principal Secretary until 1572, managing Elizabethan foreign policy through its most perilous years: the French religious wars, the threat from Mary Queen of Scots, the early stages of the Dutch revolt, and the growing tension with Spain. He was created Baron Burghley in 1571 and became Lord Treasurer in 1572 — a position from which he controlled Crown finance and patronage for another quarter-century. ^[source: hume_history_tudor_vol2_raw.txt]
Factional Relationship with Walsingham
Conyers Read’s biography of Walsingham constructs the factional relationship between the two men as the organizing dynamic of Elizabethan court politics. Both were Protestant and both committed to Elizabeth’s Protestant settlement, but profoundly different in strategic orientation:

Cecil/Burghley preferred diplomatic solutions, feared the financial cost of war, and was suspicious of the private interests (commercial and religious) that drove men like Drake. He believed England’s security lay in balanced diplomacy and trade, not in backing Protestant risings abroad that might draw England into unaffordable wars. He was comfortable with the Stationers’ Company press-control apparatus and the management of political threats through administrative means.
Walsingham believed that Catholic powers — Spain especially — would not stop until Protestant England was destroyed, and that preemptive action was the only realistic security. He was willing to spend his own money and take personal risks that Burghley would not.

The factions broadly aligned as: Burghley + Sussex (early) vs. Leicester + Walsingham + Sidney, with Essex eventually inheriting Leicester’s patronage network. On major policy questions — the French match, the Dutch intervention, Drake’s commissions — the two camps consistently diverged, with Elizabeth mediating and usually choosing a middle position that neither satisfied. ^[source: walsingham_raw.txt]
The “Protestant International” and Burghley’s Counter-Position
Walsingham, Leicester, and Sidney shared a vision of an activist “Protestant international” — a coordinated European Protestant resistance to Catholic power, with England providing military and financial leadership. Burghley was skeptical of this vision for structural reasons: it required England to spend money it did not have in support of Protestant causes whose success could not be guaranteed, and it committed England to continental military entanglements from which it would be difficult to disengage. His counter-position — patient diplomatic management, commercial agreements, and selective use of intelligence to neutralise specific threats rather than confronting Catholic power generally — was less inspiring but more sustainable. The debate between the two positions runs through every major Elizabethan foreign policy crisis. ^[source: walsingham_raw.txt, hume_history_tudor_vol2_raw.txt]
The Execution of Mary Queen of Scots
One of the most revealing episodes of the Burghley–Walsingham relationship was the execution of Mary Queen of Scots (1587). Both ministers wanted Mary dead; Burghley’s preferred method was administrative — presenting Elizabeth with the Babington Plot evidence in a way that made the execution unavoidable and then managing the political fallout. Walsingham provided the intelligence; Burghley managed the political machinery that produced the trial and conviction. The subsequent imprisonment of William Davison (who dispatched the death warrant) was partly a face-saving exercise that protected both men from Elizabeth’s displeasure. ^[source: walsingham_raw.txt, hume_history_tudor_vol2_raw.txt]
Robert Cecil and the Succession
Burghley groomed his son Robert Cecil to succeed him, introducing him to the Privy Council and gradually transferring effective workload from 1596. Robert became Principal Secretary in 1596 and was the effective manager of the Elizabethan state in its final years. After Elizabeth’s death in 1603, Robert Cecil’s most significant achievement was negotiating the Treaty of London (1604) with Spain — ending the Anglo-Spanish war that had been running since 1585. The treaty represented the victory of the Cecil/Burghley strategic approach over the Walsingham/Leicester/Essex militarist tradition: commercial peace rather than Protestant crusade. Robert Cecil died as Earl of Salisbury in 1612. ^[source: hume_history_tudor_vol2_raw.txt]
Hume’s Assessment
Hume’s assessment is relatively generous — Cecil as the essential administrator of a difficult reign, the ballast that prevented Elizabethan foreign policy from running aground on either Catholic aggression or Protestant adventurism. The same caution Walsingham found maddening Hume identifies as the quality that kept England solvent and the peace intact for most of the reign. The contrast between Burghley’s forty years of stable service and the brief, violent careers of the men who opposed him — Leicester, Essex, Walsingham himself (who died bankrupt) — is the empirical argument for Cecil’s approach. ^[source: hume_history_tudor_vol2_raw.txt]

entities/william-shakespeare.title: William Shakespeare
entities/william-shakespeare.content:
William Shakespeare (1564–1616) was the playwright, poet, and part-owner of the Globe Theatre whose works constitute the central achievement of Elizabethan literature. His career intersects this knowledge base at multiple points: his poems were published by Richard Field (his Stratford schoolfellow, trained by Thomas Vautrollier); his plays were registered in the Stationers’ Register and published as quartos through the Elizabethan book trade; the 1601 performance of Richard II during Essex’s rebellion was investigated as sedition; and the 1623 First Folio — entered by Blount and Jaggard — was the most significant single Stationers’ copyright transaction of the era. Stephen Greenblatt’s Will in the World (2004) provides the major modern literary-biographical synthesis.
Origins and Early Life
Shakespeare was born on approximately April 23, 1564, in Stratford-upon-Avon — the son of John Shakespeare, a glove-maker who rose to the position of alderman and High Bailiff before a mysterious financial collapse in the 1570s that may have required the withdrawal of young William from school. He attended the King’s New School in Stratford, where the daily schedule ran from 6 a.m. to 5:30 p.m. Instruction centred on Latin through Erasmus’s On Copiousness, Terence, and Plautus — Greenblatt notes that students performed the Latin plays, giving Shakespeare early theatrical experience. The school also involved severe corporal punishment; its intellectual culture was simultaneously rigorous and violent.
He married Anne Hathaway in November 1582 — when she was 26 and he 18, and already pregnant with their first child. Susanna was baptized six months later (May 1583); twins Hamnet and Judith followed in February 1585. The “lost years” between approximately 1585 and 1592 are undocumented. Greenblatt examines the Lancashire hypothesis — that Shakespeare may have spent part of this period in the household of Alexander Hoghton of Lea Hall, Lancashire, whose 1581 will refers to “William Shakeshafte” and mentions players and musical instruments, recommending that Thomas Hesketh (a Catholic landowner) take them into his service. Hoghton’s household was connected to Edmund Campion’s 1581 Jesuit mission; Campion passed through Lancashire on his clandestine circuit before his arrest and execution at Tyburn on December 1, 1581. The hypothesis connects Shakespeare’s lost years to the recusant underground. The one directly sourced Lost Years detail comes through John Aubrey (writing c.1680, via William Beeston): that Shakespeare “had been in his younger years a schoolmaster in the country.” ^[source: greenblatt_will_in_the_world_raw.txt]
Richard Field and the Early Publications
Shakespeare surfaces in London as an established playwright by 1592 — the year Robert Greene’s deathbed pamphlet attacks “an upstart Crow beautified with our feathers.” Greenblatt identifies Henry Wriothesley, 3rd Earl of Southampton (probably the intervening patron who quelled Greene’s attack), as the “young man” of the Sonnets and the dedicatee of both narrative poems. The publication of those poems was handled by Richard Field — a Stratford man, two years older than Shakespeare, who had been apprenticed to Thomas Vautrollier and inherited his Blackfriars press by marrying the widow Jacqueline.

Venus and Adonis (1593): The first appearance of Shakespeare’s name in print; dedicated to Southampton in carefully elegant prose signalling his literary ambitions.
The Rape of Lucrece (1594): Second poem, again dedicated to Southampton, with a warmer dedicatory letter suggesting the patronage had deepened.

Field’s press held classical texts that Shakespeare demonstrably used: North’s Plutarch’s Lives (the source for the Roman plays) was originally a Vautrollier production that Field continued printing. Greenblatt argues the Field connection was Shakespeare’s point of entry into the world of professional literary publication and the classical sources that fed his dramaturgy. ^[source: typographical_antiquities_ames_raw.txt, greenblatt_will_in_the_world_raw.txt]
Hamnet and the Plays of Grief
Shakespeare’s son Hamnet died in August 1596 at age eleven. Greenblatt connects this loss to the grief passage in King John — “Grief fills the room up of my absent child, / Lies in his bed, walks up and down with me” — written around this period, noting that Shakespeare “could not mourn in his own name but could give the words to a character in a play.” ^[source: greenblatt_will_in_the_world_raw.txt]
The Theatrical Companies
Shakespeare was a member and shareholder of the Lord Chamberlain’s Men from 1594. He held approximately one-tenth of the company — a share specified in Greenblatt’s account of the Globe construction. When James I succeeded Elizabeth in 1603, the company became the King’s Men under direct royal patronage.
In December 1598, on a snowy night, the Lord Chamberlain’s Men’s lease on The Theatre in Shoreditch having expired, they dismantled the building’s timbers and transported them across the Thames to Bankside. The builder Peter Streete used them to construct the Globe Theatre (1599). For its sign they chose Hercules bearing the world on his shoulders; for their motto, Totus mundus agit histrionem — “The whole world plays the actor.” Shakespeare held approximately one-tenth of the resulting theatre. From 1608, the King’s Men also operated the indoor Blackfriars Theatre, enabling year-round playing regardless of weather.^[source: greenblatt_will_in_the_world_raw.txt, dramatic_publication_england_raw.txt]
The Stationers’ Register and Publication
The Arber Registers document key entries:

Hamlet entered July 26, 1602 (6d, James Roberts) — preceded the first quarto (1603), which is notoriously defective (a memorial reconstruction); the second quarto (1604) is more authoritative.
Four plays “stayed” (1600): The Chamberlain’s Men had As You Like It, Henry V, Much Ado About Nothing, and Every Man in His Humor entered “to be staied” in 1600. Albright interprets this not as suppression but as ownership claims — the company reserving copyright by having a chosen publisher register the rights before a pirated version appeared.
The Sonnets (1609): Entered May 20, 1609 (6d, Thomas Thorpe) — appearing to have been published without Shakespeare’s direct involvement. The identity of the dedicatee (“Mr W.H.”) remains one of literary scholarship’s most debated questions.
The First Folio (1623): Entered November 8, 1623 (7s for Comedies, 6d per History/Tragedy, Edward Blount and Isaac Jaggard). It collected 36 plays — 18 not previously published — assembled after Shakespeare’s death by his former colleagues John Heminges and Henry Condell. ^[source: stationers_registers_arber_vol2_raw.txt, stationers_registers_arber_vol3_raw.txt, stationers_registers_arber_vol4_raw.txt]

The Richard II Affair (1601)
On February 7, 1601 — the day before the Essex Rebellion — the Lord Chamberlain’s Men were paid £2 extra (40 shillings above the normal fee) by Gelly Meyrick (one of Essex’s followers) to perform a play depicting a monarch’s deposition. One actor objected: “the play was olde and they should haue losse in playing it.” They performed Richard II regardless, with the deposition scene. The actors were questioned afterward but not prosecuted — the grounds being that the play was old and they were merely paid performers. Elizabeth allegedly said to a visitor shortly after: “I am Richard II, know ye not that?” — indicating she understood the political intent of the commission. ^[source: dramatic_publication_england_raw.txt, stationers_registers_arber_vol3_raw.txt]
Property and Retirement
Shakespeare built a systematic property portfolio in Stratford: New Place (a substantial house, purchased 1597), tithes in Stratford and surrounding villages, a Chapel Lane cottage, 107 acres of farmland. Greenblatt notes this systematic asset-building continued even after he had established himself in London — the Stratford investments representing both a financial strategy and a long-term plan for retirement. He retired to Stratford around 1612–13. He died on April 23, 1616, and was buried in the chancel of Holy Trinity Church. His will — which included the famous bequest of the “second-best bed” to his wife Anne — made no mention of manuscripts or literary property; these passed to his theatrical colleagues rather than his family. ^[source: greenblatt_will_in_the_world_raw.txt]

entities/william-tyndale.title: William Tyndale
entities/william-tyndale.content:
William Tyndale (c. 1477–1536), called by Foxe “the apostle of England in this our later age,” was the principal translator of the English New Testament and much of the Old Testament. He was strangled and burned at Vilvorde (Filford), near Brussels, in 1536 — the same year in which, Foxe notes, Catherine of Aragon died in January and Anne Boleyn was beheaded in May.
Oxford, Cambridge, and Sir John Walsh
Born about the borders of Wales and brought up from a child at Oxford (Magdalen Hall), Tyndale grew in knowledge of tongues and especially of Scripture. He read privily to certain students and fellows of Magdalen College some parcel of divinity; his manners and conversation were such that all who knew him reputed him a man of most virtuous disposition and life unspotted. He removed to Cambridge, then became schoolmaster to the children of Master Welch, a knight of Gloucestershire.
At Welch’s table abbots, deans, archdeacons, and other doctors talked of Luther and Erasmus. Tyndale showed his judgment plainly, laying open manifest places of Scripture to confute their errors. When the priests waxed weary and bore a secret grudge, Welch’s wife asked whether it were reason to believe Tyndale before doctors who might dispend hundreds of pounds. Tyndale gave no answer; he translated Enchiridion Militis Christiani for his master and lady, after which the doctorly prelates came no more to the house.
Priests of the country stormed against Tyndale in alehouses; he was warned before the bishop’s chancellor and, fearing what they would lay to his charge, departed and was no more seen in those parts.
Translation and Exile
Tyndale’s labour in translating Scripture made him the special object of the adversaries’ malice. John Frith received from Tyndale the seed of the gospel and sincere godliness. Frith’s testimony and Tyndale’s own letters survive in Foxe’s account of both men.
Betrayal and Martyrdom (1536)
After acts of Parliament establishing the king’s supremacy and making denial of the royal dignity high treason (1534, 1536), Foxe turns to Tyndale — falsely betrayed and put to death in 1536. The emperor’s decree from the assembly at Augsburg furnished the legal ground; Tyndale refused advocate or procurator and made answer for himself.
At Vilvorde he was tied to the stake, strangled first by the hangman, then consumed with fire in the morning, crying with fervent zeal and loud voice: “Lord! open the king of England’s eyes.” During imprisonment (about a year and a half) he converted his keeper, the keeper’s daughter, and others of the household; the procurator-general left testimony that he was homo doctus, pius, et bonus — learned, good, and godly.

events/babington-plot-1586.title: The Babington Plot (1586)
events/babington-plot-1586.content:
The Babington Plot of 1586 was Francis Walsingham’s masterwork of intelligence entrapment — a Catholic conspiracy to assassinate Elizabeth I and free Mary Queen of Scots, allowed to develop under Walsingham’s surveillance until Mary herself committed to paper her approval of the assassination, then destroyed. Its outcome was Mary’s trial and execution. It stands as the most elaborate and consequential intelligence operation of the Elizabethan period.
The Conspirators
Anthony Babington was a young Catholic gentleman of Derbyshire, 25 years old in 1586, who had previously served as a page to the Earl of Shrewsbury (Mary’s keeper) and had contact with the Catholic exile community on the Continent. He was the nominal head of a conspiracy that included approximately fourteen men:

John Ballard — a seminary priest who had visited the Continent specifically to secure commitments from Spain and the papacy that external support (invasion forces and financing) was available. Ballard returned with assurances — possibly exaggerated — that Philip II and Pope Sixtus V would back the enterprise. These continental assurances were the precondition Babington required before the English conspirators would move.
Chidiock Tichborne — later famous for the elegy he wrote in the Tower before his execution.
Robert Gage, and approximately ten others.

The conspiracy’s plan was threefold: foreign invasion (supported by Spain and the papacy), the assassination of Elizabeth (to be carried out by six designated men), and the liberation of Mary. ^[source: walsingham_raw.txt, hume_history_tudor_vol2_raw.txt]
Walsingham’s Penetration
Walsingham had intelligence of the conspiracy’s outlines before Babington recruited his full circle. His penetration rested on two key operatives working independently inside Babington’s trust:
Gilbert Gifford — a young English Catholic who had trained at the seminary at Rheims, where he was recruited by Walsingham before or on his return to England. Gifford’s role was to approach Mary’s household and establish what appeared to be a safe, secret postal route. He was the architect of the beer-barrel channel.
Robert Poley — another of Walsingham’s agents who had embedded himself directly in Babington’s personal circle, gaining his close friendship over months. Poley was present in Babington’s inner councils throughout the conspiracy’s development and reporting continuously to Walsingham. Poley remained active as a government agent for years afterward — he was one of the three men present at the Deptford tavern when Christopher Marlowe was killed in May 1593. ^[source: walsingham_raw.txt]
The Beer-Barrel Channel
The postal channel operated through a brewer who delivered beer to Mary’s household at Chartley in Staffordshire. Letters from the continental exiles or from Babington were concealed in a waterproof packet inside the bung of a beer barrel; Mary’s household extracted them and sent replies through the same route. The brewer was in Walsingham’s employ. Every letter was intercepted before delivery, the outer waterproof packet opened, the contents decoded by Thomas Phelippes, copied, re-encoded in the original cipher, resealed, and forwarded — giving Mary and Babington no indication the channel was compromised. Engravers in Walsingham’s service reproduced the seals used on the intercepted packets so that the resealed letters showed no sign of tampering. ^[source: walsingham_raw.txt]
Mary’s Letters
Through the beer-barrel channel, Babington sent Mary a detailed account of the conspiracy in a letter of July 1586 — including the plan for Elizabeth’s assassination, which he described as “the dispatch of the usurping Competitor.” Mary’s reply, dated July 17, 1586, approved the plan. Phelippes decoded the letter and drew a gallows on the outside to indicate its explosive significance to Walsingham. The letter also requested the names of the six men designated to carry out the assassination — a request whose very specificity demonstrated that Mary understood and endorsed the plan.
Walsingham chose to allow the conspiracy to continue briefly after receiving this evidence, so that Babington’s full circle could be identified. A postscript was added to Mary’s July 17 letter asking for the six names — an addition whose authenticity historians have disputed. If genuine, it was Mary’s own supplementary request; if forged by Phelippes (under Walsingham’s direction), it was a fabricated entrapment. The scholarly debate has not been resolved. Either way, the main body of Mary’s letter was sufficient to condemn her. ^[source: walsingham_raw.txt]
The Arrests
In August 1586, Babington became suspicious — possibly alerted by some change in Poley’s manner, possibly by the arrest of Ballard on August 4. He met with his confederates and they attempted to flee; Walsingham ordered the arrests. Babington was captured in a wood in Harrow on August 14, hiding in disguise. Over the following days the entire circle was taken. They were interrogated — some under torture — and confessed. ^[source: walsingham_raw.txt, hume_history_tudor_vol2_raw.txt]
Executions
Babington and six of his confederates were executed at Lincoln’s Inn Fields on September 20, 1586, in the particularly brutal manner reserved for traitors: hanged, cut down while still alive, and disembowelled. The first group’s execution was so violent that Elizabeth reportedly asked that the second group (executed the following day) be allowed to die hanging before the disembowelment — a mercy relative to what the first group had endured. Tichborne’s elegy, written in the Tower, survives as one of the more affecting documents of Elizabethan political execution. ^[source: walsingham_raw.txt, hume_history_tudor_vol2_raw.txt]
Consequences: Mary’s Trial
The letters obtained through the beer-barrel channel were presented as the primary evidence against Mary at her trial at Fotheringhay Castle in October 1586. Mary denied their authenticity and challenged the court’s jurisdiction over an anointed queen. The commission — forty nobles and judges — convicted her of treason on October 29, 1586. Parliament petitioned for her execution; Elizabeth delayed signing the death warrant for months, eventually signing and then attempting to prevent its formal dispatch. ^[source: walsingham_raw.txt, hume_history_tudor_vol2_raw.txt]

events/bucer-and-phagius-bones-1557.title: Bucer and Phagius Bones (1557)
events/bucer-and-phagius-bones-1557.content:
On 9 January 1557, during Cardinal Pole’s visitation at Cambridge, the bones and books of Martin Bucer and Paulus Phagius were condemned, exhumed, and burned — opening Book XII of Foxe’s Marian narrative.
Visitation
Cardinal Pole, three years after his return into England, having established the Romish religion, began the Cambridge visitation (vol4). The order and manner of the visitation, with condemning, taking up, and burning the bones and books of Martin Bucer and Paulus Phagius, anno 1557, January 9.
Proceedings

Master Stokes’s oration to the queen’s visitors
Answer of Master Scot, bishop of Chester
Oration before condemnation of Bucer and Phagius
Sentence of condemnation
Effect of Dr Perne’s sermon; Watson’s sermon on Candlemas-day
Oration of Master Acworth at the restitution of Bucer and Phagius
Dr James Pilkington’s sermon
Epitaph of Dr Redman upon the death of Martin Bucer

Bucer and Phagius had been called from Germany to Cambridge; they lay buried at Great St Mary’s (Bucer) and St Michael’s (Phagius). Foxe draws on Latin and English accounts of the exhumation and burning (editorial notes cite Golding’s 1562 English translation and the Strasbourg Latin narrative).
Despiteful handling of Peter Martyr’s wife at Oxford — grave taken up and buried in a dunghill — appears in the same book as parallel action against reformers’ remains.

events/burning-of-anne-askew-1546.title: Burning of Anne Askew (1546)
events/burning-of-anne-askew-1546.content:
Anne Askew was burned at Smithfield in June 1546 with Nicholas Belenian (priest of Shropshire), John Adams (tailor), and John Lacels (gentleman of the king’s household) — after racking in the Tower and examination before Wriothesley, Rich, and Bonner.
At the Stake
Tormented so she could not walk, Askew was brought to Smithfield in a chair. Tied by the middle with a chain at the stake, Dr. Shaxton preached; Askew, hearing and answering, confirmed where he said well and where he missed said, “There he misseth, and speaketh without the book.”
Three separate stakes; a great multitude; Wriothesley (chancellor), the old Duke of Norfolk, the old Earl of Bedford, and the lord mayor on a bench under St Bartholomew’s church. Gunpowder about the martyrs’ bodies (not under the faggots) was explained by the Earl of Bedford as meant to rid them quickly of pain.
Wriothesley sent letters offering the king’s pardon if she would recant; she refused once to look upon them, answering she came not thither to deny her Lord and Master. The same offer refused by Lacels, Adams, and Belenian. The lord mayor commanded fire put to them, crying “Fiat justitia.”
Askew, compassed in flames, slept in the Lord A.D. 1546. Lacels, Adams, and Belenian, beholding her invincible constancy and stirred by her persuasions, received greater comfort; they took their death patiently about June 1546. Foxe prints Lacels’s prison letter on the sacrament.
Context
Foxe places this burning in Henry VIII’s late reign — after the king’s oration touching reformation and alongside prohibited books including Tyndale’s Wicked Mammon. Askew’s case links the Henrician persecution of sacramentarian opinion to the Marian burnings at the same ground (smithfield).

events/burning-of-cranmer-1556.title: Burning of Cranmer (1556)
events/burning-of-cranmer-1556.content:
Thomas Cranmer was burned at Oxford on 21 March 1556 after a prolonged process of examination, multiple recantations, and final withdrawal of those recantations at the stake.
Oxford Process
Foxe’s Book XI (vol4) opens 1556 with the life, state, and story of Thomas Cranmer, Archbishop of Canterbury, martyr: orations of Brooks and Martin at St Mary’s Church, Oxford; Cranmer’s faith and profession; Story’s oration; papal commission and sentence; appeal to the next general council; degrading; copies of recantations sent abroad; Cole’s sermon; Cranmer’s prayer and letters to the queen and others.
The 21st day of March was appointed for Cranmer’s execution. On the morning of his martyrdom friars brought a seventh declaration to subscribe; he rejected it and made the declaration and prayer Foxe prints. Bonner had printed All the Submissions and Recantations of Thomas Cranmer — six or seven papers — as though Cranmer had subscribed to all, including one he had rejected.
Recantations and Final Act
Foxe narrates fourth, fifth, sixth, and seventh papers of recantation demanded; Cranmer’s miserable case after recanting — neither quietness in conscience nor help from adversaries; praise on one side, scorn on the other; the queen’s heart set against him though she received his recantation gladly.
At the stake he withdrew his recantations and thrust his hand that had signed them into the fire first (Hume’s account aligns with Foxe’s climax).

events/burning-of-latimer-and-ridley-155.title: Burning of Latimer and Ridley (1555)
events/burning-of-latimer-and-ridley-155.content:
Hugh Latimer and Nicholas Ridley were burned at Oxford on 16 October 1555 — a central set-piece in Foxe’s Marian narrative (vol7).
Before the Stake
Ridley had remained in custody from 1554 until 1555. He and Latimer conferred in prison on refusing mass and on scripture (printed dialogue in Foxe). Ridley’s last suit concerned poor men’s leases taken away by the new bishop of London after Ridley left the see.
At the Stake
A faggot kindled with fire was laid at Ridley’s feet. Latimer spoke: “Be of good comfort, master Ridley, and play the man. We shall this day light such a candle, by God’s grace, in England, as I trust shall never be put out.”
When the fire was given, Ridley cried with a loud voice, “In manus tuas, Domine, commendo spiritum meum,” repeating “Lord, Lord, receive my spirit” in English. Latimer cried vehemently, “O Father of heaven, receive my soul!” — received the flame as embracing it, stroked his face with his hands in the fire, and soon died with very little pain.
Ridley, by reason of the evil making of the fire (wooden faggots laid about the gorse and over-high), suffered longer.
Foxe notes A.D. 1555, October 16, followed at Oxford the slaughter of two.

events/cadiz-raid-1587.title: The Cadiz Raid (1587)
events/cadiz-raid-1587.content:
Drake’s raid on Cadiz harbour in April 1587 — “singeing the King of Spain’s beard” — destroyed an estimated 10,000 tons of Spanish shipping and seized vital supplies intended for the Armada, delaying the invasion of England by at least a year. It was the last great privateering operation before the Armada campaign transformed English naval activity into formal state warfare; it demonstrated both the vulnerability of Spanish Atlantic infrastructure and the effectiveness of the aggressive offensive doctrine that Walsingham and Drake had been pressing on Elizabeth for a decade. Corbett treats it as one of Drake’s most perfectly executed operations.
Background and Context
By early 1587, Walsingham’s intelligence network had confirmed that Philip II was assembling an invasion fleet at Lisbon and Cadiz. The fleet’s completion was a matter of months; Drake and Walsingham pressed Elizabeth to authorize a preemptive strike. Elizabeth authorized — and then, characteristically, sent countermanding orders limiting Drake’s scope of action. Drake, already at sea when the countermand arrived, chose not to receive it clearly enough to be bound by it. He proceeded to Cadiz. ^[source: corbett_drake_tudor_navy_vol2_raw.txt, walsingham_raw.txt]
The Raid (April 19–20, 1587)
Drake entered Cadiz harbour on April 19, 1587, with approximately 23 ships. The harbour contained a large concentration of shipping being fitted out for the Armada. Drake’s fleet fought its way through the defending galleys — fast oar-powered warships suited to harbour fighting — and spent two days destroying or seizing shipping. The damage:

An estimated 10,000 tons of shipping destroyed; Drake’s own account may be somewhat exaggerated but the damage was substantial and independently documented by Spanish sources
The staves intended for the Armada’s water casks were seized and destroyed — a logistical blow that Corbett identifies as more strategically significant than the ship losses: without seasoned staves, the barrels could not be properly sealed, and the fleet’s water supply would be compromised throughout the subsequent campaign
The San Felipe, a large Portuguese carrack returning from the East Indies, was captured as a prize on the subsequent operations along the Portuguese coast; its cargo of spices and merchandise was worth approximately £100,000

Drake wrote to Walsingham afterward that the raid “would delay the Armada by a year” — a prediction that proved roughly accurate. ^[source: corbett_drake_tudor_navy_vol2_raw.txt]
William Borough and the Council of War Dispute
During the Cadiz operation, Drake’s vice-admiral William Borough wrote a formal protest — “a letter of remonstrance” — against Drake’s high-handedness in attacking the harbour without first holding a council of war with his senior officers. Borough’s complaint was procedurally legitimate: the tradition of holding councils of war before major tactical decisions was well-established, and Drake’s unilateral action bypassed it entirely. Drake responded by court-martialling Borough for insubordination — an extreme response that alarmed the queen.
Elizabeth was unimpressed by Drake’s treatment of a subordinate; she made her displeasure known. She nonetheless kept Drake in command, recognizing that his tactical success rendered disciplinary action counterproductive. Borough returned to England under a cloud; the episode illustrates both Drake’s operational temperament (he believed councils of war produced delay and indecision) and the command tensions that would resurface during the Armada campaign. ^[source: corbett_drake_tudor_navy_vol2_raw.txt, sir_francis_drake_raw.txt]
The Broader Operation
After Cadiz, Drake operated along the Portuguese coast, raiding harbours, destroying coastal shipping, and seizing provisions intended for the Armada. He then sailed to the Azores, where he captured the San Felipe. The overall operation lasted approximately three months and inflicted logistical damage far beyond the immediate destruction at Cadiz — disrupting the supply chain for the fleet being assembled at Lisbon. ^[source: corbett_drake_tudor_navy_vol2_raw.txt]
Strategic Effect: Delaying the Armada
The Armada had been intended to sail in 1587; the Cadiz raid and subsequent operations delayed it until 1588. Corbett argues this delay was strategically decisive: it gave England another year to prepare the fleet and fortifications, another year for the diplomatic situation to evolve, and — crucially — it meant that the Armada sailed under Medina Sidonia rather than the Marquis of Santa Cruz (the original commander, who died in February 1588). Medina Sidonia was competent but lacked Santa Cruz’s aggressive naval experience. The unseasoned staves for the water casks meant that provisions spoiled; the provisioning problems that plagued the fleet in 1588 originated at Cadiz in 1587. ^[source: corbett_drake_tudor_navy_vol2_raw.txt]
“Singeing the King of Spain’s Beard”
The phrase attributed to Drake — “I have singed the King of Spain’s beard” — is the most celebrated remark in Elizabethan naval history. Whether Drake actually used it is uncertain; it appears in various contemporary sources in different forms. It captures the character of the Cadiz operation: not a decisive fleet engagement but a disruptive, humiliating raid that demonstrated Spanish vulnerability and English daring. Philip II was furious; the Spanish court’s dignity was injured as much as the fleet. The phrase passed into the language as a description of the audacious spoiling attack that sets back an adversary without defeating him. ^[source: corbett_drake_tudor_navy_vol2_raw.txt, hume_history_tudor_vol2_raw.txt]

events/circumnavigation-1577-1580.title: Drake's Circumnavigation (1577–1580)
events/circumnavigation-1577-1580.content:
Drake’s circumnavigation of the globe (December 1577 – September 1580) was the second in history (after Magellan-Elcano, 1519–22) and the first completed under a single commander. It was simultaneously a privateering operation of global scale (raiding the undefended Spanish Pacific coast), a geopolitical provocation (demonstrating that English ships could reach any ocean), and a voyage of exploration (mapping the California coast as Nova Albion). The voyage returned approximately 200,000 ducats of royal plunder; Drake was knighted by the queen aboard the Golden Hind at Deptford in April 1581. The geopolitical significance was stark: “the entire system of Spanish imperial security was exposed as resting on the assumption that no one could reach the Pacific from Europe.”
Preparation, Investors, and Secrecy
The expedition was organised in secret. The true objective — circumnavigation via Magellan’s Strait and raids on Spanish Pacific ports — was known only to Elizabeth, Walsingham, Leicester, and Sir Christopher Hatton. The crew was told they were “bound for Alexandria.” The cover story successfully deceived even the Spanish ambassador Mendoza, who “could only confuse rumours that Drake was bound for Nombre de Dios.” The principal investors almost certainly included the queen herself, who maintained plausible deniability while sharing the profits; Walsingham and Leicester were among the known investors.
Drake sailed from Plymouth in December 1577 with five ships: the Pelican (100 tons, his flagship), the Elizabeth, the Marigold, the Swan, and the Christopher. The Swan and Christopher were scuttled for their stores before the fleet reached the Strait of Magellan, leaving three ships. ^[source: corbett_drake_tudor_navy_vol1_raw.txt]
The Doughty Affair at Port St Julian
The defining crisis of the voyage occurred at Port St Julian (a harbour on the Patagonian coast where Magellan had previously wintered and executed a mutineer) in June 1578. Thomas Doughty was a gentleman, a lawyer, a friend of Drake’s, and — crucially — a servant of Sir Christopher Hatton, the expedition’s investor whose coat of arms would later grace the flagship. Doughty had been “subtly undermining Drake’s authority with hints that the backers expected Doughty to share the command” — or so the prosecution alleged. Carpenter Edward Bright testified to having heard Doughty’s private boasts at Plymouth. Drake convened a formal “court of forty men” and tried Doughty publicly.
Doughty was convicted. Drake had no royal commission clearly authorising him to execute a gentleman at sea; Corbett judges Doughty’s guilt “probable” but the death sentence “legally doubtful.” Nonetheless Drake beheaded him. He “communed with him before the end and dined with him afterward — ‘we are yet friends,’ Drake told him.” After the execution, Drake renamed the Pelican the Golden Hind — Hatton’s family emblem, a cringing diplomatic gesture to his dead adversary’s patron.
The speech Drake made to the assembled crew afterward established the meritocratic discipline Corbett identifies as the foundation of the Elizabethan naval ethos: “gentlemen must haul and draw with the mariner, and the mariner with the gentleman. I would know him that would refuse to set his hand to a rope.” The Doughty affair and this speech became the formative statement of English naval culture. ^[source: corbett_drake_tudor_navy_vol1_raw.txt]
The Straits of Magellan
Drake navigated the Straits of Magellan in 14 days — the fastest passage of the century; Magellan himself had taken 37 days. Emerging into the Pacific in August 1578, the fleet immediately encountered catastrophic storms. The Marigold sank with all 29 men aboard — the worst single casualty of the voyage. The Elizabeth, commanded by Captain John Winter, was separated from the Golden Hind in the storm and eventually turned back to England; Winter later claimed he had searched for Drake but been unable to find him. Drake in the Golden Hind continued alone.
The storms drove Drake far south — further south than any ship had previously been, revealing that Tierra del Fuego was not the tip of a great southern continent but an island with open sea beyond it. Corbett identifies this inadvertent geographic discovery as one of the voyage’s most significant contributions to knowledge. ^[source: corbett_drake_tudor_navy_vol1_raw.txt]
The Pacific Raids: Valparaíso, Callao, the Cacafuego
Drake’s raids on the undefended Spanish Pacific ports inflicted both material damage and strategic shock. Spanish Pacific possessions had no defences because no foreign ship had previously entered the Pacific from the Atlantic. Drake’s arrival exposed a structural vulnerability of the Spanish imperial system.
At Valparaíso he took a cargo of gold and wine from a ship in harbour. At Callao (the port of Lima, the viceregal capital) he found 30 ships but they carried no bullion — it had just departed on the treasure galleon Nuestra Señora de la Concepción, known to the Spanish as Cacafuego (“Fire-Spitter”). Drake pursued her north along the Peruvian coast and took her on March 1, 1579, after a chase — disguising the Golden Hind to delay the Cacafuego’s captain from recognising the threat. The Cacafuego carried:

Twenty-six tonnes of silver ingots
Thirteen chests of silver coins (pieces of eight)
Eighty pounds of gold
A cargo of jewels and precious stones

Drake spent six days transferring the cargo. The Golden Hind was, as Corbett reports, “literally ballasted with silver.” The Spanish response was to send Sarmiento de Gamboa south to intercept Drake at the Magellan Strait — too late. Sarmiento predicted that Drake would seek the hypothetical Straits of Anian (a supposed north-west passage above the Americas), a prediction that Drake’s subsequent northern exploration seemed to confirm. ^[source: corbett_drake_tudor_navy_vol1_raw.txt]
Nova Albion and the California Coast
Drake explored the California coast northward to approximately 48°N latitude — further north than any European had previously explored in the Pacific. Cold, thick fog, and the failure to find any strait entrance eventually forced him to give up the search for a north-west passage. He turned south and made a landing somewhere on the California coast — naming it Nova Albion and leaving a brass plate claiming it for the English Crown. The exact location of the landing remains disputed among scholars: Drake’s Bay, Bolinas Bay, and the San Francisco Bay entrance have all been proposed, and the evidence is insufficient to resolve the question.
Greenblatt quotes Drake’s own account of the Miwok people who came to the landing site in great numbers, performing ceremonies that Drake and his men interpreted as offering him sovereignty — a misreading of local protocol that nonetheless became the basis of England’s California claim. ^[source: corbett_drake_tudor_navy_vol1_raw.txt, sir_francis_drake_raw.txt]
Return: The Moluccas, the Indian Ocean, and Near-Disaster
Drake sailed west across the Pacific, reaching the Moluccas (Spice Islands), where he negotiated a trade agreement with the Sultan of Ternate and loaded cloves. The return through the Indian Ocean included a near-disaster: the Golden Hind ran onto a reef and was held fast for approximately 20 hours before breaking free. Drake continued around the Cape of Good Hope and north through the Atlantic.
Before entering Plymouth Sound on September 26, 1580, Drake sent a pinnace ashore to determine whether Walsingham was still in power and the political situation favourable — if not, the plunder could be politically disavowed and the voyage’s sponsors might find it convenient to denounce him. The news was good; Walsingham was in power. Drake anchored. The voyage had lasted nearly three years. ^[source: corbett_drake_tudor_navy_vol1_raw.txt]
The Knighting and Its Diplomatic Meaning
Elizabeth came to Deptford on April 4, 1581, to see the Golden Hind and to knight Drake. She arranged for a French envoy — the Sieur de Marchaumont — to perform the ceremony. The choice was deliberate: it made the knighting simultaneously an act of royal favour and a diplomatic message to Spain, communicating that France was associated with the honor and that England had no intention of apologising for the Pacific raids. Philip II had formally demanded restitution; Elizabeth declined. Drake received the bulk of the plunder; the queen received a large share.
Corbett identifies the Deptford knighting as the moment when the Elizabethan government publicly committed to the strategic logic of Drake’s operations — that English interests were best served by aggressive disruption of Spanish Atlantic commerce, not by diplomatic accommodation. The circumnavigation had changed the strategic calculus of the Atlantic world: Spain’s Pacific possessions were no longer invulnerable, and English sea power had demonstrated a global reach. ^[source: corbett_drake_tudor_navy_vol1_raw.txt]

events/execution-of-anne-boleyn-1536.title: Execution of Anne Boleyn (1536)
events/execution-of-anne-boleyn-1536.content:
Anne Boleyn was beheaded on Tower Green within the Tower of London on May 19, 1536 — three years and four months after her coronation as Queen of England. The charges were adultery with five men (including her brother), incest, and conspiracy to murder the king. The charges were almost certainly fabricated by Thomas Cromwell, acting to neutralise the Boleyn faction and facilitate Henry VIII’s marriage to Jane Seymour. The event is the central narrative of Hilary Mantel’s Wolf Hall: Bring Up the Bodies — probably the most sustained literary engagement with the episode in any language.
Sequence of Events: April–May 1536
The destruction of Anne Boleyn proceeded with extraordinary speed once Cromwell decided to act — from first arrest to execution in less than three weeks:
Late April 1536: Mark Smeaton, a court musician, was brought to Cromwell’s house at Stepney and interrogated — not with torture but with silence, patience, and darkness. Cromwell used only psychological pressure; Mantel is explicit that no rack was employed. Smeaton confessed to adultery with the queen. His confession was the hook on which Cromwell built the subsequent case.
April 30, 1536: Henry Norris (Groom of the Stool — the king’s most intimate household servant) was arrested. The charge of adultery with the queen was implausible given the surveillance of the court and the access controls on the Privy Chamber, but Norris’s position — closer to Henry than any man except Cromwell — made the charge politically available and politically devastating.
Francis Weston and William Brereton were arrested in the following days.
May 2, 1536: Anne herself was arrested and taken to the Tower. George Boleyn (her brother) was arrested the same day on the charge of incest.
May 15, 1536: Anne and George Boleyn were tried before a court of twenty-six peers in the Tower. The presiding judge was their own uncle, the Duke of Norfolk. Norfolk pronounced the death sentence on his niece with a steady voice and with no visible hesitation. Lord Percy — Henry Percy, heir to the Earl of Northumberland, who had been in love with Anne before Henry’s interest separated them (Wolsey having broken the attachment on royal instructions years before) — fainted during the proceedings and was carried from the court.
May 17, 1536: Archbishop Cranmer pronounced Anne’s marriage to Henry void — making Elizabeth technically illegitimate two days before her mother’s death. Norris, Weston, Brereton, Smeaton, and George Boleyn were executed on Tower Hill. Thomas Boleyn, Anne’s father, was not prosecuted; his cooperation with the investigation, or at minimum his neutrality, appears to have purchased his survival.
May 19, 1536: Anne Boleyn was beheaded on Tower Green. ^[source: wolf_hall_bring_up_the_bodies_raw.txt, hume_history_tudor_vol1_raw.txt]
The Execution Itself
The executioner was brought from Calais — a swordsman rather than the English axeman who had dispatched the male accused two days earlier. The choice was presented as a mercy, but it imposed its own demands: execution by sword required the condemned to kneel upright and unsupported, without the block that an axe beheading used, exposing the neck to the blade while maintaining position. Anne had requested the Calais swordsman herself.
Contemporary accounts emphasise her composure on the scaffold. The swordsman — Mantel describes him cleaning his Toledo steel blade afterward, the physical instrument of an act that required technical precision regardless of its meaning — performed the execution cleanly in a single stroke.
Her body was placed in an arrow chest that served as a coffin; no proper funeral preparations had been made. She was buried in the Chapel of St Peter ad Vincula within the Tower. ^[source: wolf_hall_bring_up_the_bodies_raw.txt]
The Construction of the Case: Sources
Mantel’s Bring Up the Bodies presents Cromwell’s investigative process in detail that goes beyond what any single historical source can confirm:
Lady Worcester — pregnant and physically vulnerable — was brought to a small room with cakes and a cushion. Cromwell listened while she spoke about Anne being “free with her body,” about certain gentlemen being overfamiliar. She came back again, and each time she came she said more.
Lady Rochford (Jane Parker, George Boleyn’s wife) provided hints about nocturnal visitors to Anne’s apartments — hints that implicated her own husband as well as the queen.
These two women’s testimony, combined with Smeaton’s confession and Norris’s arrest, provided the minimal factual armature around which Cromwell constructed a case whose outcome was determined before the evidence was complete. ^[source: wolf_hall_bring_up_the_bodies_raw.txt]
Cromwell’s Self-Examination
In The Mirror and the Light, Mantel has Cromwell return to the question of what he did in 1536. The Boleyns had destroyed Wolsey; he had wanted them destroyed in part for that reason. He asks himself whether what he had done was justice or revenge — and finds he cannot cleanly answer. The case he built was not more fraudulent than many Tudor state trials; the question he cannot resolve is whether he would have found a way to build it even if Anne had been innocent of the charges and her enemies had been guilty of nothing except ambition. ^[source: the_mirror_and_the_light_raw.txt]
Hume’s Assessment
Hume is relatively clear that the charges were fabricated: “the utter improbability of the crimes imputed to her, the irregular manner of her trial, and the precipitancy of her condemnation, all tend to give great reason for doubt.” He situates the fall of Anne within Henry’s broader pattern of disposing of inconvenient women and blames the king as much as Cromwell. He notes the irony that the daughter born of the marriage Henry needed the Reformation to contract — Elizabeth — would become the greatest of English monarchs. ^[source: hume_history_tudor_vol1_raw.txt]

events/execution-of-mary-queen-of-scots-.title: Execution of Mary Queen of Scots (1587)
events/execution-of-mary-queen-of-scots-.content:
Mary Queen of Scots was beheaded at Fotheringhay Castle, Northamptonshire, on February 8, 1587 — nineteen years after she had fled to England seeking Elizabeth’s protection, and twenty-seven days after Elizabeth signed the death warrant. Her execution was the culmination of the Babington Plot trial; it removed the Catholic dynastic claimant around whom every major Elizabethan assassination conspiracy had circled; and it precipitated the international crisis that Philip II used as additional justification for building the Armada. It is one of the best-documented events of the Elizabethan period, with accounts from English and Scottish observers.
The Trial at Fotheringhay
Mary was tried before a commission of forty nobles and judges at Fotheringhay Castle in October 1586. The primary evidence was the correspondence obtained through the Babington beer-barrel channel — letters in which Mary had approved the plan to assassinate Elizabeth, using the phrase “dispatch of the usurping Competitor.” Mary challenged both the court’s jurisdiction (as an anointed queen she denied that English law applied to her) and the authenticity of the letters (she claimed they had been forged or altered). The commission convicted her of treason on October 29, 1586. Parliament petitioned for her execution; Elizabeth, aware of the dynastic and diplomatic implications of executing an anointed queen, delayed signing the death warrant for nearly three months. ^[source: walsingham_raw.txt, hume_history_tudor_vol2_raw.txt]
The Death Warrant, Paulet, and Davison
Elizabeth signed the death warrant on February 1, 1587. She then appears to have attempted to arrange for Mary to be killed by private action, suggesting to Sir Amyas Paulet (Mary’s keeper at Fotheringhay) that he might “find some way to shorten the life” of Mary without requiring the formal execution. Paulet refused in terms that have been quoted ever since: “my conscience and my honour” would not permit private assassination; he had been appointed to keep Mary safely, not to kill her. The reply was everything Elizabeth did not want — a moral commitment that made the legal warrant unavoidable.
Elizabeth’s Secretary William Davison held the signed warrant. He convened the Privy Council, which resolved to dispatch the warrant to Fotheringhay without waiting for further instruction from Elizabeth. The warrant arrived at Fotheringhay on February 7. Elizabeth subsequently imprisoned Davison in the Tower, fined him £10,000, and declared she had never intended the warrant to be dispatched — a performance that historians from Hume forward have treated as a characteristic attempt to disclaim responsibility while achieving the desired result. Burghley and the other councillors who had authorised the dispatch were collectively blamed but not individually punished; Davison bore the cost of the Council’s collective decision. ^[source: walsingham_raw.txt, hume_history_tudor_vol2_raw.txt]
The Execution
Mary was executed in the great hall of Fotheringhay Castle on the morning of February 8, 1587. She entered wearing black; beneath the black outer gown she wore red — the colour of Catholic martyrdom — which was removed on the scaffold, so that she died visibly as a martyr. The choice of colour was deliberate; Mary had known for weeks that execution was coming and had prepared her self-presentation with care.
The beheading was botched. The executioner required two or three blows of the axe — a failure that entered both Protestant and Catholic accounts of the event, each reading it differently (Protestant accounts minimised it; Catholic accounts used it as evidence of the horror of the proceedings). When the executioner lifted her head by what he thought was her hair, her red wig detached and the head fell — she had been grey beneath. Her small dog was found hiding beneath her skirts, refusing to leave the body; it had to be removed before the body could be tended. ^[source: walsingham_raw.txt, hume_history_tudor_vol2_raw.txt]
Diplomatic Consequences
Mary’s execution provoked a formal crisis with Scotland: James VI protested formally but calculated carefully. His own succession to the English throne depended on maintaining Elizabeth’s goodwill; to break with England would be to trade a hypothetical kingdom for a demonstrated grievance. He protested without breaking. Philip II of Spain used the execution as additional justification for the Armada — adding the cause of avenging Mary (who had named him her heir in preference to her Protestant son) to his existing religious and strategic grounds. The execution thus accelerated the Armada timetable, though the fleet’s assembly was already underway. France protested and recalled its ambassador briefly.
Dynastic Irony
Mary’s son James VI succeeded Elizabeth as James I of England in 1603 — fulfilling in Protestant form the Catholic dynastic claim his mother had been executed for asserting. Elizabeth’s resistance to naming a successor meant that the person who actually succeeded her was the son of the queen she had executed for plotting to replace her. Hume finds this irony characteristic: Elizabeth’s entire political style was one of managed deferral, and the succession question was the case in which the costs of that style were most visible. James’s succession also meant that the Elizabethan Catholic threat — the structural danger that had justified Walsingham’s entire career — ended not through military victory but through Protestant dynastic accident. ^[source: hume_history_tudor_vol2_raw.txt]

events/oxford-disputations-1554.title: Oxford Disputations (1554)
events/oxford-disputations-1554.content:
In 1554, under Mary I, Thomas Cranmer (Archbishop of Canterbury), Nicholas Ridley (Bishop of London), and Hugh Latimer were sent from the Tower to Oxford to dispute against Catholic doctors — the order, manner, and circumstances of the disputation and their condemnation are set out in Foxe’s Book XI (vol6).
Sendings-Down
How Thomas Cranmer, Bishop Ridley, and Master Latimer were sent down to Oxford to dispute appears with the arguments, reasons, and allegations used. The sum and effect of the communication between Dr Ridley and Secretary Bourne with others at the lieutenant’s table in the Tower precedes the Oxford material.
The Disputations

Ridley: Disputation at Oxford between Dr Smith with his other colleagues and doctors, and Bishop Ridley
Latimer: Disputation had at Oxford, the 18th day of April, 1554, between Master Hugh Latimer, answerer, and Master Smith and others, opposers

Address to the reader; disputation of Master Harpsfield answering for his form to be made doctor. Observations or censures upon the disputations — what judgment to give touching the adversaries’ arguments and the martyrs’ answers.
Prison Documents
A copy of a declaration drawn and sent abroad out of prison by Master Bradford, Master Saunders, and divers other godly preachers, concerning their disputation and doctrine — the same against Doctor Ridley and against Master Latimer. Answers and resolutions to the arguments by number and order.
Ridley’s report and narration concerning the misordered disputation had against him and his fellow-prisoners at Oxford. Ridley’s letter to the prolocutor; Cranmer’s letter to the council sent by Dr Weston, who refused to deliver it; Ridley to Cranmer.
Tables of principal arguments against Doctor Cranmer follow.
