Contents — Chapter by Chapter
Chapter I: The Indies Voyage 1585 (lines ~232–1358)
Drake’s 1585 Indies expedition marks the transition from undeclared reprisal warfare to formal Anglo-Spanish hostility. Elizabeth’s commission contained implicit authority for aggressive action against Spanish colonial infrastructure. The expedition assembled approximately 2,300 men (soldiers and sailors), led by experienced commanders including Frobisher and Carleill, with an operational plan targeting San Domingo, Cartagena, Panama, and Havana. Corbett frames this as deliberate provocation designed to precipitate open war, though Philip remained unwilling to commit fully to English conquest until his broader European strategy aligned. Epidemic disease, appearing mid-Atlantic, claimed hundreds of men and compromised combat strength throughout the campaign.
Chapter II: San Domingo and Cartagena (lines ~1359–2992)
Drake’s 1585 fleet attacked the Caribbean’s most valuable Spanish possessions, sacking San Domingo (the oldest European settlement in the Indies and the jewel of Philip’s colonial empire) after a difficult mountain march to force the defences. Corbett emphasises the scale of Drake’s strategic vision: he aimed not merely to plunder but to destroy the supply infrastructure sustaining Spanish Atlantic power and to seize advanced bases — notably Havana and Panama — for future operations. Despite achieving the tactical objectives at San Domingo and Cartagena, sickness and Spanish reinforcements curtailed the campaign’s ambitions. The voyage returned with significant prizes and demonstrated Spanish colonies’ vulnerability, precipitating Philip’s decision to build a formal invasion fleet.
Chapter III: Operations on the Spanish Coast (lines ~2993–5018)
Following Drake’s triumph and the Babington Plot’s exposure (1586), Elizabeth enters a phase of diplomatic ambiguity, keeping Drake poised for action while avoiding outright declaration of war. She permits preparation of a Portuguese expedition under Don Antonio (the legitimate Portuguese claimant), even exploring Ottoman alliance possibilities, but repeatedly suspends offensive action when diplomatic overtures seem promising. Corbett details Philip’s strategic response: rather than pursuing the English Enterprise directly at cost, he decides to build a powerful ocean fleet to secure his sea lanes and colonies — a more economical path to protecting Spanish interests. Drake is kept “in constant communication” with Don Antonio, serving both as a deterrent to Spain and as a negotiating tool.
Chapter IV: Drake’s Plan of Campaign (lines ~5019–6916)
Drake’s post-Indies intelligence convinced Elizabeth of an imminent Armada, but she refused to mobilise the fleet preemptively or dispatch Drake to harass Spanish preparations — a decision Corbett partially defends on diplomatic grounds but characterises as strategically misguided. The chapter traces the Armada’s fitful concentration at Lisbon: delayed by Santa Cruz’s pursuit of a Portuguese fleet, damaged by gales, and fractured by Spanish internal disagreement. Experienced admirals such as Recalde recognised the inherent weakness of invading England without a secure harbour; the impetuous Leyva and Philip’s stubborn adherence to original instructions overrode such counsel. By autumn 1587, the fleet could not sail; the golden opportunity for English preemption had passed, leaving England unprepared and Spain determined to proceed. Drake’s 1587 Cadiz raid (not a separate chapter but covered in context) destroyed substantial Spanish stores and delayed departure by months.
Chapter V: Attempts to Attack the Armada (lines ~6917–8079)
The English fleet gathered at Plymouth under Lord Admiral Howard numbered approximately 100 sail (69 galleons and great-ships, including 16 Royal Navy vessels), with total crews around 10,000 men; Drake served as Vice-Admiral, Hawkins as Rear-Admiral. Spain’s fleet had been reconstituted to approximately 114 sail after its initial dispersion following the Cadiz raid and Santa Cruz’s death. Howard and Drake’s attempts to attack the Spanish fleet at Coruña were thwarted by summer storms that forced the English back to Plymouth. The fundamental strategic problem: without a favourable wind and tactical surprise, neither fleet could force engagement decisively, and the Armada, once regrouped and moving up the Channel, became increasingly difficult to intercept from behind.
Chapter VI: The Fleets in Contact (lines ~8080–10062)
Howard plans to blockade and destroy the Armada at Coruña while detaching a flying squadron to intercept the Indies treasure fleet — a sound strategy that proved unexecutable against contrary winds. Corbett praises Howard’s command style: lacking Drake’s tactical genius, his “high dignity” and “assured tact” unified a fleet of competing aristocrats and sea-captains where Drake’s rough temperament might have bred faction and jealousy. Spanish leadership remained demoralised; Sidonia doubted his own fitness to command; Recalde and senior officers urged modifications to Philip’s plan but were overridden. The chapter portrays both fleets as frustrated — the English by weather and logistics, the Spanish by their admiral’s caution and the fundamental contradiction of invading a fortified island from open water without an English harbour as base.
Chapter VII: Portland and the Isle of Wight (lines ~10063–11365)
Upon encountering the English fleet off Plymouth on July 31, 1588, the Spanish concluded they must fight for the Isle of Wight — the only harbour on the eastern Channel that could serve as an advanced base for Parma’s crossing. The chapter details the tactical engagement off Portland: the English attempt to gain the weather gauge fails initially; Spanish galleasses operate effectively in the calm; Frobisher becomes dangerously isolated near Portland Bill but is rescued. Drake’s controversial dimming of his stern lantern during a night chase — he abandoned formation to pursue Spanish stragglers — confuses the English fleet’s order and earns Howard’s reproach. Corbett analyses the fundamental asymmetry: English ships’ superior sailing qualities, firepower concentration, and trained gun crews against Spanish superiority in numbers and boarding strength. By the Isle of Wight action, it becomes clear that Spanish tactics (massed crescent formation, boarding assault) cannot overcome English nimbleness and gunnery, yet the English cannot inflict decisive damage with available ammunition.
Chapter VIII: The Battle of Gravelines (lines ~11366–13276)
Corbett’s magisterial account of the decisive engagement of July 29, 1588. Sidonia’s fleet, lacking intelligence of Parma’s readiness and anchor-bound at Calais, is dispersed by fire-ships (Drake and Hawkins’s initiative) — forcing an emergency evacuation that breaks the massed formation. With the Armada scattered northeastward toward Gravelines, the English fleet delivers sustained volleys at close range: Spanish crews were appalled by English accuracy and rate of fire; boarding attempts failed repeatedly; ships lost formation in confusion. The English inflicted irreplaceable losses (seven major ships sunk or destroyed, many more crippled) while exhausting Spanish powder and shot. Corbett stresses that superior English seamanship and gun discipline — trained by Drake’s insistence on target practice — proved decisive; Spanish courage and numbers could not overcome the technological and tactical revolution. Line-ahead gunnery was the instrument; Drake’s school had trained the instrument. Gravelines established the broadside-gunned sailing warship as the decisive weapon of European naval power.
Chapter IX: The Lisbon Expedition (lines ~13277–15355)
Despite the Armada’s destruction, contemporaries felt grave disappointment — the English had not achieved the overwhelming victory expected, Spain’s navy had demonstrated resilience, and English gunnery was recognised as inadequately trained (provoking a petition to revive Henry’s Corporation of Gunners). Drake faced a changed political landscape: Leicester’s death and Walsingham’s exhaustion removed his patrons. A 1589 expedition to Portugal under Drake and Norreys (to support Don Antonio) failed disastrously — not from naval action but from plague, logistics failures, and disagreement over strategic objectives. Drake’s navy successfully attacked Coruña and destroyed ships there, but Norreys’ army could not take Lisbon, and the expedition returned discredited. Corbett argues that the campaign revealed Drake’s limitations in joint army-navy command and, more importantly, demonstrated Elizabeth’s reluctance to pursue unlimited war when diplomatic and commercial opportunities seemed available.
Chapter X: Drake’s Disgrace (lines ~15356–17043)
Drake’s successful Armada campaign paradoxically isolated him politically. Elizabeth and the older aristocratic establishment — jealous of his rise — held him responsible for the Portugal expedition’s failure, though his navy operations were sound; blame attached to Norreys and the army, but Drake shared in the discredit. With Leicester dead and Walsingham following (1590), Drake lost his advocate at Court. Strategic doctrine shifted from Drake’s offensive grand strategy (attacking Spanish sources of power at their origin) to Hawkins’s commerce-raiding model — privateering against merchant convoys rather than systematic destruction of enemy capacity. This pivot was economically attractive to Elizabeth but strategically incomplete: it never threatened Spain’s recovery. Drake was kept from active command during the crucial years 1590–94, his expertise wasted while the war devolved into petty corsairing. Corbett implies that the loss of Drake’s “master hand” explains the war’s eventual stagnation.
Chapter XI: The Last Voyage (lines ~17044–22974)
In 1595, with new Spanish fleets reported and Ireland threatened by Spanish intrigue, Drake regained favour and led an expedition to repeat his 1585 Indies successes. Corbett frames this as a tragic miscalculation: Drake believed Spain remained as vulnerable as a decade earlier, not grasping that Philip had transformed his navy into a permanent, professionally managed force with dedicated escort squadrons (the Indian Guard and Tertia). The expedition was too weak, and the strategic vision — to strike Panama and compel Philip to disperse resources — was sound in theory but impossible given Spain’s new naval reality. Drake’s final council-of-war disputes with Hawkins, the missed interception of treasure fleets, and the mounting sickness (Hawkins died off Puerto Rico in November 1595; Drake died of dysentery off Portobello on January 28, 1596) are recounted in detail. Corbett frames the last voyage as a tragedy of outdated assumptions: Drake’s contempt for Spanish seamanship, earned in 1585 when Spain was unprepared, blinded him to Spain’s post-Armada professionalisation and the impossibility of repeating easy triumphs.

Useful For

armada-1588 — the most analytically substantial account: fleet compositions, engagement sequences (Portland, Isle of Wight, Gravelines), fire-ship tactics, and Corbett’s argument that English victory derived from trained gunnery and line-ahead formation rather than improvised heroism
battle-of-gravelines — the fullest scholarly treatment of the July 29, 1588 engagement; Corbett’s argument on the decisive role of gunnery discipline
drake-francis — the admiral phase of Drake’s career: Indies Voyage 1585, Cadiz 1587, Armada 1588, Lisbon 1589, last voyage 1595–96; the arc of triumph, disgrace, and death
elizabethan-navy — Howard’s command style, the English fleet composition, the Navy’s administrative reform under Hawkins; Corbett’s distinction between Howard’s aristocratic leadership and Drake’s tactical genius
elizabethan-strategy — Elizabeth’s strategic ambivalence as the central theme; the persistent gap between Drake’s offensive vision and the queen’s diplomatic restraint; the shift from amphibious grand strategy to commerce-raiding after 1589
hawkins-john — Hawkins as Rear-Admiral in the Armada campaign; his commerce-raiding doctrine (contrasted with Drake’s); his death off Puerto Rico 1595
cadiz-1587 — Drake’s pre-Armada raid covered in the Chapter IV context; described as “singeing the King of Spain’s beard” and delaying the Armada by months
walsingham-secretary — Walsingham as Drake’s Court patron; his death in 1590 as the political turning point in Drake’s career

sources/de-republica-anglorum-smith.content:
De Republica Anglorum: A Discourse on the Commonwealth of England
Author: Sir Thomas Smith (1513–1577)
Editor: L. Alston (with a Preface by F. W. Maitland)
Publisher: Cambridge University Press, 1906
Original composition: 1562–1565 (written while Smith was Elizabeth’s ambassador in France)
First published: 1583 (posthumously)
Source type: Primary source (constitutional/political treatise)
Raw text: de_republica_anglorum_raw.txt

Overview
Sir Thomas Smith’s De Republica Anglorum is a foundational description of the English constitution and commonwealth as it existed under Queen Elizabeth I. Written while Smith was serving as ambassador to France (1562–1566), the work offers a contemporary’s account of how England was governed — its monarchy, parliament, laws, courts, and social hierarchy. It is one of the most cited primary sources on Tudor governance.
Smith was a distinguished scholar and statesman: a Cambridge regius professor of civil law, fellow of Queens’ College, public orator, secretary of state under both Edward VI and Elizabeth I, ambassador to France, and a privy councillor. He was a key figure in the introduction of Erasmian Greek pronunciation and the reform of English spelling.
The book is divided into three books. Book I describes the forms of commonwealths and the social orders of England. Book II describes the institutions of government — Parliament, the monarchy, courts, and legal procedures. Book III covers appeals and their absence in English criminal procedure.

Contents
Book I — Of the Diversities of Commonwealths and the Social Orders of England
Chapter 1 — Of the diversities of commonwealths. Smith opens with the three classical forms of government drawn from Aristotle and Plato: monarchy (rule by one, for the common good), aristocracy (rule by the best few), and democracy or politeia (rule of the multitude). Each is defined by its purpose — governance oriented to the common good — as distinct from its corrupt counterparts discussed in Chapter 3. Smith frames the entire work within this ancient taxonomy before applying it to England.
Chapter 2 — What is just or Law in every commonwealth. Smith engages Thrasymachus’s challenge from Plato’s Republic — that justice is merely whatever the stronger party ordains — and rejects it. His own definition: law is what the whole body of a commonwealth has established for the common good, not what any single faction imposes for its own advantage. This sets the constitutional standard against which England’s specific institutions are then measured.
Chapter 3 — An other division of commonwealths. The six forms completed: each of the three good forms has a corrupt counterpart. Monarchy degenerates into tyranny (the monarch ruling for himself alone); aristocracy into oligarchy (the few ruling for their own benefit); democracy into mob rule or ochlocracy (the multitude exploiting the rest). Smith follows Aristotle’s schema closely.
Chapter 4 — Example of changes in government. Illustrated through Roman history — kings giving way to consuls, consuls to dictators, dictators to emperors. The lesson is that constitutional change is natural and follows from the accumulating pressures of circumstance. No form is permanent; all are subject to internal decay and external shock.
Chapter 5 — Of the question what is right and just. When is disobedience against unjust government warranted? Smith examines Dion against Dionysius of Syracuse, and Brutus against Caesar. His conclusion is characteristically cautious: rebellion against a tyrant may be theoretically justifiable but is “alwayes a doubtfull and hasardous matter.” He stops well short of endorsing resistance theory — the practical statesman’s hedge.
Chapter 6 — That commonwealths are not simple but mixed. No pure form of government exists in reality. Like the four Aristotelian elements, all real governments are compounds. England is not a pure monarchy but a mixed constitution combining monarchical, aristocratic, and democratic elements — a claim Smith will substantiate through the rest of the book.
Chapter 7 — The definition of a King and of a Tyrant. Three differences distinguish king from tyrant: how authority was obtained (just succession vs. usurpation), how it is administered (by law vs. by will), and to what end (the common good vs. self-interest). Smith notes that these three criteria produce four permutations: a man can be a tyrant by entry but rule justly (Octavius/Augustus), or come to power legitimately but rule tyrannically (Nero). The full tyrant scores badly on all three; the good king scores well on all.
Chapter 8 — Of the absolute king. Absolute power — power unchecked by law — is legitimate in one sphere only: war, where the speed of decision makes legal process impossible. In peace, absolute power corrupts. Smith cites Plato: no man can bear unchecked authority without becoming unjust, which is why Rome limited its dictators to six months. The English king is not absolute in peacetime; the Privy Council, Parliament, and common law all constrain him.
Chapter 9 — Of the name King and the administration of England. The etymology of “cyning” from the Saxon. The English monarch holds authority directly from God, without investiture by any external power — no pope, no emperor. Smith argues that King John’s submission to the papacy in 1213 was never binding on England, because it was not enacted by Parliament. Parliament’s consent is the constitutional threshold that makes obligations binding on the realm.
Chapter 10 — What is a commonwealth. A society of free men, governed by common accord, for the common good. Slaves are excluded: they are instruments, not members, of the polity. Smith questions whether Ottoman despotism qualifies as a true commonwealth at all — if the subjects are not free, the polity is merely a household writ large.
Chapter 11 — The first sort or beginning of a house or family (oikonomia). The family as the first and most natural society: husband and wife in complementary roles, parents and children, master and servants. Smith follows Aristotle’s dictum that man cannot live alone without being either a beast or a god. The household (oikonomia) is the foundation from which larger political arrangements grow.
Chapter 12 — The first and natural beginning of a kingdom (basileia). As the household grows into a tribe, the patriarch continues to rule absolutely — basileia is the natural political consequence of family governance extended over time and distance.
Chapter 13 — The first and natural beginning of aristocracy (aristokratia). When the patriarch dies, his sons deliberate together and take turns in authority. From this fraternal consultation emerges the aristocratic form — deliberative rule among equals who share a common standing.
Chapter 14 — The first original beginning of democracy (demokratia). Growing equality among men makes oligarchic exclusion unsustainable; free men refuse to be shut out of honour and profit. Democracy arises not from a deliberate design but from the pressure of social equality asserting itself against a restricted ruling group.
Chapter 15 — That the commonwealth must be according to the nature of the people. Smith’s shoe-to-foot metaphor: government must fit the governed. A people accustomed to liberty will not endure tyranny without becoming servile or rebellious; an undisciplined people without strong authority falls into disorder. There is no universal best constitution — the question is always which form fits the particular people in question.
Chapter 16 — The division of parts and persons of the commonwealth. Women are excluded from governance of the commonwealth — except when royal authority is attached to blood and title, in which case a queen absolute has the same authority as a king. England is divided into four sorts: nobilitas maior (lords temporal and spiritual), nobilitas minor (knights, esquires, and gentlemen), citizens and burgesses, and yeomen. A fourth sort — labourers and artisans — are outside the active governing structure. Lords and Commons in Parliament represent the first three sorts.
Chapter 17 — Nobilitas maior: dukes, marquises, earls, viscounts, barons. The titled peerage: created by the king or inherited. Smith gives income requirements (baronage needs £1,000 per year minimum) and compares the English peerage to Roman senators and patricians. All bear the title “Lord” and have voice in the upper house of Parliament.
Chapter 18 — Of the second sort of gentlemen: knights. Knights are made, not born. Smith describes the dubbing ceremony — the formula “sus ou sois chivalier au nom de Dieu et de Saint George” — and notes that knights may be compelled at coronations if they hold income of £40 per year or more. He covers the Order of the Garter (founded by Edward III, 26 knights), knights bachelor, and the distinction between knights banneret (made in the field under the royal standard) and ordinary knights.
Chapter 19 — Of esquires. Esquires bear coats of arms and are not strictly separated from gentlemen; originally they were armour-bearers for lords. Smith treats them as the upper stratum of the gentry, not a formally distinct order.
Chapter 20 — Of gentlemen. Gentlemen are defined by blood, lineage, and the continuity of “old riches or prowesse remaining in one stock.” Smith uses the “gilded copper” metaphor for families whose quality has declined: they still pass as gold at a distance but are not the genuine article. The king can create new gentlemen as a husbandman plants new trees — replacing what time has degraded.
Chapter 21 — Whether the manner of England in making gentlemen so easily is to be allowed. Smith defends England’s relatively permeable gentry: any man who studies law, attends university, professes the liberal sciences, or can live without manual labour and bear the outward charges of gentility (dress, servants, liberality) may call himself a gentleman and be called “master.” A herald will grant him arms. Smith argues this costs the crown nothing (unlike France, where fiscal distinctions between estates matter), because in England gentlemen pay more toward public charges, not less, and bear the costs of military service and household display themselves.
Chapter 22 — Of citizens and burgesses. A third estate between gentlemen and yeomen. Citizens and burgesses are freemen of incorporated towns, of sufficient substance to bear public charges. In the shire they have little standing, but in Parliament they are essential: ancient cities return four burgesses, lesser boroughs return two, to give consent in the name of their communities.
Chapter 23 — Of yeomen. Smith calls yeomen the most important commoners in the commonwealth — more travailed in service than any other group. A yeoman is a legalis homo who holds at least 40 shillings of yearly revenue from free land. They do not call themselves gentlemen but carry more prestige than labourers. Yeomen are the backbone of military service — the English foot soldiers who made France “afraid”; the French gentleman on horseback was England’s superior, but the English yeoman on foot was France’s superior. Smith traces the word “yeoman” to the Dutch “yonker man” (a lesser gentleman), adopted in mockery during the wars and domesticated over time. Cato and Aristotle both praised this middling, land-owning, self-sufficient sort as the best citizens.
Chapter 24 — Of the fourth sort who do not rule. Day labourers, poor husbandmen, copyholders, merchants without free land, and all artisans — the Roman capite censi. They have no voice in the commonwealth and are governed rather than governing. But they are not entirely neglected: in cities, for lack of yeomen, they serve on juries; in villages they become churchwardens, alecunners, and constables. Smith closes Book I with a summary: England is governed by three active parts — the Prince, the gentlemen (in two degrees: barons and lesser nobility), and the yeomanry.

Book II — Of Parliament, the Monarchy, Courts, Trials, and Legal Procedures
Chapter 1 — Of the Parliament and its authority. Smith’s central constitutional claim, in language he intends to be definitive: “The most high and absolute power of the realme of Englande, consisteth in the Parliament.” Parliament can abrogate old laws, make new ones, legitimate bastards, establish forms of religion, define succession to the crown, appoint subsidies, restore attainted persons. “All that ever the people of Rome might do either in Centuriatis comitijs or tributis, the same may be doone by the parliament of Englande.” Every Englishman is taken to be present in Parliament — by procuration if not in person — and the consent of Parliament is taken to be every man’s consent.
Chapter 2 — The form of holding Parliament. The Prince sends writs to every lord spiritual and temporal, and to the sheriffs of every shire to return two knights of the shire elected by all gentlemen and yeomen (those with 40 shillings of free land). Ancient cities return four burgesses; boroughs two. On the first day the Lords assemble in robes in the upper house; the Chancellor sits under the Prince as the Prince’s voice. On woolsacks sit the judges (to advise on points of law, but without a vote) and the Secretaries of State. The Commons assemble separately, elect a Speaker, present him at the bar of the upper house, where he disclaims ability, is confirmed by the Chancellor, and then makes four petitions: freedom of speech within the house, freedom from arrest during Parliament, power to discipline their own members, and right to confer with the Lords or the Prince if needed. Bills are read three times in each house and may be amended by committee. The upper house votes individually — “content” or “not content” — with each lord also casting votes by proxy for absent lords. The lower house votes by voice (yea or no), with division by physical separation if the result is doubtful. No bill is law until both houses agree and the Prince gives assent in person on the last day of the session: “Le roy le veult” — or withholds it: “Le roy s’aduisera,” which kills the bill entirely.
Chapter 3 — Of the Monarch, King or Queen of England. The Prince has absolute power in war and peace — declaring war, making alliances, receiving ambassadors — with advice only from the Privy Council, which he himself appoints and dismisses. He proclaims the coin of the realm (controlling weight, fineness, and value) by proclamation alone. He appoints all great officers and judges, both temporal and spiritual. He holds wardship over those holding land in chief. Martial law in the field is absolute: the Prince’s word is law. All writs and criminal prosecutions run in the Prince’s name. England’s king is, Smith argues, “farre more absolute” than the Duke of Venice or the Spartan kings — because the Privy Council is entirely his creature, not an independent check.
Chapter 4 — The chief points wherein commonwealths differ. Five functions distinguish one government from another: lawmaking, war and peace, money provision, officer appointments, and justice. Parliament handles lawmaking and taxation jointly with the Prince; the Prince alone handles war and appointments; and the administration of justice remains to be described.
Chapter 5 — Three forms of trial or judgment in England. Three modes of definitive judgment exist: by Parliament (the highest), by battle, and by the great assize of twelve men. Each is considered in turn.
Chapter 6 — Trial by Parliament. Parliament may judge between private parties or between the Prince and a subject, in criminal or civil matters, following the same bill procedure as for legislation. In practice it is rare: Parliament, occupied with public affairs, is reluctant to involve itself in private quarrels.
Chapter 7 — Trial by battle. Technically still available and not formally abrogated. Rarely used, partly because the clergy always condemned it as unlawful, partly because customs change with time. Smith says he could not learn that it was ever repealed — it simply fell into disuse.
Chapter 8 — Trial by assise or twelve men. Smith introduces the English jury as England’s defining legal institution, contrasting it explicitly with the civil law countries of France and Italy, where judges decide. In England, the decisive verdict is given not by the judge but by twelve laymen — and this applies to civil matters as much as criminal.
Chapter 9 — Of pleas or actions. Criminal pleas are “pleas of the crown” — the Prince is party to every criminal prosecution because the life of his subjects is held only under the Prince’s protection. When a subject is robbed of life or limb, the Prince is damaged and demands an account. Civil pleas are personal (for contract or injury) or real (possessory or writs of right). A “writ” (breve) is the English equivalent of the Roman actio.
Chapter 10 — Of the chief tribunals, benches, or courts of England. Westminster Hall contains three permanent tribunals, fixed there by parliamentary agreement after it proved cumbersome for courts to follow the king. At the entry on the right: the Common Pleas, for civil matters of land and contract. At the upper end on the right: the King’s Bench, for pleas of the crown and criminal matters. On the left: the Chancery, presided over by the Chancellor and masters. Each has its distinct jurisdiction and procedure.
Chapter 11 — Of terms and the Chancery. The common law sits only four times a year (Michaelmas, Hilary, Easter, Trinity terms) — fewer than a third of the year’s days. Smith defends this by reference to Cato’s argument that excessive litigation is a social vice: those who love pleading should feel the cost; industrious men settle their matters at home by neighbourly judgment. The Chancery fills the gap that the common law’s rigidity creates: as the Roman praetor moderated jus summum, the Chancellor provides equity — ex aequo et bono, according to good conscience rather than the strict letter of the law. The Chancery operates by civil law procedure (written bills, witness examination) rather than jury trial.
Chapter 12 — Of judges in common law and the manner of trial. The Prince appoints two chief justices (King’s Bench and Common Pleas) and six or more puisne judges, all drawn from the senior counsellors and serjeants-at-law. They sit at term in their courts, hearing pleadings from counsel on both sides until the case reaches its “issue” — the precise legal or factual question on which everything turns.
Chapter 13 — Of the two manner of issues. Two kinds of issue exist. If both parties agree on the facts but disagree on the law (demurrer), the judges decide — and if the point is difficult, all the judges meet in checquer chamber to pronounce. If the parties disagree on what happened (issue of fact), the twelve men decide. Smith explicitly contrasts England’s procedure with civil law: in England, counsel argue to a legal question first, and fact is then tried by the jury; on the continent, fact is established by witnesses and torture before advocates argue the law. Smith praises the English system as “the most wise, most just, and most well devised meane found out” in Europe.
Chapter 14 — Of the sheriff and the Court of Exchequer. The sheriff (reeve of the shire, vice-comes in Latin) is the key executive officer of the shire, responsible for executing the commands of the courts. The Exchequer (fiscus principis) is the royal treasury and accounting court, where customs, subsidies, and revenues are received. Barons of the Exchequer hear questions that arise under its jurisdiction, decided by twelve men as in common law. The sheriff collects fines and amercements ordered by the courts; particular receivers handle routine revenues.
Chapter 15 — Of the twelve men. The sheriff summons twenty-four to ensure twelve can be assembled after absences and challenges. Either party may challenge individual jurors (for insufficient income, kinship with the other party, enmity, etc.); two of the panel are empanelled first to try the challenges. Once twelve are sworn, sergeants declare the issue from each side, witnesses give evidence openly in public — before judges, justices, parties, and all present; cross-examination is permitted. When the judge has heard enough, he recapitulates briefly for the jury, gives them the written evidence, and bids them retire. A bailiff keeps them without bread, drink, fire, or light until they agree unanimously — all twelve must agree, not merely a majority. The verdict is delivered in the fewest possible words (“guilty” or “not guilty”). The winning party customarily gives the jury dinner; that is all they receive.
Chapter 16 — Of hundreds, lathes, rapes, and wapentakes. The subdivisions of the shire — each named differently by region. Hundreds were originally the 100 townships (or the 100 men) that composed them; lathes and rapes derive from harvest service; wapentakes from Danish weapon-inspection musters. Each hundred has high constables appointed by the Justices of Peace, and its own bailiff appointed by the lord (if a liberty) or by the sheriff.
Chapter 17 — Of the court baron. Every owner of a manor may hold a court baron from three weeks to three weeks for his tenants. Tenants form the “homage” rather than an enquest. Court barons handle admissions of copyholders, deaths of tenants, intrusions by tenants against each other or the lord, and small disputes. Any party who prefers can remove a case to Westminster by writ. The court baron serves those who prefer neighbourly settlement over the delay and expense of the common law.
Chapter 18 — Of the leete or law day. A manorial court with special Crown grant or long prescription, held twice yearly. Its original function was broader: swearing men to the Prince, taking pledges, inquiring into conspiracies, affrays, and murders, and overseeing measures of bread and ale. It may reach those outside the manor’s homage. Smith traces the name from the Saxon lant (law) and “day.”
Chapter 19 — Of the proceedings in causes criminal; justices of the peace. Before criminal procedure can be understood, Smith explains three key officers. Justices of the Peace are chosen from the nobility and gentry of the shire and from learned lawyers; they hold commission at the Prince’s pleasure. Numbers grew from four to eight and now commonly reach thirty to forty per shire. A subset (the “Quorum”) must be present for certain acts. At quarter sessions (four times yearly) they inquire into felonies, riots, vagabonds, and misdemeanors. Each year or alternate year the Privy Council sends articles from penal laws to the Justices for local enforcement — a mechanism Smith praises as “the most benefitte that can be devised for the common wealth of Englande,” if honestly executed.
Chapter 20 — Of hue and cry. Every Englishman has a duty to join the hue and cry when theft or murder is reported. Constables raise the parish; the pursuit goes from parish to parish by chain. The parish that fails to pursue pays the victim’s damages to the king as a fine. Suspects are bound by recognizance to appear at the gaol delivery; witnesses are similarly bound to give evidence.
Chapter 21 — Of the coroner. If any person dies violently and the murderer is unknown, the body may not be buried before the coroner views it. The coroner — a gentleman learned in law — empanels a jury from bystanders and inhabitants, who may range at large and return a verdict after twenty to thirty days as the evidence allows. The verdict is given openly in public, in the street. Smith argues the title derives from the Crown’s interest in every violent death of a subject — the Prince’s strength “doth stande and consist in the force of his people.”
Chapter 22 — Of constables. Originally custodes pacis with authority closer to that now held by Justices of Peace; today they are primarily the executors of the Justices’ commands. They may command the peace in affrays, pursue suspects, enter houses to search, and hold men in the stocks until a Justice examines them. Made at leet courts and called headboroughs or tithingmen in different localities, they are commonly artisans or labourers of limited education and authority.
Chapter 23 — Of sessions of gaole delivery and definitive criminal proceedings. Twice yearly — in Lent and summer vacation — the Prince commissions judges from Westminster Hall to circuit the shires and deliver the gaols. The full machinery of justice is assembled in each town: judges, Justices of the Peace, the sheriff with his under-sheriff, and five inquests of twenty-four yeomen each. Prisoners are called by name and arraigned. The arraignment formula is exact: “Thou art endicted of such a felonie… What sayest thou, art thou guiltie or not guiltie?” If the prisoner refuses to answer, he is judged “mute by contumacy” and condemned to peine forte et dure — pressed to death under stones and weights. Some strong men chose this death to preserve their heirs from the forfeiture of goods that a felony conviction would bring. If the prisoner pleads not guilty, the formula is “I will be tryed by God and the Countrie” — and the clerk replies that the twelve honest men present are his country. Evidence is given publicly; the judge summarises; the jury retires; the verdict — “guilty” or “not guilty” — is final.
Chapter 24 — Certain orders peculiar to England touching punishment. For felony, manslaughter, robbery, murder, and rape — hanging until dead. Nothing more: no heading, dismembering, breaking on the wheel, impaling, or other forms of bodily torture used on the continent. Judges cannot aggravate or mitigate punishment; only the Prince and Privy Council can, and they rarely do. Special cases: a wife who kills her husband is burned alive (petit treason); a servant who kills his master is drawn on a hurdle (petit treason); a poisoner is boiled (by Henry VIII’s act). Then Smith’s most quoted passage: “Torment or question which is used by the order of the civill lawe and custome of other countreis to put a malefactor to excessive paine, to make him confesse of him selfe, or of his felowes or complices, is not used in England, it is taken for servile.” The argument against torture is both moral and practical: a tormented man will confess to anything, even to having killed his own father; the twelve-man verdict is unaffected by confession; and “the nature of English men is to neglect death, to abide no torment.” An ancient law makes it a felony for a gaoler to torture a prisoner. England achieves “as few murthers committed as any where” without it.
Chapter 25 — Of treason and the trial of the higher nobility. Treason follows the same jury procedure as felony, but the punishment is worse: hanged, drawn down alive while still breathing, bowels removed and burned before the face, then beheaded and quartered, the parts set up in diverse places. A duke, marquess, or other baron of Parliament charged with treason is tried by his peers — the Lords of Parliament rather than a yeoman jury — each giving his vote separately, beginning from the youngest lord. A single Lord is appointed Constable of England for the day; at the end of judgment he breaks his staff of office and abdicates the role.

Book III — Of Appeals and Their Absence in England
Chapter 1 — Of what in other countries is called appeal or provocation. In England there is no appeal from a jury verdict of guilty or not guilty, unlike civil law countries where sentences may be challenged in higher courts. If the judges think the jury went against the evidence, the judge may “reprive” (remand) the prisoner and petition the Prince for a pardon — but no formal appeal mechanism exists. Smith presents this not as a deficiency but as a strength: the finality of the twelve-man verdict is precisely what gives it authority.

Significance for the 16th Century England Wiki
De Republica Anglorum is the single most important primary source for understanding how Elizabethan governance actually worked from the inside. It is valuable for:

Parliamentary sovereignty: Smith’s articulation of Parliament’s absolute authority — the source from which all later constitutional arguments derive
Social hierarchy: the division into four sorts, with precise income qualifications and the mechanics of social mobility through the gentry
The jury system: the only detailed contemporary description of how twelve-man verdicts were reached in both civil and criminal cases
Torture’s absence: Smith’s explicit prohibition and reasoned argument against it — a primary source for claims about English criminal justice’s distinctiveness
The Chancery’s role: how equity supplemented the common law’s rigidity
Justices of the Peace: the mechanism by which the Privy Council’s commands were executed across the shires
The constitution as mixed: Smith’s synthesis of monarchy, aristocracy, and democracy in England’s actual institutions

sources/dramatic-publication-england.title: Albright — Dramatic Publication in England, 1580–1640
sources/dramatic-publication-england.content:
Evelyn May Albright, Dramatic Publication in England, 1580–1640: A Study of Conditions Affecting Content and Form of Drama. Modern Language Association of America Monograph Series. D. C. Heath / Oxford University Press, 1927. ~1.1 MB extracted from zip (per-page OCR, 462 pages). University of Michigan library copy digitised via Internet Archive.
A scholarly study of the institutional, legal, and commercial conditions governing both performance and print publication of plays in the late Elizabethan and Jacobean periods. “Publication” is used in its technical sense to include both public performance and printed sale. Covers a range of companies, not only Shakespeare’s, and draws heavily on Henslowe’s Diary, Stationers’ Registers, Privy Council records, State Papers, and Herbert’s office-book. The study originated in a 1909 Shakespeare seminar at the University of Chicago under Professor Manly. ^[source: dramatic_publication_england_raw.txt]
Quality Assessment
Per-page OCR from an Internet Archive scan (462 pages concatenated from the zip in page order). The main argumentative text of each chapter is readable. Typical OCR noise throughout: occasional misread characters, split words at line ends, library stamps overlapping text on some pages. Footnotes are densely packed and contain frequent extraction errors — individual footnote citations should be verified against the original rather than quoted directly from this file. Best used by keyword search (grep -n) rather than raw line numbers. ^[source: dramatic_publication_england_raw.txt]

Contents and Coverage
Preface (lines 68–108)
Albright defines her scope: “publication” covers both public performance and printed book sale, treating them as two distinct but related acts of making a play available to an audience. The study addresses the legal, commercial, and institutional framework — not literary interpretation of the plays themselves. Method is archival: Privy Council records, Stationers’ Registers, Henslowe’s Diary, Herbert’s office-book, State Papers. ^[source: dramatic_publication_england_raw.txt]
Chapter I: Organisation and Control of Dramatic Companies (lines 474–2751)
Status of actors. Albright argues the popular equation of actors with rogues and vagabonds applies to strolling players, not to members of the London patent companies. The 1572 statute required players to be retainers of “a baron of this realm or other honourable personage of greater degree” — this gave licensed company members a defined legal status. Richard Burbage’s company applied to the Earl of Leicester for a license in terms of being his “household servants.” Five actors from the King’s Men (including Shakespeare) marched in James I’s coronation procession and each received 4½ yards of red cloth from the royal wardrobe. Fifteen players were gowned in black at James’s funeral. The 1604 statute (1 Jas. I, c.7) shifted formal legal responsibility away from the patron and onto the individual actor. ^[source: dramatic_publication_england_raw.txt]
Companies and licences. The 1578 Privy Council order approved companies: Children of the Chapel, the Lord Chamberlain’s, the Earl of Warwick’s, the Earl of Leicester’s, the Earl of Essex’s, and the Children of Paul’s — and specified that no others should play. By 1622 Herbert’s office-book lists only five principal adult companies licensed. Provincial companies maintained separate touring licences, and touring records document dozens of appearances across England from 1558 to 1642. ^[source: dramatic_publication_england_raw.txt]
Actor contracts and economics. From Henslowe’s Diary: Thomas Heywood bound himself exclusively to the Admiral’s Men for two years with a £40 penalty for playing elsewhere. Robert Dawes’s contract specified payment by shares in proceeds rather than a fixed fee. The economic structure divided proceeds between actor-sharers (who received half profits from galleries, boxes, and tiring-house receipts) and housekeepers (who owned the theatre building and received the other half). Housekeepers acquired their share by money payment and by “merit and antiquity.” ^[source: dramatic_publication_england_raw.txt]
Regulation: the Master of the Revels. Edmund Tilney served as Master of the Revels under Elizabeth; Herbert under James and Charles. By 1588 there were twelve licensers operating under Archbishop Whitgift’s authority. The Master of the Revels licensed plays for performance; the Lord Chamberlain stood between the companies and the Privy Council; the city of London’s Mayor had authority over performances within city boundaries. Companies in the liberties (Southwark, Shoreditch) were under Privy Council jurisdiction rather than the Mayor’s. In 1622, Herbert’s records show the theatres subject to closure when plague deaths exceeded a threshold (thirty per week under one patent, forty under later ones). ^[source: dramatic_publication_england_raw.txt]
Chapter II: Literary and Dramatic Censorship (lines 2752–8820)
Part I: Censorship of Literature in General (lines 2752–4200)
Albright traces censorship from the 1382 Act of Parliament targeting Wycliffe’s followers, through Archbishop Arundel’s controls on Oxford manuscripts, to the first controls on printed books under the early Tudor monarchs. Cardinal Wolsey enforced Leo X’s bull against Lutheran books in 1520. A prohibitory index was established in 1526; a royal proclamation issued 1538. Mary I’s commissioners in 1557 extended controls. ^[source: dramatic_publication_england_raw.txt]
The officers of censorship across the period were: bishops and archbishops (with authority to license books in theology and divinity), the Star Chamber (with authority to decree press regulations), and the Mayor of London (with authority over printing within city boundaries). In practice these jurisdictions overlapped and competed. Whitgift’s 1599 proclamation specified “noe playes be printed excepte they bee allowed.” The Star Chamber decrees of 1566 and 1586 were the principal instruments of general press regulation. ^[source: dramatic_publication_england_raw.txt]
William Prynne’s Histriomastix (1633) resulted in a £5,000 fine, public pillory, loss of both ears, and imprisonment. Albright compares England’s censorship regime with France and Spain and concludes England operated with more freedom than either. She documents the persistence of both publishers and readers in circulating condemned books: Thomas Woodcock was committed to Newgate in 1578 for renewed sale of An Admonition to the Parliament; Raleigh’s History of the World circulated without a title-page after James condemned it. Albright quotes Calvert writing to Winwood in 1605 that a suppressed book on the peace negotiations was “not to be had” but he would send one when he found it. ^[source: dramatic_publication_england_raw.txt]
Part II: Censorship of the Drama (lines 4200–8820)
Albright identifies eight categories of offence in the eyes of the dramatic censor: (1) religious controversy — favorable or unfavorable exploitation of any creed or denomination; (2) sacrilege, and after 1606 use of oaths containing the name of Christ or God or obvious substitutes; (3) realistic portrayal of living kings, especially their weaknesses, vices, or policies; (4) satirical or hostile portrayal of foreign kings or high officials; (5) discussion of foreign politics or international relations; (6) cartooning of real persons of any rank, especially noblemen; (7) seditious sentiments or discussion of facts likely to produce popular discontent or desire for change of government; (8) excessive indecency. ^[source: dramatic_publication_england_raw.txt]
Religious discussion. Elizabeth gave an order before April 1559 prohibiting plays in derision of the Catholic religion, the mass, the saints, or God. A further proclamation of May 16, 1559 categorically forbade political and religious problems on stage, charging mayors and justices to permit no play “wherein either matters of religion or of the governance of the estate of the common weall shalbe handled or treated.” ^[source: dramatic_publication_england_raw.txt]
Anti-Catholic portrayals ran throughout both reigns regardless of this prohibition. Bishop Gardiner had appeared as the type of the Catholic intriguer even in plays under Mary. Venetian and Spanish diplomatic correspondence documents protests about the English stage’s treatment of Catholicism. In 1618 Busino reported that “never represent any theatrical piece, not even satirical tragicomedy without larding it with the vices and iniquity of some Catholic churchman.” The Fortune players were fined £1,000 in 1639 for setting up an altar with basin and candlesticks on stage and bowing before it; they claimed it was an old play revived for a heathen gods scene. ^[source: dramatic_publication_england_raw.txt]
Puritans were ridiculed on stage throughout the period by Jonson, Marston, Middleton, and others. In the Martin Marprelate controversy (1589), the Martinists were satirized in plays by the Queen’s Men and Paul’s Boys. The Privy Council ordered a temporary suppression of all plays in London (November 8, 1589); Lord Strange’s Men refused to comply and two of their members were sent to the Counter. ^[source: dramatic_publication_england_raw.txt]
Treatment of contemporary matters: specific cases. Albright documents several named cases: ^[source: dramatic_publication_england_raw.txt]


Richard II (Shakespeare): the deposition scene was reportedly suppressed or omitted during Elizabeth’s reign. The Essex faction commissioned a performance of an old play about Richard II on February 7, 1601, the day before the Essex rising. One player objected “the play was olde and they should have losse in playing it because fewe would come” but it was staged for £2 extra payment.


A Game at Chess (Middleton, 1624): depicted Philip IV of Spain and Count Gondomar allegorically in a chess game. Ran nine days before suppression. Albright documents it as the clearest case of systematic attack on a foreign king and his ambassador passing the censor.


The Isle of Dogs (Nashe/Jonson, 1597): caused the Privy Council to suppress all plays in London for the summer and to order demolition of The Curtain and The Theatre.


Eastward Ho (Chapman/Jonson/Marston, 1605): Chapman and Jonson imprisoned for passages mocking the Scottish at James I’s court.


Sir Thomas More (manuscript, Harley 7368): the manuscript shows Tilney’s censorship marks throughout; Tilney struck the riot scenes dealing with immigrants (“Ill May Day” scenes) and required their replacement. Albright’s account of the manuscript is that it was too sensitive for the stage in its submitted form.


Massinger’s plays: several referenced as suppressed or censored for criticism of royal policies; The Roman Actor (1626) includes a defence of free speech on the stage.


Chapter III: Authorship and Ownership of Plays (lines 8821–11458)
Albright opens by noting Sidney Lee’s estimate that only 600 of approximately 3,000 plays acted in the period reached print. She then documents the conditions of dramatic authorship that governed whether plays were published at all. ^[source: dramatic_publication_england_raw.txt]
Authorship as hack-work and revision. Playwrights routinely appropriated plots and whole lines from earlier plays. Henslowe’s Diary documents regular payments for “altering and mending of old plays,” for additions, prologues, and epilogues. Albright cites Davenport’s King John and Matilda as expanded from an earlier play; Shakespeare’s remodelling of old plays as common practice among best writers, not just second-rate ones. ^[source: dramatic_publication_england_raw.txt]
Company ownership. Once a playwright sold a play to a company it became company property; the playwright had no residual rights. Albright documents the legal mechanics of play ownership through an extended quotation from Richard Jones’s agreement of January 3, 1589 with Edward Alleyn, selling Jones’s share in “playing apparalles, play bookes, instrumentes, and other commodities” for £37 10s. The plays were specified property transferred in “playne and open market.” Alleyn is shown as a key broker in play transfers between companies: he sold I. Tamar Cam to the Admiral’s Men for £2 on October 2, 1602. ^[source: dramatic_publication_england_raw.txt]
“Staying” of entries. In 1600, the Chamberlain’s Men had four plays — As You Like It, Henry V, Every Man in His Humor, and Much Ado About Nothing — entered as “to be staied” on the Stationers’ Registers. Albright interprets this as the company reserving copyright by having a chosen publisher register the rights, rather than as suppression of publication. She documents what she identifies as a wave of piracy or threatened piracy around 1600, naming unscrupulous stationers Pavier, Danter, Ferbrand, and Ling as handling suspect texts at this period. ^[source: dramatic_publication_england_raw.txt]
Chapter IV: Conditions Affecting the Time of Publication (lines 11459–12668)
Albright examines the claim that theatrical companies systematically withheld plays from print to protect stage receipts. She finds the evidence mixed. ^[source: dramatic_publication_england_raw.txt]
Evidence for withholding: Heywood stated certain actors thought publication against their peculiar interest. The Whitefriars contract explicitly prohibited one play (“Torrismont”) from being put into print before a term expired. The possibility that reading a play in advance might dull audience interest is noted as a contemporary belief. ^[source: dramatic_publication_england_raw.txt]
Evidence against systematic withholding: Many plays were published while actively being staged. Shirley’s The Royal Master was entered on the Stationers’ Registers March 13, 1638, published the same year, and an acting licence was taken out after the print entry. Court revivals show old plays were regularly preferred; the prologue to The Lover’s Progress (Beaumont and Fletcher) claims the status of a new play for a revision. John Chamberlain wrote in 1614 that “of five new plays there is not one that pleases; and therefore they are driven to furbish over their old.” ^[source: dramatic_publication_england_raw.txt]
Albright provides a decade-by-decade count of plays published (1580–1640) and a plague year table cross-referencing theater closures with publication numbers. Her conclusion is that no simple correlation exists between plague years or Puritan suppression and publication surges. For 1600 specifically — fifteen plays published, eleven from the Admiral’s and Chamberlain’s Men — she attributes the cluster to a bad outlook for stage receipts following the Privy Council’s restriction order and the illness of the Chamberlain, George Carey, rather than to piracy or compulsion. She identifies Henry V Q1 as a text that “can hardly be regarded as a legitimate text on any explanation of its defects.” ^[source: dramatic_publication_england_raw.txt]
Chapter V: Sources of Play Texts Printed (lines 12669–13885)
Albright surveys contemporary and modern theories about how play texts reached the printer. She opens by noting the persistence of the assumption (citing Pope’s dismissal of quartos as “whole heaps of trash”) that early printed play texts are necessarily defective and illegitimate. She contrasts this with Pollard’s discriminating work in Shakespeare Folios and Quartos and Shakespeare’s Fight with the Pirates. Pollard’s conclusion: the players handed printers authorised texts of fourteen Shakespeare plays for quarto publication, three of them improved versions for re-issue. Pollard’s “bad quartos” are Romeo and Juliet Q1, Henry V Q1, Merry Wives Q1, and Hamlet Q1. ^[source: dramatic_publication_england_raw.txt]
Indicators of legitimacy and their limits. Markers of an authorised text include: author’s dedication or preface, actor’s dedication or preface, entry in Stationers’ Registers, publisher’s note of source. Albright documents that none of these markers is conclusive by itself and that absence of entry does not prove piracy. ^[source: dramatic_publication_england_raw.txt]
Sources of copy: author’s own manuscript; scriveners’ copies; actors’ individual roles; borrowed manuscripts; private transcripts; prompt-books. ^[source: dramatic_publication_england_raw.txt]
Piracy by stenography. Albright treats the shorthand-reporter theory with scepticism. She acknowledges shorthand textbooks were available and that one non-dramatic writer (noted at line ~3740 of the raw file) was said to have taken down sermons by shorthand. But she argues no reliable evidence proves this was done systematically with plays. ^[source: dramatic_publication_england_raw.txt]
Memorial reconstruction. An actor who had played a role could reconstruct the text from memory, with his own part as the anchor. Albright examines Greg’s theory that the Merry Wives Q1 was pirated by the actor playing the Host, arguing the Host’s speeches in Q1 and Folio are inconsistent in ways that cut against Greg’s theory. She documents how an actor-pirate’s version would tend to be accurate in his own speeches and defective in others’. ^[source: dramatic_publication_england_raw.txt]
Prompt-books. The bookkeeper’s working manuscript differed from the author’s foul papers: prompt-books contain actors’ names, stage directions added during rehearsal, bookkeeper’s notes and annotations. Albright notes that a play printed from prompt-book copy and a play printed from author’s manuscript will differ in ways unrelated to textual corruption. ^[source: dramatic_publication_england_raw.txt]
Chapter VI: Printing and Publishing Conditions (lines 13886–17245)
Typography and the monopoly system. The common contemporary criticism was that typography declined after 1560. Albright quotes Plomer attributing this to the monopoly system, which placed profitable printing work in the hands of half a dozen men; drama fell outside the class of privileged works and was handled by smaller printers competing for unprofitable jobs. She documents that Star Chamber decrees of 1566 and 1586 regulated press conditions. Albright tests Plomer’s argument by examining individual printers’ records and finds the relationship between monopoly exclusion and print quality more complicated than the broad assertion suggests. ^[source: dramatic_publication_england_raw.txt]
The Stationers’ Company. Entry on the Stationers’ Registers functioned as a form of copyright claim, not as a printing licence. The two were distinct: a book could be licensed for printing but not entered, and vice versa. The Company enforced fines for printing without entry or in violation of another member’s copyright. Albright documents specific Stationers’ actions: members’ shops nailed up, fines levied, books called in. The Company also assisted in censorship enforcement by collecting and burning condemned titles — she gives the example of the 1599 “bishops’ ban” requiring the Stationers to collect and burn several named works. ^[source: dramatic_publication_england_raw.txt]
Printers and publishers specialising in drama. Albright names Charlewood, Creede, Eld, Allde, and others as printers whose output was concentrated in play quartos. She documents the flow of plays between publishers by tracing individual titles through their entry and transfer records on the Registers. The Widow Brome is identified as publishing four Lyly plays in 1591–92 following the dissolution of the Children of Paul’s, suggesting plays entered the print market when companies dissolved or were suppressed. ^[source: dramatic_publication_england_raw.txt]
Print economics. Play quartos were cheap books. Albright discusses the low returns to publishers from play printing, the typical print runs, and the distribution of plays through bookstalls and at the theatres themselves. She notes the paradox that publishers had little financial incentive to pirate plays, which cuts against some memorial-reconstruction theories that assume aggressive publisher demand. ^[source: dramatic_publication_england_raw.txt]

sources/foxe-acts-monuments.content:
John Foxe, The Acts and Monuments — Foxe’s Book of Martyrs. Eight OCR text files in this knowledge base, drawn from Victorian editions of Foxe’s work (Pratt / Townsend / Seeley imprints). Copied from the printing-press knowledge base.
Foxe (1516–1587) published in English in 1563; the first edition was printed by John Day, dwelling over Aldersgate, beneath St. Martin’s (described in the Life of Foxe in foxe-acts-monuments-vol1-townsend.txt). The same volume carries Foxe’s dedications to Queen Elizabeth (1563 and 1570), prefaces To the Persecutors of God’s Truth, To the True and Faithful Congregation, and Townsend’s Life of the Martyrologist.

Contents by reign (Tudor England scope)
From the table-of-contents headings in the OCR files:

Henry VII — opens Book VI in vol3 (1485)
Henry VIII — Book VIII in vol3 and vol5-pratt (1511 through supremacy, Frith, Tracy, marriage to Anne Bullen, persecutions under Stokesley and later bishops)
Edward VI — Book IX in vol6 (1547–1552): Latin service abolished, altars taken down, Ridley’s table letter, Gardiner’s trial sessions, Somerset
Mary I — Books X–XII in vol6, vol7, vol4: religion altered, Jane Grey, Bonner’s monitions, Oxford disputations, burnings from 1555 through 1558, Cranmer’s process, Bucer/Phagius at Cambridge (1557), commission of Philip and Mary
Elizabeth — dedications and closing material in vol1-townsend; accession narrative at end of Marian books in vol4

Pre-Tudor material (early church through Lollards) occupies vol1-townsend, vol2, and much of vol3-1841 — useful for background, not the primary Tudor mining set.

Hub for lesser Marian names
Pages for individual minor martyrs are not planned. Names that appear only in Foxe’s regional lists belong on the concept page marian-persecutions (Phase 1), grouped by diocese or year.
Star martyrs with dedicated entity/event pages: Latimer, Ridley, Cranmer, Rogers, Hooper, Bradford, Philpot, Askew, Frith, Tyndale, and related events (see tracker).

sources/hazlitt-livery-companies.content:
W. Carew Hazlitt, The Livery Companies of the City of London: Their Origin, Character, Development, and Social and Political Importance. London: Swan Sonnenschein & Co. / New York: Macmillan & Co., 1892. ~31,305 lines extracted from a zip of 724 OCR’d page files. Pennsylvania State University Libraries copy.
A comprehensive survey of all the London livery companies, written by Hazlitt of the Inner Temple in response to the Royal Commission on Livery Companies whose oral inquiry sat in 1882–83. Covers approximately seventy companies in individual chapters, preceded by a long Preface and General Introduction on the gild system from its medieval origins. Each company chapter typically includes: history and charter; governance (Master, Wardens, Court of Assistants, Livery, Yeomanry); finances and property; hall history; notable members; and Literary Notices — a bibliography of company-specific publications and documents. Hazlitt draws on the 1882 Return (companies’ replies to the Commission), Rivington’s Company records, and published company histories. ^[source: hazlitt_livery_companies_raw.txt]
Quality Assessment
OCR from the Pennsylvania State University Libraries copy of the 1892 first edition. Prose text is generally readable. Each company chapter’s running head (e.g. “THE MINOR COMPANIES.”, “THE GREAT COMPANIES.”, “THE STATIONERS.”) repeats on every page and appears as a repeated line in the OCR. Illustrative plates — arms, common seals, printer’s devices, hall views, monograms, autographs — produce garbled OCR character strings between text passages but are identifiable as image noise.
