sources/hume-history-tudor-vol1.title: Hume — The History of England Under the House of Tudor, Vol. I
sources/hume-history-tudor-vol1.content:
David Hume, The History of England Under the House of Tudor, Vol. I. First published A. Millar, London, 1759. Digital edition: Oxford Text Archive, 2011. ~9.7 MB extracted from mobi via HTML. Covers Henry VII (1485–1509), Henry VIII (1509–1547), Edward VI (1547–1553), and Mary I (1553–1558).
Hume’s 18th-century narrative history of the Tudor dynasty’s first three reigns and the Marian restoration. The analysis is consistently Enlightenment in temper: religious zeal is always traced to self-interest or passion; rulers are judged by “prudence,” “enlarged views,” and “wisdom”; constitutional liberty is the implicit standard against which power is measured. Hume wrote against the partisan Whig and Tory historiographies of the previous century, and his Tudor volumes show this corrective ambition — he is sympathetic to neither Catholic nor Protestant bigotry, and sees both Henry VIII and Cranmer as figures of mixed capacity and rampant self-deception. ^[source: hume_history_tudor_vol1_raw.txt]
Quality Assessment
All sections are readable. The file was post-processed on 2026-05-07 to fix a mobi extraction artifact that had placed each word on its own line in the Edward VI and Mary sections. The paragraph-reconstruction algorithm joined those lines back into prose. ^[source: hume_history_tudor_vol1_raw.txt]



































ReignBody-text line range (original)Readable?NotesHenry VII218–3942YesClean prose; unaffected by artifactHenry VIII3943–23166YesClean prose; unaffected by artifactEdward VI23167+YesFixed: paragraphs reconstructed from one-word-per-lineMary Imid-file onwardYesFixed: paragraphs reconstructed from one-word-per-line
Line numbers in the fixed file are substantially different from the original (total now ~26,215 lines vs. ~79,793). Use keyword search (grep -n) rather than raw line numbers for navigation. ^[source: hume_history_tudor_vol1_raw.txt]
Additional artifacts throughout: footnote markers embedded as † ‡ * superscripts and reference numbers; OCR letter-substitutions shown as bullet characters (•); illegible passages rendered as 〈◊〉; and column-format page footnotes occasionally break into the body flow.
Contents and Coverage
Henry VII (3 Chapters; lines 218–3942)
Ch I — Accession and the problem of legitimacy (line 218)
Hume opens not with victory at Bosworth but with Henry’s dynastic predicament: his Lancastrian title is weak (derived through a legitimated but adulterous line), his right of conquest is invidious, and his claim through his wife Elizabeth of York would subordinate him to her. Hume argues Henry chose “present possession” — raw power solidified by survival — as his actual foundation, and that his lifelong antipathy to the Yorkist party was both a personal passion and a political mistake: by treating Yorkists as enemies he taught them to examine his title’s flaws and find them. Covers the marriage to Elizabeth of York, Lambert Simnel’s rebellion and the Battle of Stoke (1487), Perkin Warbeck’s first appearance, and the Duchess of Burgundy’s intrigues. ^[source: hume_history_tudor_vol1_raw.txt]
Ch II — Foreign affairs and Perkin Warbeck (line 1008)
European survey: Scotland under James III; Spain under Ferdinand and Isabella; the Low Countries under Maximilian; France under Charles VIII annexing Brittany. Hume analyses the shifting alliance logic of early Tudor diplomacy with characteristic attention to “interest” rather than honour or religion. The Perkin Warbeck imposture is treated as a serious diplomatic crisis, credible to European courts because Henry’s title was genuinely vulnerable. Trial and execution of Sir William Stanley for Warbeck complicity. ^[source: hume_history_tudor_vol1_raw.txt]
Ch III — Perkin’s end, Arthur, and Henry’s character (line 2180)
Perkin’s return from Scotland, the Cornish insurrection against taxation (Battle of Deptford Bridge), Perkin’s capture and execution, and the execution of the Earl of Warwick — the last legitimate Plantagenet — to clear the path for the Spanish match. Marriage of Prince Arthur to Katherine of Aragon; Arthur’s death; marriage of Princess Margaret to James IV of Scotland. Hume’s assessment of Henry VII: a king who accumulated immense treasure and maintained peace, but whose avarice and partisan spirit left him unloved and whose title never felt secure. His laws — Star Chamber, the uses statute, fiscal reform — are assessed as instruments of a centralising monarchy. ^[source: hume_history_tudor_vol1_raw.txt]
Henry VIII (7 Chapters; lines 3943–23166)
Ch I — The new reign and Wolsey’s rise (line 3943)
Henry VIII’s accession is greeted with widespread joy — the contrast with his father’s unloved final years is the chapter’s governing theme. Hume catalogues Henry’s gifts: handsome, learned, musical, athletic, apparently generous. Empson and Dudley are sacrificed to popular anger (Hume gives Empson’s defence of strict law-enforcement considerable weight). Wolsey emerges as the king’s minister through his willingness to accommodate Henry’s desire for pleasure and magnificence; Surrey does the same. The dissipation of Henry VII’s treasures begins at once. Battle of Flodden (1513) and its Scottish context. ^[source: hume_history_tudor_vol1_raw.txt]
Ch II — Wolsey’s administration and the Field of Cloth of Gold (line 5578)
Wolsey’s foreign policy in the context of the Habsburg-Valois struggle: the League of Cambrai, the Battle of Pavia (1525) and the captivity of Francis I, the Sack of Rome (1527) by imperial forces. Field of the Cloth of Gold (1520). Henry’s early opposition to Luther: he writes the Assertio Septem Sacramentorum, earns the title “Defender of the Faith.” Hume is sardonic about the theological pretensions of a king who would soon repudiate Rome. The divorce question begins to form in the background. ^[source: hume_history_tudor_vol1_raw.txt]
Ch III — Digression on the Ecclesiastical State (line 6784)
Hume suspends the narrative to argue that established churches are socially useful precisely because they bribe the clergy into indolence: competitive, market-driven religion produces enthusiasm, superstition, and faction, while an endowed establishment produces torpor — which is safer for the civil order. The Church of Rome failed on this logic by making the clergy too powerful, too wealthy, and answerable to a foreign potentate whose interests diverged from the nation’s. Protestantism failed in the opposite direction by releasing private judgment, which encourages the very enthusiasm that makes men ungovernable. ^[source: hume_history_tudor_vol1_raw.txt]
Ch IV — The Divorce and the Break with Rome (line 8860)
Detailed account of Henry’s divorce campaign: Katherine’s age and infirmities, the Leviticus argument (Hume notes drily that Henry “being so great a casuist and a divine, proceeded to examine the question by his own learning”), the papal politics complicated by Katherine’s nephew the Emperor Charles V, Wolsey’s manipulation of the question for his own ends, and Anne Boleyn’s role. Wolsey’s fall (1529) is traced to his failure to secure the divorce. Cranmer is appointed Archbishop. Parliament of 1529 begins the legislative Reformation. The Act of Supremacy (1534) is treated as a political rather than theological event. ^[source: hume_history_tudor_vol1_raw.txt]
Ch V — The Reformation’s human cost (line 10944)
Extended analysis of why people converted: not theological conviction but the pleasure of opposing authority, the fervor of new preachers, and resentment of clerical extortion. Henry’s religious position is anatomised: he hated Lutheran doctrine because Luther had insulted him personally, and he made the real presence a point of honour. The executions of John Fisher and Thomas More are given substantial treatment; Hume is respectful of both men’s integrity while criticising their inflexibility. The dissolution of the monasteries is assessed as economically and morally complex — monasteries were corrupt but also poor relief. Anne Boleyn’s fall (1536): Hume treats the charges of adultery with cautious scepticism. Birth of Edward; death of Jane Seymour. The Pilgrimage of Grace is mentioned but not developed at length. ^[source: hume_history_tudor_vol1_raw.txt]
Ch VI — The Six Articles and the fall of Cromwell (line 13693)
The Act of Six Articles (1539) — Hume reads it as Henry asserting his personal orthodoxy on the real presence against both Lutherans and Catholics. Lambert’s disputation with the king. Anne of Cleves: the marriage arranged by Cromwell, Henry’s disgust on meeting her, and the rapid fall of Cromwell. Hume’s assessment of Cromwell is notably hostile: he is an “artful and dextrous” minister but one who manipulated the king’s passions and enriched himself through the dissolution. The execution of Cromwell is presented as judicially corrupt but historically intelligible. Catherine Howard’s story and fall. ^[source: hume_history_tudor_vol1_raw.txt]
Ch VII — Scotland, France, and Henry’s death (line 15351)
Henry’s war with Scotland: the Battle of Solway Moss (1542), James V’s death (“The crown came with a woman, and it will go with one”), and the birth of Mary Queen of Scots. Hume quotes James’s dying words in full. War with France; the campaign that takes Boulogne. Execution of the Earl of Surrey for heraldic presumption. Henry’s final illness and death. Hume’s full character assessment: immense ability, brutal tyranny, theological vanity, but also the political genius that broke the power of the papacy and the nobility simultaneously. He sees Henry as the decisive figure in England’s transition from medieval to modern governance. ^[source: hume_history_tudor_vol1_raw.txt]
Edward VI (2 Chapters) — Readable after fix
Body text fully reconstructed from one-word-per-line artifact. Use grep -n for navigation. ^[source: hume_history_tudor_vol1_raw.txt]
Ch I: Somerset as Protector — Hume opens the reign by noting the paradox that Henry’s will, designed to prevent any single minister seizing control, was immediately circumvented. The executors voted to name a Protector, and Somerset (Seymour) took the role. Gardiner’s principled resistance to the new homilies and to the dissolution of chantries is given extended treatment — Hume is sympathetic to Gardiner’s argument that wholesale religious change required parliamentary authority. The assassination of Cardinal Beaton in Scotland is treated as a consequence of his brutality toward reformers (George Wishart burned). Battle of Pinkie (1547): English victory over a larger Scottish force, won by combined artillery and cavalry. The young Mary Queen of Scots is sent to France for safety. Thomas Seymour’s intrigues against his brother Somerset — Hume’s account of how Seymour cultivated the young Edward VI and sought to outmanoeuvre the Protector — ends with Seymour’s attainder and execution, Somerset acquiescing in his brother’s death.
Ch II: Kett’s Rebellion (1549) — the agrarian rising in Norfolk, driven by enclosures and the collapse of the old manorial order. Hume takes Kett’s rebels seriously as a social phenomenon rather than mere disorder. Fall of Somerset: the council turns against the Protector after the double crisis of Kett’s rising and the western Prayer Book rebellion; Northumberland (Warwick) replaces him. Lady Jane Grey and the succession manoeuvre: Hume analyses the legal fragility of the device altering the succession and why it collapsed the moment Mary appeared in public as queen. Death of Edward VI and the brief nine-day reign of Jane. ^[source: hume_history_tudor_vol1_raw.txt]
Mary I (2 Chapters) — Readable after fix
^[source: hume_history_tudor_vol1_raw.txt]
Ch I: Northumberland’s failure and Mary’s accession — the speed with which the political class deserted Lady Jane Grey once Mary raised her standard in Suffolk. Hume’s account of Northumberland’s arrest and recantation to Rome is notably sardonic (“Whether that such were his real sentiments, which he had formerly concealed, could not easily be determined”). Catholic restoration: Gardiner returned as chancellor; Bonner restored to London; the Edwardian bishops displaced. Marriage negotiations with Philip II of Spain and the parliamentary resistance. Wyatt’s Rebellion (1554): the Kentish rising against the Spanish match; Hume treats Wyatt as a genuine patriot rather than a dynastic schemer. Execution of Lady Jane Grey, whom Hume regards as an innocent casualty of others’ ambition.
Ch II: Hume’s philosophical digression on religious toleration. He argues toleration is a social policy question, not a theological one, and that persecution achieves nothing except creating martyrs, whose deaths convince more people than any preaching. The Marian burnings (Latimer, Ridley, Cranmer) are treated in this frame: Hume is horrified but analytical. Cranmer’s recantation and then his final withdrawal of it at the stake (“he stretched out his right hand into the flame, and held it there with a steady resolution”) is given full dramatic weight. War with France and the loss of Calais (1558). Death of Mary: Hume’s closing assessment is the harshest in the volume — she is judged to have accomplished nothing except making Catholicism synonymous with foreign domination and religious violence. ^[source: hume_history_tudor_vol1_raw.txt]

sources/hume-history-tudor-vol2.title: Hume — The History of England Under the House of Tudor, Vol. II
sources/hume-history-tudor-vol2.content:
David Hume, The History of England Under the House of Tudor, Vol. II. First published A. Millar, London, 1759. Digital edition: Oxford Text Archive, 2011. ~7.1 MB extracted from mobi via HTML. Covers the reign of Elizabeth I in full (1558–1603) across 7 chapters.
Hume’s Elizabeth is a figure of genuine greatness but also of vanity, dissimulation, and occasional meanness: a ruler whose prudence was extraordinary but whose womanhood (on Hume’s accounting) introduced irrationalities — jealousy of Mary, coquetry with suitors, the Essex infatuation — that a man would have suppressed. The volume covers Philip II’s character, the French Wars of Religion, the Dutch Revolt as Elizabeth experienced it, and the strategic logic of the Anglo-Spanish conflict. ^[source: hume_history_tudor_vol2_raw.txt]
Quality Assessment
Better than Vol. I overall, but deteriorates with chapter depth. The first three chapters (lines 125–~4530) are clean, readable prose. From Chapter IV onward the indentation from the mobi conversion deepens progressively, producing prose that is still readable but visually cluttered with leading spaces. No chapter suffers the one-word-per-line collapse that afflicts Vol. I’s Edward VI and Mary sections. Usable throughout, though quotation requires care with whitespace. ^[source: hume_history_tudor_vol2_raw.txt]
Same artifact types as Vol. I: † ‡ * footnote markers embedded in text; 〈◊〉 for illegible passages; some OCR letter-substitutions (•); occasional 〈1 page duplicate〉 markers where the scan doubled a page. ^[source: hume_history_tudor_vol2_raw.txt]













































ChapterLine rangeQualityCh I125–1923CleanCh II1924–4530CleanCh III4531–7061Readable (minor indentation)Ch IV7062–8716Readable (moderate indentation)Ch V8717–11164Readable (heavier indentation)Ch VI11165–12711Readable (heavy indentation)Ch VII12712–endReadable (heaviest indentation)
Contents and Coverage
Chapter I — The Elizabethan Settlement and Scotland (lines 125–1923)
The accession. Elizabeth enters London through cheering crowds; Hume describes her declining to fall on her knees in the Tower as another prisoner (a Marian one) had done, but instead giving thanks for her deliverance. She receives the Bible from a boy on a triumphal arch and presses it to her bosom — Hume calls this an “innocent artifice” and does not mean it disparagingly: Elizabeth’s management of public affection was a political art.
Philip II’s proposal is declined deftly. Hume gives Elizabeth’s reasoning in full: marrying Philip would confirm her illegitimacy (a parallel to her father’s marriage to Katherine), would place her on a “precarious” throne dependent on Spanish power, and would alienate the nation. She keeps Philip hoping anyway, which is treated as prudent dissimulation.
The religious settlement. Extended account of Cecil’s advice to Elizabeth on the political logic of restoring Protestantism: the pope cannot ratify her title without destroying his own authority; Philip and France can never combine against her; English Catholics will conform to their new sovereign as they have conformed to every previous one. Hume treats the Elizabethan settlement as a political calculation brilliantly executed, not a religious conviction. The Acts of Supremacy and Uniformity pass against an episcopate that refuses to cooperate — most bishops are deprived. ^[source: hume_history_tudor_vol2_raw.txt]
Scotland and the Reformation. John Knox, Mary of Guise (the regent), the Lords of the Congregation, French troops in Scotland, English intervention, and the Treaty of Edinburgh (1560). Hume’s Knox is a bigot of genius — indispensable to the Protestant cause, deeply hostile to monarchy, and personally insulting to every queen he encounters. Mary Queen of Scots arrives in Scotland: Hume introduces her as a figure of beauty, charm, and political naivety — not yet a threat, but surrounded by enemies.
Elizabeth’s government. Hume closes the chapter with a long appreciation: open in address, “rejoiced in the concourse of her subjects,” expert at managing Parliament and the people, and possessed of “masculine spirit.” He acknowledges the irony that the woman he called “masculine” ruled for 45 years more successfully than most kings. ^[source: hume_history_tudor_vol2_raw.txt]
Chapter II — Mary Queen of Scots and the French Wars (lines 1924–4530)
Philip II’s character. Opens with one of the finest portrait passages in the volume: Philip is “endowed with great industry and sagacity, a remarkable caution in his enterprizes, an unusual foresight in all his measures… ever cool and unmoved by passion.” But “prejudices had on him a more pernicious effect than ever passions had on any other monarch.” His vow after the tempest — to dedicate his life to extirpating heresy — is Hume’s pivot: an intelligent man converted by religion into an engine of destruction. The Elizabeth-Philip opposition is framed as the collection’s central geopolitical conflict: the more virtuous sovereign was “happily thrown into the more favourable cause.” ^[source: hume_history_tudor_vol2_raw.txt]
France. The French Wars of Religion as background: Catherine de’ Medici’s failed balancing act, the Huguenots and the Guises, English occupation of Havre de Grace (1562) and its humiliating loss, the Massacre of Vassy. Hume’s account of French religious violence is sustained and horrified: “in a nation renowned for polished manners” — the comparison with civilisation is always implicit.
Mary Queen of Scots: the catastrophe. Darnley, the most detailed sequence in the chapter: Rizzio’s murder (Mary’s Italian secretary, stabbed in her presence, Darnley a participant), Darnley’s own murder at Kirk o’Field (explosion; Hume treats Mary’s complicity as highly probable), Mary’s marriage to Bothwell within months, the Scottish nobles’ insurrection, Mary’s imprisonment at Lochleven, her escape into England. Hume’s assessment: Mary was not a plotter by nature but was used by others — Bothwell, the Guises, the seminary priests — and her passions (love, resentment, pride) consistently overrode her judgment. The conferences at York and Hampton Court: Elizabeth refuses to decide, keeps Mary in limbo — Hume calls this “a species of refined and complicated policy.” ^[source: hume_history_tudor_vol2_raw.txt]
Chapter III — Plots, the Duke of Norfolk, and St. Bartholomew’s (lines 4531–7061)
The Puritans. Hume opens with a character sketch of Puritanism: not a coherent theology but a disposition — opposition to ceremony, hostility to bishops, embrace of private judgment — that naturally tends to republicanism. He is more sympathetic to the Puritans as civic actors than as theologians, but hostile to their theocratic ambitions in Scotland under Knox.
The Duke of Norfolk’s conspiracy. Norfolk as Mary’s proposed husband: the “Ridolfi plot” is traced in detail, with Hume noting that Walsingham’s intelligence penetrated it thoroughly. Norfolk is executed (1572). Elizabeth’s reluctance to sign his death warrant: Hume sees this as neither sentiment nor policy but a kind of royal paralysis when confronted with the execution of a peer. The pattern will recur with Mary.
St. Bartholomew’s Massacre (1572). Among the most powerful passages in the volume — Hume’s account of the Paris murders is controlled fury: “that signal of massacre was given by the great bell of the palace; and Guise himself led on the perpetrators.” Catherine de’ Medici and Charles IX’s complicity. The scale of the killing across France. Hume draws the line between the Massacre and England’s accelerating anti-Catholic legislation: the seminary priests trained at Reims were responding to this as much as causing it.
The Low Countries. Don John, Parma, the Pacification of Ghent, Elizabeth’s agonised and reluctant support for the Dutch rebels: she hates the precedent of subjects resisting their sovereign, but cannot afford a Spanish-controlled Channel coast. ^[source: hume_history_tudor_vol2_raw.txt]
Chapter IV — Drake, the Anjou Courtship, and Escalation (lines 7062–8716)
Sir Francis Drake. Hume’s account of Drake’s circumnavigation and knighthood is compact and strategic — he is interested in the diplomatic fallout and what Drake’s success signals about the Anglo-Spanish balance, not the adventure narrative. “This man, sprung from mean parents in the county of Devon, having acquired considerable riches by some depredations on the Spaniards in the isthmus of Panama…” — Hume’s prose efficiently places Drake in the context of Elizabethan state piracy. Use alongside sir-francis-drake for the full account.
The Anjou courtship. Elizabeth genuinely considered marrying Anjou, Hume argues, and was half in earnest. Walsingham and the council opposed it; the people’s hostility alarmed her. The courtship dragged on, giving England diplomatic cover with France, until Anjou died in 1584. Hume sees the whole affair as Elizabeth at her most womanlike — not a compliment in his register.
The tightening net. Morton’s execution in Scotland; the young James VI under French influence; Spanish troops in Ireland under San Josepho (massacred by Lord Gray after surrender — Elizabeth expressed displeasure); the assassination of William of Orange (1584); the Bond of Association. Hume traces the escalating logic by which England moved from covert to open war with Spain. ^[source: hume_history_tudor_vol2_raw.txt]
Chapter V — Babington, Mary’s Execution, and the Armada (lines 8717–11164)
The Babington Plot. Detailed reconstruction: Ballard’s mission from Rheims, Savage’s assassination vow, Babington’s recruitment of a circle of Catholic gentlemen, their letter to Mary proposing assassination of Elizabeth and her liberation, Mary’s reply. Walsingham’s penetration of the correspondence via a mole in the beer-barrel delivery. The conspirators’ capture, trial, and executions (September 1586).
Mary’s trial. Hume’s extended analysis of the commissioners’ difficulty in persuading Mary to submit to trial: she refused to acknowledge the jurisdiction of a court that was trying a queen. She eventually appeared, made her defence, and was condemned. Hume weighs Elizabeth’s four months of indecision before signing the death warrant with characteristic balance: it was partly political calculation (would James retaliate?), partly genuine horror at the precedent, partly — he suggests — the women’s rivalry for legitimacy that had structured the entire reign.
Mary’s character assessment. Hume gives Mary one of his most sustained and ambivalent portraits: beauty, charm, courage, political intelligence — all real. But also recklessness, passion, the inability to sustain any consistent policy, and the fatal pattern of placing herself in the hands of men (Bothwell, the Guises, Babington’s circle) who used her. He is not the hostile Protestant Hume of legend; he is the Enlightenment historian who cannot forgive irrationality.
Drake at Cadiz (1587). “Singeing the king of Spain’s beard”: Hume places Drake’s Cádiz raid here as the prelude to the Armada, giving it military and psychological weight. Philip’s Armada plans; English preparations; Howard as Lord Admiral, Drake as vice-admiral.
The Armada (1588). Hume’s account is strategic and compressed: the fireships at Gravelines, the Spanish flight north around Scotland, the storms. He emphasises English discipline and Spanish tactical failures rather than providential deliverance (Hume never invokes Providence). The Portugal expedition (1589): its failure and Drake’s disgrace. ^[source: hume_history_tudor_vol2_raw.txt]
Chapter VI — France, Henry IV, and Essex Ascending (lines 11165–12711)
The assassination of the Duke of Guise (December 1588): Henry III has Guise killed in the Château de Blois; Hume calls it “cruel” but concedes “the necessity of it.” The friar Jacques Clément assassinates Henry III (1589) — Hume’s note on the century’s spirit of religious violence: “that bloody spirit of bigotry which distinguishes this century, and a great part of the following one, beyond all other ages of the world.”
Henry IV. The King of Navarre’s accession: the League under Mayenne, Philip’s ambitions to dismember France. Elizabeth’s subsidies to Henry: £22,000, “a larger sum than, as he declared, he had ever seen before.” The campaigns: Coutras, Ivry, the siege of Paris. Parma’s relief of Paris. Henry IV’s conversion to Catholicism (1593): “Paris is worth a mass.” Hume treats this pragmatically — a rational concession to political reality, not apostasy.
Essex ascending. Robert Devereux, Earl of Essex, appears here as Elizabeth’s new favourite — young, charismatic, militarily ambitious, politically reckless. Hume establishes the psychological dynamic early: Elizabeth indulged Essex where she would have contained other men. The pattern anticipates the catastrophe of Chapter VII. Naval enterprises: the Islands Voyage, the attack on Cádiz (1596 — a success that inflamed Essex’s ambitions). ^[source: hume_history_tudor_vol2_raw.txt]
Chapter VII — Ireland, Essex’s Fall, and Elizabeth’s Death (lines 12712–end)
Ireland. Hume opens with a long and remarkably harsh analysis of English colonial failure in Ireland: four centuries of nominal dominion maintained by insufficient force, laws that excluded the Irish from English protections, private conquest that produced a lawless settler class that “degenerated into mere Irish.” The argument is Enlightenment in structure — institutional analysis of why a colonial system produces the violence it claims to suppress. Tyrone’s rebellion (1593–1603) is the climax.
Essex in Ireland. Elizabeth sends Essex to Ireland with a large army and high expectations; he wastes it in marches, signs an unauthorised truce with Tyrone, and returns to England without leave. Hume’s account of Essex’s dash from Ireland, his unexpected appearance in Elizabeth’s bedchamber before she had dressed, and her controlled response — gracious on the day, punitive within weeks — is one of the volume’s most vivid scenes. Essex’s disgrace, his intrigues with James VI of Scotland, his insurrection (February 1601): a hundred horsemen in the streets of London who find no followers. His trial and execution. Hume is colder on Essex than most later historians: he sees a man of charm and military talent destroyed by self-dramatisation and an inability to calculate odds.
Mountjoy and Tyrone. Charles Blount, Lord Mountjoy, succeeds where Essex failed: systematic campaign, scorched-earth in Ulster, breaking Tyrone’s support. Spanish troops land at Kinsale (1601) and are defeated. Tyrone submits just days after Elizabeth’s death — she never knows the Irish war is won.
Elizabeth’s death and character. She declines into silence after Essex’s execution, refusing food, refusing to go to bed, sitting on cushions on the floor of her chamber for days. She dies on 24 March 1603.
Hume’s full character assessment occupies several pages and is the volume’s centrepiece. He catalogues her gifts at length: “masculine understanding,” prudent government, management of Parliament, use of talented ministers, the creation of a prosperous and confident England. He then qualifies systematically: vanity about her appearance and her suitors; excessive parsimony with money and with honours; jealousy of capable women (Mary Queen of Scots, her own ladies); indecision at crisis moments (Norfolk, Mary, Essex). His conclusion: “on the whole, she possessed the virtues of kings, with some of the weaknesses of women.” ^[source: hume_history_tudor_vol2_raw.txt]
The survey of arts, manners, commerce, and learning that closes the chapter covers the Elizabethan economy, overseas trade and the merchant companies, the state of the navy, printing and literacy, the Elizabethan literary flowering (Spenser, Sidney, Shakespeare mentioned by name), and the condition of the universities. ^[source: hume_history_tudor_vol2_raw.txt]

sources/nature-of-the-book-johns.title: nature-of-the-book-johns
sources/nature-of-the-book-johns.content:
The Nature of the Book: Print and Knowledge in the Making
Author: Adrian Johns
Publisher: University of Chicago Press, 1998 (paperback 2000)
Pages: xxi + 753
Source type: Secondary source (cultural history / history of the book)
Raw text: nature_of_the_book_raw.txt (OCR from image-based EPUB, ~379 KB)

Overview
Adrian Johns’s The Nature of the Book is a landmark revisionist work in the history of print culture. It directly challenges Elizabeth Eisenstein’s thesis (in The Printing Press as an Agent of Change) that the printing press brought inherent fixity, standardization, and credibility to texts. Johns argues instead that these qualities of print were not automatic products of the technology — they had to be socially constructed through a complex and contested process involving printers, authors, booksellers, readers, and the state.
The book focuses primarily on England from the late 16th through the early 18th centuries (roughly 1580–1720), making it centrally relevant to this wiki’s 16th-century England period. It traces how the “credibility” of printed knowledge was established through the practices of the Stationers’ Company, the politics of licensing, the physical construction of printing houses, and the social regulation of the book trade.
Johns uses the term “literatory life” (from the 17th-century spelling “literatory”) to describe the entire social world of print: the workshops, the trade networks, the negotiations between authors and stationers, and the cultural practices that made printed knowledge trustworthy (or not).

Contents























































ChapterTitleFocus1Introduction: The Book of Nature and the Nature of the BookSets out the argument against Eisenstein; introduces the social construction of print credibility2Literatory Life: The Culture and Credibility of the Printed Book in Early Modern LondonThe physical and social world of London’s printing houses; the Stationers’ Company; the practices of printing3”The Advancement of Wholesome Knowledge”: The Politics of Print and the Practices of ProprietyLicensing, censorship, and the politics of regulating the press in early modern England4John Streater and the Knights of the Galaxy: Republicanism, Natural Knowledge, and the Politics of PrintingA case study of John Streater, a republican printer, and the intersection of print and politics in the Interregnum5Faust and the Pirates: The Cultural Construction of the Printing RevolutionHow the idea of a “printing revolution” was itself constructed in the 17th century; piracy, authorship, and the myth of Gutenberg6The Physiology of Reading: Print and the PassionsEarly modern theories of how reading affected the body and mind; the physical and emotional experience of reading7Piracy and Usurpation: Natural Philosophy in the RestorationThe politics of knowledge in the Royal Society; print and the credibility of experimental philosophy8Histories of the Heavens: John Flamsteed, Isaac Newton, and the Historia Coelestis BritannicaA detailed case study of the publication of Flamsteed’s star catalogue and Newton’s Principia; the social politics of astronomical printing9ConclusionSummary of the argument and implications for understanding print culture

Key Themes and Arguments





































ThemeSummaryAgainst “fixity by technology”Print did not automatically fix texts; piracy, unauthorized editions, and textual corruption were rampant. Fixity was achieved through social institutions (the Stationers’ Company, the licensing system), not technologyThe “literatory life”The culture, practices, and social world of the printing house — a full ethnographic account of how books were actually made in early modern LondonCredibility as a social achievementFor knowledge to be trusted in print, the entire system of production had to be trusted. Printers and booksellers had to establish reputations for honestyPiracy and intellectual propertyPiracy was widespread; the concept of authorial property was contested throughout the period. Johns traces the emergence of proprietary authorshipPrint and the passionsEarly modern readers understood reading as a physiological process that affected the humors and passions — a dimension lost in modern histories of readingPolitics of natural knowledgeThe Royal Society’s claim to produce credible knowledge was intertwined with the politics of print; publishing scientific works was a political actThe Flamsteed-Newton caseA detailed narrative of the conflict over the publication of the Historia Coelestis Britannica, revealing the power dynamics of print in the Republic of Letters

Significance for the 16th Century England Wiki
The book’s first half (chapters 1–3) is directly about the Elizabethan and Jacobean print trade:

Chapter 2 — detailed account of London printing houses, the Stationers’ Company, and the daily practices of the book trade in the late 16th century
Chapter 3 — the political regulation of print: licensing, the Stationers’ Register, the Star Chamber decrees on printing (1586), and the Elizabethan state’s attempt to control the press
The book documents the material culture of printing: how presses were built, how type was cast, how pages were composed and proofread
It provides an alternative to the Eisenstein thesis, which is also covered in this wiki (see The Printing Press as an Agent of Change)


Relationship to Other Sources in This Wiki

































SourceRelationshipThe Printing Press as an Agent of Change (Eisenstein)Johns’s primary intellectual antagonist; directly challenges the “print revolution” thesisStationers’ Registers (Arber)Johns relies heavily on the Stationers’ Company records for his account of London print cultureTypographical Antiquities (Ames)Ames is one of the early historians of English printing whose work Johns discussesDramatic Publication in England (Albright)Both treat different aspects of the same print culture in Elizabethan/Jacobean LondonCopyright in Historical Perspective (Patterson)Patterson’s legal-historical account of copyright complements Johns’s social-historical accountHazlitt’s Livery CompaniesThe Stationers’ Company was one of the livery companies of London, placing Johns’s work in the broader context of City of London institutional history

Sources
Johns, Adrian. The Nature of the Book: Print and Knowledge in the Making. Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1998.

sources/printing-press-agent-of-change-e.title: printing-press-agent-of-change-eisenstein
sources/printing-press-agent-of-change-e.content:
The Printing Press as an Agent of Change: Communications and Cultural Transformations in Early Modern Europe
Author: Elizabeth L. Eisenstein
Edition: 1st paperback edition
Publisher: Cambridge University Press, 1980 (original hardcover 1979)
Pages: xxi + 794
Source type: Secondary source (historical synthesis)
Raw text: eisenstein_printing_press_raw.txt

Overview
Elizabeth Eisenstein’s The Printing Press as an Agent of Change is a landmark — and explicitly provisional — work in the history of communications. It argues that the invention of movable type in the mid-15th century constituted a “communications revolution” that fundamentally transformed early modern European society — reshaping religion, science, politics, and culture. Eisenstein is careful to frame this as a provisional argument: “I have not reached any final formulation but have merely become convinced that beyond this provisional resting point, diminishing returns will set in.”
Scope: Western Europe’s literate elites (primarily Latin-reading professionals — clergy, lawyers, physicians, humanist scholars). Eisenstein explicitly sets aside Eastern Europe, the Near East, and the New World. She also sets aside questions of mass literacy and popular culture — her argument is about what printing did to the circulation of knowledge among those who could already read Latin. This is important context: the source page is not a general argument about print and society, but a specific argument about print and elite knowledge culture.
What Eisenstein is NOT arguing: She is not a technological determinist. Her argument is that print enabled certain transformations, not that it caused them mechanically. Typographical choices were contingent and practical, and she explicitly rejects oversimplified claims about type-styles reflecting ideology.

Contents
Part I: Introduction to an Elusive Transformation (Chapters 1–3)
Chapter 1 — The Unacknowledged Revolution. Eisenstein’s opening argument is that printing’s consequences have been systematically underestimated precisely because they are so foundational: historians, who themselves work through printed texts, cannot easily observe what print transformed. While Francis Bacon and contemporaries recognised printing (alongside gunpowder and the compass) as one of the three most consequential inventions, academic historians have never given it the sustained analytical treatment it deserves. The chapter frames the central methodological problem: how do you reconstruct the mentality of scribal culture when all your evidence comes through print?
Chapter 2 — Defining the Initial Shift. The core contrast between scribal and print cultures. Eisenstein offers a concrete measure of scale: a person born in 1453 would, by age fifty, have witnessed the production of approximately 8 million printed books — more than all European scribes had produced in the preceding millennium. She identifies six features that distinguished print culture from manuscript culture: dissemination (multiplication of identical copies); standardization (each copy the same, enabling comparison and correction across distance); reorganization (title pages, indexes, running headers, footnotes — new navigational apparatus that changed how texts were used); data collection (tables, charts, and illustrated material could be accumulated and compared); preservation (texts fixed against the corruptions of successive copying); and amplification (cumulative cross-referencing across works). Master printers emerged as cultural impresarios bridging the university and the commercial world.
Chapter 3 — Some Features of Print Culture. A sustained development of the “standardization” theme. Eisenstein argues that the shift from oral-mnemonic learning (where knowledge was transmitted through verse and recitation) to reading-based learning was a genuine cognitive transformation, not merely a change in medium. Print created what she calls a “fixity” of texts — the same text simultaneously present in identical form across Europe — that manuscript culture structurally could not achieve. This fixity is what made the Reformation irreversible where earlier reform movements had been suppressible: once Luther’s ideas were in print, no bishop could confiscate every copy.

Part II: Classical and Christian Traditions Reoriented (Chapters 4–5)
Chapter 4 — The Renaissance Recapitulated. The Renaissance underwent two distinct phases. The first (early quattrocento Italy) was a fragile, geographically limited revival of classical learning, dependent on scarce manuscripts and personal networks of scholars. The second (post-1470, north of the Alps) was a permanent international transformation enabled by print. Eisenstein contrasts Petrarch’s revival — inherently transient, dependent on manuscript availability and living teachers — with the post-Aldine spread of humanism that reached Northern Europe through printed grammars, dictionaries, and editions. Greek studies, apparently threatened by Constantinople’s fall in 1453, actually flourished because printed grammars liberated Northern scholars from dependence on émigré teachers.
Chapter 5 — The Permanent Renaissance. Printing transformed a localized, fragile revival into a durable, expansive movement. The chapter’s four subdivisions trace specific mechanisms: The Recovery of Antiquity — print “permanently secured” classical texts that medieval scribes had preserved but could not stabilize; Eisenstein is insistent that humanists did not “discover” classical texts but made them permanently available in a way manuscript culture could not. The Great Book of Nature — the transition from text-based to observation-based learning. The Renaissance in the North — how printed editions carried Italian humanism north without the need for personal transmission. The Shift from Copying to Editing — scribal culture’s task was faithful reproduction; print culture’s task became critical collation, comparison, and emendation. The scholar who collated multiple manuscripts to establish a correct text was doing something that had no scribal equivalent.

Part III: The Book of Nature Transformed (Chapters 6–9)
Chapter 6 (introduction) and Chapter 7 — Technical Literature Goes to Press. Printing transformed natural philosophy by making technical literature — mathematical tables, anatomical illustrations, surveying manuals, engineering drawings — widely available and systematically comparable. Eisenstein’s central example is Vesalius’s De Fabrica (1543): a collaboration between anatomist, artist, and printer that produced exactly repeatable pictorial statements linked to textual commentary — something structurally impossible in manuscript culture, where every illustration diverged from its original in copying. Technical manuals on mining, fortification, and surgery emerged as new genres, elevating mechanical arts by giving them print authority. Artisan-authors (Agricola, Paré, Palissy) achieved eponymous fame and influenced learned élites by using print to cross the gap between workshop knowledge and university learning.
Chapter 8 — Expanding the Community of Science. Print created a “community of science” — scholars in different cities and countries who could compare observations against identical reference texts. Before print, two astronomers in different cities had no reliable way to compare their tables; after print, they worked from identical editions of Ptolemy and could identify divergences precisely. Eisenstein argues this cumulative comparability was the structural precondition for the Copernican revolution: Copernicus could identify the accumulated errors in the Ptolemaic tables because he had access to multiple editions of the same original. The “data-processing” capacity of print — its ability to accumulate, compare, and cross-reference observations across time and space — was the foundation of empirical science, not any individual act of observation.
Chapter 9 — The Book of Nature Transformed. A synthesis: the “book of nature” could not be read systematically until printing standardized the recording of observations, tables, and diagrams. Exact repeatability of pictorial and numerical data — not just words — enabled the development of experimental and observational procedures. Print also created a problem of authority: when dozens of printed editions of Galen or Ptolemy existed, which was correct? The pressure to collate and correct drove the development of critical editing, which in turn undermined the authority of the ancients and prepared the way for Bacon’s programme of new observation.

Part IV: The Scripture Revised (Chapters 10–12)
Chapter 10 (introduction) and Chapter 11 — The Eucharistic Controversy. Printing created the conditions for the Reformation in two ways. First, it distributed biblical texts widely in vernacular translations, making scripture accessible to lay readers and creating “book religion” — Protestant bibliolatry and Catholic devotional literature both depend on print. Second, it standardized the text of scripture in a way that made doctrinal precision both possible and explosive: once the same text was in everyone’s hands, disagreements about its meaning became public controversies rather than internal clerical disputes. The eucharistic controversy — the debate over transubstantiation that divided Lutherans from Zwinglians and both from Catholics — was conducted through printed tracts at a speed and scale that manuscript controversy could not have achieved. Printed indulgences preceded the Reformation crisis; printed polemics defined and spread it. The mass production of Bibles in vernaculars meant that “book religion” developed on both sides of the confessional divide.
Chapter 12 — Conclusion. Eisenstein resists a triumphalist conclusion. Print enabled the Reformation and the Scientific Revolution, but it also enabled Catholic Counter-Reformation propaganda, alchemical literature, and astrological almanacs. The press did not automatically produce truth or progress; it amplified whatever intellectual movements were already in motion. Her final argument is that printing is the necessary but not sufficient cause of the major transformations of early modernity: without it, the Reformation could not have mobilized mass populations; without it, the Scientific Revolution’s cumulative data-gathering was impossible; without it, the Renaissance revival of antiquity would have been as transient as earlier revivals. But print alone did not produce any of these things — it created the infrastructure within which human choices, conflicts, and accidents then unfolded.

Key Themes and Arguments









































ThemeSummaryThe “Unacknowledged Revolution”The printing press is arguably the most significant transformation in Western history, yet historians treat it as a footnote rather than a causeFixity and StandardizationPrint fixed texts in a way manuscript could not — enabling identical diagrams, maps, and biblical texts across distances. But this applied to elite Latin-literate culture primarily.”Securing” vs. “Discovering” antiquityHumanists did not discover classical texts — medieval scribes had preserved them. What print did was permanently secure them against the corruption that destroyed manuscripts. This is Eisenstein’s subtler claim about the RenaissanceReformation and PrintThe Protestant Reformation was the first movement to fully exploit the printing press for mass communication. Luther’s pamphlets and the 95 Theses spread through print networks that manuscript culture could not have replicated at that speedScientific RevolutionPrint enabled the standardization of scientific illustrations, maps, and data-tables; it created a cumulative “community of science” across EuropeThe Mapmaking RevolutionPrinting made possible accurate, repeatable maps — the same diagram could appear in every copy of a workEucharistic ControversyThe decision to print the Bible in vernacular languages, the translation debates, and the fixity of the printed liturgy all sharpened confessional divisionsMethodological cautionThe work stops roughly at Newton/Locke — the rise of learned journals and editorial offices replacing the master-printer as knowledge-gatekeeper

Significance for the 16th Century England Wiki
Eisenstein does not have sustained England-specific chapters — her argument is about Western Europe’s elite lettered culture. Use this source for:

The English Reformation framing: why Protestant reform spread so rapidly via print when earlier reform movements had not (the Lollards without print vs. the Lutherans with it)
Bible printing and standardization: the Great Bible (1539) placed in every parish church is a specific instance of Eisenstein’s “fixity” argument — an identical text distributed uniformly
Print and the Reformation’s irreversibility: once Protestant ideas were fixed in print and distributed across Europe, suppression became structurally harder than it had been for manuscript heresies
Contrast with Johns: Eisenstein argues print’s fixity was technologically produced; Johns argues it was socially constructed — both positions are relevant for understanding the Stationers’ Company and Tudor censorship

Do NOT use Eisenstein for claims specific to the Stationers’ Company, English printing patents, or Tudor censorship mechanisms — she does not discuss these in detail. Johns and Patterson are more directly useful for those topics.

Relationship to Other Sources in This Wiki





























SourceRelationshipThe Nature of the Book (Adrian Johns)Johns explicitly challenges Eisenstein’s thesis, arguing that print did not automatically confer fixity or credibility — these had to be socially constructed. The Eisenstein-Johns debate structures the entire historiography of the English print tradeCopyright in Historical Perspective (Patterson)Patterson’s legal-historical account of copyright uses the print-revolution framework but focuses on institutional and legal development, not cultural transformationTypographical Antiquities (Ames)A primary-source catalog of early English printing that provides some of the evidence base for Eisenstein’s claims about English printingStationers’ Registers (Arber)The institutional record of the English print trade — more relevant to Johns than to EisensteinDramatic Publication in England (Albright)Tests print-culture questions against the specific case of English play publication

Sources
Eisenstein, Elizabeth L. The Printing Press as an Agent of Change: Communications and Cultural Transformations in Early-Modern Europe. 1st paperback ed. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1980.

sources/raleigh-history-of-the-world-vol.content:
Sir Walter Ralegh (c.1552–1618), The History of the World. This file is Volume I of the 1736 London “Eleventh Edition” (“printed from a Copy revis’d by Himself”), with William Oldys’s life of the author, Ralegh’s 1603 trial, a full contents of all five books, Ralegh’s Preface, chronological-table matter, and the text of Book I only (Beginning and First Ages… from the Creation unto Abraham). ~58,316 lines / ~2.6 MB plain text downloaded from Internet Archive DjVuTXT. ^[source: raleigh_history_of_the_world_vol1_raw.txt]
Internet Archive: item TheHistoryOfTheWorldInFiveBooks1736 — stream / DjVuTXT · download
Extractable? Yes. Archive.org already ships a ready *_djvu.txt OCR extract (~2.6 MB). No local unzip/OCR step was needed beyond download.
Ralegh wrote the History in the Tower under James I (first published 1614). For this Tudor knowledge base, the Oldys Life and Trial are the main Elizabethan/Jacobean mining set; Book I is ancient/biblical universal history (Creation → flood → nations → Nimrod/Ninus/Semiramis), useful for Ralegh’s voice and Tower-period thought rather than Tudor narrative proper. ^[source: raleigh_history_of_the_world_vol1_raw.txt]

Quality Assessment
Google-digitized OCR of an 18th-century folio. Long-s → f is constant. Soft hyphenation and broken words across line ends are common. “Digitized by Google” interstitial pages appear often. Running headers (The LIFE of, The History of the World. Book I.) repeat. Body prose of Life, Trial, Preface, and Book I is generally recoverable. ^[source: raleigh_history_of_the_world_vol1_raw.txt]

Contents — mining notes
Oldys Life (~6911–32849)
Long early-modern biography: Devon origins; France/Low Countries service; Humphrey Gilbert and American ventures; Elizabethan court rise; Ireland; Armada-era naval/military reputation; Guiana; James I’s accession; fall, imprisonment, and death. Rich in names, voyages, and faction. Best first stop for elizabeth-i / privateering / court pages. ^[source: raleigh_history_of_the_world_vol1_raw.txt]
Trial (~32850–37170)
Winchester, 17 November 1603: commissioners (Suffolk, Devon, Northampton, Salisbury, etc.); indictment (Cobham, Aremberg, Arabella Stuart, Spanish money); proceedings for high treason. Jacobean aftermath of the Elizabethan career. ^[source: raleigh_history_of_the_world_vol1_raw.txt]
Preface (~338–2523)
Ralegh’s famous preface from the Tower: reputation, fortune, providence, and the use of universal history — including sharp reflections on English kings and contemporary politics. Often mined separately from the biblical books. ^[source: raleigh_history_of_the_world_vol1_raw.txt]

sources/raleigh-history-of-the-world-vol.content:
Sir Walter Ralegh (c.1552–1618), The History of the World. This file is Volume II of the 1736 London “Eleventh Edition” (“printed from a Copy revis’d by Himself”). It carries the continuous text of Books II–V (Abraham → Roman conquest of Macedon/Asia), plus chronological tables and the general Index. ~145,067 lines / ~5.1 MB plain text from Internet Archive DjVuTXT. ^[source: raleigh_history_of_the_world_vol2_raw.txt]
Internet Archive: item TheHistoryOfTheWorldInFiveBooks1736 — stream / DjVuTXT · download
Extractable? Yes — same ready DjVuTXT as Vol. I; download only.
Companion: raleigh-history-of-the-world-vol1 holds Oldys’s Life, the 1603 Trial, the Preface, Contents of all five books, and Book I. For Tudor mining, Vol. I’s Life/Trial remain primary; Vol. II is Ralegh’s Tower-period universal history (biblical → Greek → Macedonian → early Roman). The famous closing meditation on Death (“O eloquent, just and mighty death… Hic jacet”) and the aborted “second and third volume” addressed to Prince Henry are at the end of Book V. ^[source: raleigh_history_of_the_world_vol2_raw.txt]

Quality Assessment
Same Google-digitized 1736 folio OCR as Vol. I: long-s → f, soft hyphens, “Digitized by Google” interstitials, noisy running headers (Book II., The History of the World). Chapter titles are recoverable; some mid-book chapter banners are OCR-garbled (XXL for XXI). Chronological tables are sparse/columnar and hard to read as continuous prose — use the Index for name lookup instead. ^[source: raleigh_history_of_the_world_vol2_raw.txt]

sources/raleigh-history-of-the-world-vol.content:
Alexander Ross (1591–1654), The History of the World: The Second Part, in Six Books. London, 1652 (John Clark). This is not Sir Walter Ralegh’s own Book III. It is Ross’s continuation of Ralegh’s History, beginning where Ralegh stopped (end of the Macedonian kingdom / ~150 BC) and running to 1640/1641. Internet Archive files it as “Volume 3” under the same item that holds the 1736 Ralegh set — hence the KB filename raleigh_…_vol3_raw.txt. ~64,607 lines / ~3.1 MB plain text from DjVuTXT. ^[source: raleigh_history_of_the_world_vol3_raw.txt]
Internet Archive: item TheHistoryOfTheWorldInFiveBooks1736 — stream / DjVuTXT · download
Extractable? Yes — ready DjVuTXT; download only. Title-page OCR mangles the author name (aAL8XJSh…R^OSSl); imprint year is clear: M.DC.LII.
Companions: raleigh-history-of-the-world-vol1 / raleigh-history-of-the-world-vol2 are Ralegh’s own 1736 text (Life/Trial/Books I–V). For Tudor mining, this Ross volume is the valuable one: Book VI has continuous English/Scottish chapters from Lancastrians through Elizabeth, Mary Queen of Scots, James VI & I, and Charles I. ^[source: raleigh_history_of_the_world_vol3_raw.txt]

Quality Assessment
17th-century folio OCR (Google-digitized scan). Long-s → f is constant. Soft hyphens, broken words, and noisy running headers (Book VI., Hiftory of the World) are common. Chapter banners are often recoverable; some are OCR-garbled (Chap.ztf. for XXVI, Chap.2^. mid-block). Chronology pages are sparse/columnar. Alphabetical Table is usable for name lookup.
