sources/sir-francis-drake.title: Sugden — Sir Francis Drake
sources/sir-francis-drake.content:
John Sugden, Sir Francis Drake. Random House, 2012. ~1.25 MB, 23,038 lines extracted text. The standard modern biography of Drake, based on extensive archival research across English and Spanish sources including the Conway Papers (Cambridge), the Public Record Office, and Spanish colonial documents printed in I. A. Wright’s English Voyages to the Caribbean.
Comprehensive life from Drake’s origins in Devon through the Hawkins slaving voyages, his private war against Spain in the Caribbean, the circumnavigation (1577–1580), the knighthood, the raid on Cádiz (“singeing the King of Spain’s beard”), the Armada campaign of 1588, and the final ill-fated Caribbean expedition where he died in January 1596. Corrects the two dominant academic traditions that preceded it: the Corbett school (Drake as founder of naval empire) and the revisionist school (Drake as mere filibuster). Sugden presents Drake as an unusually complex social climber — privateer, civic leader, MP, property magnate — who rose from near-poverty to knighthood in a society built on inherited status. ^[source: sir_francis_drake_raw.txt]
Sugden’s preface states his purpose plainly: to rescue Drake from “the extremes of the prevailing interpretations” and to write a rounded biography rather than “the conventional collection of voyages.” His use of Spanish sources gives the biography its distinctive double vision — we see every English raid through Spanish eyes too, and Philip II emerges as almost an equal protagonist. ^[source: sir_francis_drake_raw.txt]
Quality Assessment
Clean born-digital epub, fully readable throughout. Maps included in the epub (not extractable as text) cover Drake’s circumnavigation route, the West Indies and Spanish Main, the Iberian Peninsula, and the Armada battles in the Channel — the source page can substitute for these with geographic descriptions in the text. Footnotes name principal and disparate sources and are retained in the extraction. Spelling modernized by Sugden in quotations from primary sources; dates given Old Style (Julian calendar). ^[source: sir_francis_drake_raw.txt]
Contents — Chapter-by-Chapter
Preface (lines 180–313)
Sugden opens with Pope Sixtus V’s rueful admiration — “Just look at Drake! Who is he? What forces has he? And yet he burned twenty-five of the King’s ships at Gibraltar…” — and with the simple fact that Drake’s name, four centuries later, remains a household word that has inspired Montgomery, Churchill, and Thatcher. He surveys the two academic traditions he is writing against (Corbett’s naval empire thesis vs. the revisionist privateer thesis), explains his use of English and Spanish sources together, and announces that his subject is not just the sea raider but also the social climber: Drake the businessman, property owner, parliamentarian and magistrate. ^[source: sir_francis_drake_raw.txt]
Ch 1: ‘By God’s Faith!’ (lines 315–840) — Origins in Devon
Drake’s family was long settled near Tavistock on the edge of Dartmoor. The dissolution of the monasteries (1539) is the first historical context: the Tavistock abbey lands had passed to the Russell family, and Francis Drake’s father, Edmund, was a Protestant lay reader of the new dispensation, farming land once owned by monks. Edmund’s religion was militant: when the Prayer Book rebellion of 1549 swept Devon in the Catholic cause, Edmund fled east with his family. He eventually became a lay minister serving sailors at Chatham — and it was among the sailors and their ships at Chatham that young Francis first learned the sea.
Drake’s apprenticeship was with the Hawkins family of Plymouth. John Hawkins was the dominant figure in Devon’s maritime world, and his family’s connections to the Drakes were close. Francis served first on small coastal and Channel vessels, learning the trade of a mariner, before becoming captain of a small bark on a trade voyage to the Bay of Biscay. He was still a young man, barely out of his teens, when Hawkins chose him for the third slaving voyage in 1567. Sugden is careful about Drake’s age — the records are uncertain — but places his birth probably around 1540–1545. ^[source: sir_francis_drake_raw.txt]
Ch 2: Beyond the Line (lines 841–1459) — Spain’s claim to the Americas and Philip II
Sugden suspends Drake’s story to give a full portrait of his adversary. Philip II — who had been briefly King of England as Mary I’s consort — is presented as the central fixed point around which the entire book orbits. Philip is almost entirely unlike Drake: reclusive, indecisive, agonizing, ruled by papers and self-doubt, yet capable of “almost pathological resolution” when committed. The contrast is structural: Drake bold, gregarious, decisive, forward-pressing; Philip cautious, secretive, reactive, desk-bound. Both men understand themselves as instruments of God; both understand the war as religious as much as political.
The chapter explains the Treaty of Tordesillas (1494) which divided the non-Christian world between Spain and Portugal, and the Spanish doctrine of “beyond the line” — that violence committed in the Americas did not count as war in Europe, allowing Philip to attack English ships in the Caribbean while remaining nominally at peace with Elizabeth. This legal fiction governs Drake’s entire early career: his raids are technically piracy, not warfare, because England does not recognize Spain’s monopoly claim. ^[source: sir_francis_drake_raw.txt]
Ch 3: The Troublesome Voyage of John Hawkins (lines 1460–2354) — The Slaving Voyages and San Juan de Ulúa (1568)
The pivot of Drake’s life. Hawkins fitted out six ships at Plymouth in September 1567 — including two of the queen’s warships, the Jesus of Lubeck (flagship) and the Minion — for what was the fourth Hawkins slaving voyage to West Africa and the Spanish Main. Drake commanded the small bark Judith. Sugden is unflinching about the nature of the enterprise: raiding Portuguese vessels for enslaved Africans and selling them illegally to Spanish colonists is described as it was, piracy and human trafficking, dressed up in extreme Protestant piety (the Jesus’s quartermaster was “a notorious Lutheran, the greatest that existed in England,” who held compulsory services and preached against the Pope with a rope’s end at hand).
The voyage ends in disaster at San Juan de Ulúa (Mexico), where a Spanish flota arrived while the English were refitting in the harbour. The new Viceroy, Don Martin Enriquez, negotiated a truce — and then attacked. The English lost four of their six ships. Hawkins escaped on the Minion with overcrowded, starving survivors; Drake escaped on the Judith and — controversially — did not return for Hawkins in the morning. Hawkins held this desertion against Drake for years (“that bark, the same night, forsook us in our great misery”). Sugden gives Drake the benefit of the doubt: the offshore winds were dangerous, the Judith overcrowded, and the Atlantic crossing unknown territory for Drake. But he notes that Drake’s “resolution, for the first time, failed him.”
The aftermath: the men left behind faced the Inquisition. Sugden names them, one by one — William Orlando who died in Seville dungeons, Robert Barrett of Saltash burned at an auto da fe, Michael Morgan tortured and sentenced to the galleys — making the human cost of the slaving voyages vivid. The chapter ends with Drake, returning to Plymouth after four months at sea, having made his decision: “Francis Drake declared war upon the King of Spain.” ^[source: sir_francis_drake_raw.txt]
Ch 4: Drake’s War (lines 2355–3210) — Building the Vendetta, 1569–1572
Drake returned to an England where diplomatic calculation worked against him. Elizabeth and Philip were moving toward the Convention of Bristol (1574), which required her to discourage her corsairs. Drake was advised to keep a low profile, and for two years after his return nothing is known of his activities. When he reappears it is on the margins of the dismal English colonization project in Ireland — he served briefly under Walter Devereux, Earl of Essex, providing naval support for what Sugden treats as a squalid affair that tells us little about Drake’s abilities but something about his willingness to do ugly work for powerful patrons.
The chapter develops the international backdrop: France in civil war, Spain consolidating in the Netherlands under the Duke of Alba, the gradual shift of English attention from France to Spain as the primary threat. Drake’s personal decision after San Juan de Ulúa aligns with this national reorientation. His private war is not politically eccentric — it anticipates what England’s strategic position will require. ^[source: sir_francis_drake_raw.txt]
Ch 5: ‘The Mouth of the Treasure of the World’ (lines 3211–3883) — Nombre de Dios and the Panama Silver Train (1572–1573)
Drake’s first independent command of any significance. He left Plymouth on Whit Sunday 1572 with seventy-three volunteers in two small ships, the Pasco and the Swan, with three prefabricated pinnaces stored in pieces and provisions for a year. He was aiming at Nombre de Dios, the Atlantic port where silver from the Potosí mines was gathered for shipment to Spain — “the mouth of the treasure of the world,” as Drake called it.
The raid on Nombre de Dios: Drake’s assault force of seventy-three men attacked a town of several hundred. Drake himself was shot in the leg and refused to let his men know he was wounded, continuing to direct the attack until he fainted from blood loss and the English withdrew. They had reached the treasure house; they had not been able to carry it away. Sugden’s account is detailed on tactics — drums and trumpets, six shields and twelve pikes, the timing of the assault at 2–3 a.m.
The Panama silver train: having allied with the cimarrones (escaped African slaves who lived as guerrillas in the isthmus jungle and were at permanent war with Spain), Drake marched forty-eight men across the isthmus of Panama to intercept the mule-trains carrying silver between Panama City and Venta Cruces. He climbed a great tree that allowed him to see both the Atlantic and the Pacific simultaneously — “the first Englishman, or at least the first that we have exact notice of, that saw that sea.” He returned to England in August 1573 with enough plunder to make him wealthy, and a reputation across the West Country. ^[source: sir_francis_drake_raw.txt]
Ch 6: ‘Despite … All the Spaniards in the Indies’ (lines 3884–4569) — Consolidating the Caribbean Campaign
The cimarrone alliance is developed at length: Drake’s relationship with Pedro and the other cimarron leaders is the most interesting moral dimension of the Caribbean campaigns. The cimarrones had every reason to hate the Spanish — Sugden quotes their account of how their town had been sacked, men, women and children killed or captured. Drake treated them with genuine respect and they trusted him. His fleet of pinnaces and alliances with displaced, stateless people created a mode of warfare the Spaniards could not easily counter: light, fast, intelligence-driven, operating from hidden harbours and forest paths.
The chapter also follows the fate of Drake’s brothers. His brother Joseph died of fever in Panama. His brother John was killed in a skirmish. By the time Drake sailed home he was one of the only survivors of his original company. Sugden uses this to establish something about Drake’s psychological formation: he was a man acquainted with large and repeated personal loss who learned to press forward regardless. ^[source: sir_francis_drake_raw.txt]
Ch 7: Services Ashore and Afloat (lines 4570–5094) — Ireland and the Political Interlude, 1573–1577
Drake’s triumphant return to Plymouth coincided with the worst possible diplomatic moment: Elizabeth was moving toward accommodation with Spain. The most dangerous corsair on the ocean had to disappear for a while. The chapter covers his brief involvement in Irish operations under Walter Devereux, Earl of Essex — Sugden notes the ugly character of the Irish campaign without dwelling on it. He is more interested in what the interlude reveals about Drake’s social ambitions: his cultivation of Essex, and through Essex of the Devereaux family connection, anticipates his later cultivation of Leicester and finally of Essex’s son as patrons. Drake understood from early in his career that a man of his birth needed powerful sponsors, and he worked systematically to find them. ^[source: sir_francis_drake_raw.txt]
Ch 8: The South Seas Project (lines 5095–5806) — Planning the Circumnavigation
Sugden reconstructs the planning of the circumnavigation from fragmentary evidence, since the backers required secrecy. The investors included Leicester, Walsingham, Hatton, and almost certainly the queen herself, though Elizabeth maintained deniability. The original plan, carried in documents never intended for Spanish eyes, was probably to raid the Pacific coast of Spanish America — not specifically to circumnavigate. The cover story told to most of the crew was that they were bound for Alexandria.
The Doughty problem begins here. Thomas Doughty was a gentleman, a friend of Drake’s, and a servant of Hatton. He joined the expedition as a senior figure, but from the beginning showed a disposition to undermine Drake’s authority with hints that the backers expected Doughty to share the command. Sugden traces this carefully, using the depositions of the carpenter Edward Bright, who heard Doughty’s private boasts at Plymouth. Doughty is presented not as a villain but as a man whose expectations of shared authority in a venture that required absolute command were structurally incompatible with Drake’s leadership style. ^[source: sir_francis_drake_raw.txt]
Ch 9: The Atlantic Voyage (lines 5807–6591) — Departure 1577; Magellan Strait; Doughty’s Execution
The Pelican (later renamed the Golden Hind), Elizabeth, Marigold, Swan, and Benedict left Plymouth on 13 December 1577. The seizure of the Portuguese pilot Nuño da Silva in the Cape Verde Islands — taken with his ship, his charts, and his knowledge of South American waters — is treated as necessary piracy: Drake needed the charts and the expertise. The Mary (Drake’s prize, renamed after his wife) becomes the site of the Doughty problem’s first open flare: Doughty was appointed captain of the prize and immediately began creating trouble with the men.
Doughty’s execution at Port St Julian (Patagonia): Drake convened a jury of forty men, was examined himself, presented evidence from Bright and others of Doughty’s private undermining, and had Doughty tried, found guilty, and beheaded. He communed with him before the end and dined with him afterward — “we are yet friends,” Drake told him. Sugden’s treatment is measured: Doughty was probably guilty of something, possibly of sharing information about the voyage with Burghley, who was not one of the backers and would have opposed it; but whether the offence merited death under any proper legal standard is another matter. Drake had no royal commission and his authority to execute a gentleman was extremely doubtful. He knew he would one day have to answer for it — hence the renaming of the Pelican as the Golden Hind, honouring Hatton (Doughty’s patron) with his family’s emblem.
The Magellan Strait passage: fourteen days, the fastest of the century (Magellan took thirty-seven days). Drake emerges into the Pacific to face an immediate catastrophe — the worst storm the fleet had ever encountered drove them south for weeks, destroying the Marigold with all twenty-nine aboard and separating the Elizabeth (whose captain, Winter, eventually turned back to England). Drake was left with one ship in the South Pacific. ^[source: sir_francis_drake_raw.txt]
Ch 10: War Comes to the Pacific (lines 6592–7536) — Raiding the Pacific Coast of Spanish America
Drake’s solo raid on the entirely undefended Pacific coast — the Spanish had never imagined anyone could reach it from the west. He struck north along the Chilean and Peruvian coast, taking ship after ship, none of them armed, because the Spanish had never needed to arm ships in what they regarded as a private sea. The climax was the capture of the Nuestra Señora de la Concepción, the great treasure galleon nicknamed “the Cacafuego” by her crew — she carried twenty-six tonnes of silver, thirteen chests of silver coins, eighty pounds of gold, and a cargo of jewels and precious stones. Drake spent six days transferring the cargo to the Golden Hind.
The chapter covers the pursuit mounted by the Viceroy of Peru — Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa sent south to the Magellan Strait to intercept Drake, too late. Philip II in Madrid is shown receiving the reports of the Pacific raid with mounting consternation and beginning to endorse papers with “to be put with what relates to Drake.” Sugden notes that the Pacific raid, though it yielded treasure worth perhaps £140,000 in English money, was strategically more important as a demonstration: the entire system of Spanish imperial security was exposed as resting on the assumption that no one could reach the Pacific from Europe. ^[source: sir_francis_drake_raw.txt]
Ch 11: The World Encompassed (lines 7537–8269) — The Route Home; California; the Spice Islands; Return 1580
Drake faced three possible routes home: back through the Magellan Strait (too dangerous, and the Spaniards were waiting); the hypothetical North-west Passage; or across the Pacific. He attempted the North-west Passage first, reaching 48° north along the California coast — further north than any European had previously explored in the Pacific — before cold, fog and the failure to find any strait entrance persuaded him to give up. He careened the Golden Hind in a quiet harbour in northern California (its exact location still disputed between Drake’s Bay, Bolinas Bay, and the San Francisco Bay entrance) and made contact with the coastal Miwok people, who performed ceremonies of welcome that the English interpreted as an offer of sovereignty and Drake claimed the country for Elizabeth as “Nova Albion.”
The trans-Pacific crossing: the Spice Islands (Moluccas), where the Sultan of Ternate — engaged in his own war against the Portuguese — made Drake welcome and arranged the loading of six tonnes of cloves. A near-disaster on a reef that held the Golden Hind fast for twenty hours. The return around the Cape of Good Hope and up the Atlantic to England, arriving at Plymouth on 26 September 1580 — nearly three years after departure. The investors’ shares of the treasure were enormous: the queen’s share alone may have been worth £160,000. ^[source: sir_francis_drake_raw.txt]
Ch 12: The Golden Knight (lines 8270–8986) — Elizabeth’s Reception; Knighthood on the Golden Hind; Diplomatic Fallout
Philip II had filed a formal claim for restitution. Elizabeth listened to it, and then knighted Drake on the quarterdeck of the Golden Hind at Deptford on 4 April 1581, using a gilded sword — and making clear that the treasure would not be returned. The knighthood was the central fact of Drake’s social career: it transformed him from a corsair of uncertain legal status into Sir Francis Drake, with the full machinery of honour and respectability behind him.
The chapter is notably attentive to Drake’s anxiety about his coat of arms. His initial response to knighthood was to deny his humble origins and claim that his family “had borne arms of long time.” He borrowed a dragon crest from the Drakes of Ashe in Devon (a different family), fussed endlessly about the design, and only in the last years of his life settled into accepting the crest as originally granted by the queen — the globe with the Golden Hind riding it and a hand directing from the clouds. Sugden reads this as the social climber’s characteristic insecurity: Drake was not yet comfortable inside his own new skin.
He also bought Buckland Abbey (the converted Cistercian monastery four miles north of Plymouth) from Richard Grenville — through an intermediary, because Grenville would not sell to him directly — spending £3,400 to establish his country seat. ^[source: sir_francis_drake_raw.txt]
Ch 13: ‘What Has Become of Drake?’ (lines 8987–10043) — The Years of Relative Inactivity, 1581–1584
A quieter chapter covering Drake’s adjustment to his new social position — and the years in which Elizabeth, hoping to avoid provoking Philip, kept her most dangerous instrument sheathed. Drake was elected mayor of Plymouth (1581–82), served as Member of Parliament, worked on Plymouth’s water supply, and continued to cultivate his network of patrons (Leicester above all, then Walsingham). He married again after the death of his first wife Mary. He was also involved in planning a Moluccas expedition under Edward Fenton that came to nothing.
Sugden uses this period to develop Philip’s counter-moves: the fortification of the Strait of Magellan (a settlement attempt under Sarmiento that ended in disaster and starvation — the survivors were found years later by Thomas Cavendish and called “Port Famine”). Philip was also buying Portugal’s throne (1580), annexing its empire, and beginning to think seriously about the enterprise of England. The chapter ends with Drake’s 1585 commission: Elizabeth had finally resolved on open support for the Dutch rebels and was prepared to use her most effective weapon. ^[source: sir_francis_drake_raw.txt]
Ch 14: Playing the Dragon (lines 10044–10895) — The 1585 Caribbean Expedition; Sacking Cartagena and San Domingo
Drake’s largest Caribbean expedition: 25 ships and 2,300 men, a semi-official operation with the queen investing ships and Leicester investing money. The expedition sacked Santiago in the Cape Verde Islands (no treasure), crossed the Atlantic to Hispaniola, and took Santo Domingo — the oldest city in the Americas and the administrative capital of Spanish Caribbean — by landing soldiers at night on the beach west of the city and marching around the defences. The sack lasted a month; the Spanish governor negotiated a ransom (Drake’s demolition squads were systematically destroying one building a day until the ransom was paid). Net proceeds: about 25,000 ducats, far less than hoped.
Cartagena followed — the principal city of the Spanish Main, forewarned and better defended. Drake landed soldiers at the Caleta, the narrow neck of land forming the harbour entrance, after a diversionary attack by Frobisher’s ships on the harbour chain. The infantry assault on the Caleta met Spanish galleys, lance, and arquebuses; the men panicked initially but recovered. Cartagena fell after hard fighting. Again, a ransom negotiation rather than plunder — 107,000 ducats, less than a third of what Drake demanded. He demolished the city building by building for weeks.
The expedition failed financially but succeeded militarily: it demonstrated to Philip that Spain’s Caribbean empire was fundamentally indefensible against a large English force. In Madrid, Philip’s ambassador wrote: “Drake is so highly valued by the queen and these people that we must endeavour to get rid of him by other means.” The chapter ends with Drake touching at the fledgling Roanoke Colony in Virginia on the return — taking off the surviving colonists (including Ralph Lane) and effectively ending the first Roanoke settlement. ^[source: sir_francis_drake_raw.txt]
Ch 15: ‘A Fearful Man to the King of Spain!’ (lines 10896–11532) — The Cádiz Raid and Cape St Vincent (1587)
Philip II began assembling his Armada in late 1586. Elizabeth authorized Drake to “impeach” the Spanish preparations — a deliberately ambiguous commission that he used to the fullest extent possible. He sailed for Cádiz in April 1587 with four queen’s ships and twenty-three private vessels and arrived to find thirty-seven Spanish ships in the harbour, several of them large, loading provisions and stores for the Armada.
Drake attacked immediately, over the protests of his vice-admiral (William Borough, who wanted a formal council of war first). He spent thirty-six hours in the harbour, sinking, burning, or capturing thirty-seven ships and enormous quantities of stores — “singeing the King of Spain’s beard.” Borough wrote a formal protest against Drake’s high-handedness, and Drake had him court-martialled on the return. Elizabeth quietly dropped the charges against Borough — she was unimpressed by Drake’s treatment of a subordinate — but kept Drake in command.
Cape St Vincent: Drake seized the cape as a base, ravaged coastal shipping, and destroyed the barrel staves stored in the area. The stave destruction had strategic significance: without seasoned barrel staves, the Armada’s provisions would spoil in the casks cut from green wood. This may have contributed to the fleet’s provisioning problems in 1588. Drake’s own estimate of the raid’s importance was grandiose — he wrote to Walsingham that it would delay the Armada by a year. He was roughly right. ^[source: sir_francis_drake_raw.txt]
Ch 16: ‘Stop Him Now, and Stop Him Ever!’ (lines 11533–12352) — Spanish Armada Preparations; Mary Queen of Scots
Mary Queen of Scots was executed at Fotheringay in February 1587, removing Philip’s last reservation about the enterprise of England: while Mary lived he feared that overthrowing Elizabeth would benefit France. With Mary dead, Philip himself came forward as the legitimate Catholic heir. His leading admiral, Santa Cruz, died in February 1588 and was replaced by Medina Sidonia — who famously protested his own appointment in terms of comic self-deprecation (“he would certainly make a mess of it”) before accepting.
Sugden gives Elizabeth’s strategic hesitations full weight. She understood that Spain was the only counterweight to France; she had already spent most of her reserves on the Netherlands and on Drake; she feared war’s costs. Her refusal to strike preemptively was not cowardice but a calculation about sustainability. Drake’s view — that only an aggressive offensive could save England — and Elizabeth’s view — that she must husband her resources — represent a genuine strategic debate, not simply boldness versus timidity. ^[source: sir_francis_drake_raw.txt]
Ch 17: ‘The Sooner We Are Gone, the Better’ (lines 12353–13307) — English Preparations; Drake as Vice-Admiral
Howard as Lord Admiral, Drake as Vice-Admiral: the joint command structure. Sugden is good on the English fleet’s composition and on the debate about strategy — Drake wanted to take the fleet to Spain to intercept the Armada before it left port; Howard was more cautious; Elizabeth at one point ordered them back to their home ports. The wait at Plymouth while the wind held them bottled in and the Armada approached was agonizing.
The Armada itself is described from the Spanish side: 125 ships, 19,000 soldiers and 8,000 sailors, massed prayers and confessions, their standard inscribed “Arise, O Lord, and vindicate thy cause.” Medina Sidonia’s plan (link with Parma’s army in the Netherlands for an invasion of Kent) is described alongside its fatal assumption: that flyboats could convey Parma’s men from the shallow Flemish ports to the Armada’s deep-draft ships without being destroyed by the Dutch. ^[source: sir_francis_drake_raw.txt]
Ch 18: ‘It Was Impossible to Come to Hand-Stroke with Them’ (lines 13308–14292) — The Armada Channel Battles
Sugden opens by demolishing the bowling-on-Plymouth-Hoe story: it dates from a Dutch pamphlet of 1624, was originally a Spanish boast about the Armada’s approach rather than an English anecdote about Drake’s sangfroid, and was not attributed to Drake until 1736. “On such flimsy foundations rests the most famous of all yarns about Sir Francis Drake.”
The seven days of Channel fighting: the English could not close with the Armada (which kept tight defensive formation) and the Armada could not detach transports to seize a port (Medina Sidonia’s orders forbade unnecessary engagements until the junction with Parma). The tactical problem for both sides is described precisely — the Spanish formation was too strong to break, the English guns too light to penetrate Spanish hulls at long range. One notable incident: Drake extinguished the lantern that his ships were following during a night pursuit and went off to capture a straggling Spanish ship for himself, leaving Howard and the rest of the fleet in darkness and confusion. He later said his lantern had failed. Sugden treats this as characteristic — Drake’s instinct for personal profit operating even during a fleet action. ^[source: sir_francis_drake_raw.txt]
Ch 19: ‘God Hath Given Us So Good a Day’ (lines 14293–14870) — The Fireships at Gravelines; Spanish Flight
The Armada anchored off Calais on 27 July 1588, waiting for Parma. Howard and Drake sent eight fireships into the anchorage at midnight. No ship was actually burned — the Spanish cut their anchor cables and scattered into the North Sea — but the panic had destroyed the Armada’s tight defensive formation, and it was never re-formed. Drake offered his own ship, the Thomas Drake, as one of the fireships.
The Battle of Gravelines (29 July): the only full day of close action, the English having finally exhausted their ammunition and powder supply in the process of bringing the Armada to near-destruction. The Rosario (captured earlier by Drake — his personal trophy), the San Salvador, and eight other Spanish ships were wrecked or sunk. The Armada fled into the North Sea without the ability to return south, pursued by Howard and Drake as far as the Firth of Forth before the English turned back for lack of provisions.
Philip II received the news in his monastery at the Sierra de Guadarrama: “I hope that God has not permitted so much evil, for everything has been done for His service.” His annotated dispatches trace his reluctance to accept the magnitude of the disaster. ^[source: sir_francis_drake_raw.txt]
Ch 20: ‘This Will Cause an Evil Summer’ (lines 14871–16106) — The Portugal Expedition (1589); Failure and Disgrace
The counter-armada of 1589 is Drake’s most important failure and the one Sugden analyses most critically. The plan had three objectives: destroy Armada survivors in Spanish ports; take Lisbon for Dom Antonio (Portuguese pretender); seize the Azores. These were sequenced badly and the vital first objective (destroying ships at Santander) was missed — Drake and Norris went south to Corunna instead, wasting time in a siege that achieved nothing militarily. By the time they reached Lisbon the army was weakened by disease and Dom Antonio’s promised Portuguese uprising failed to materialize. The Azores attempt was abandoned for lack of provisions.
Sugden’s verdict: if Lisbon had been dropped from the plan, and Drake had been sent simply to destroy the Armada survivors and then take the Azores, the result could have been decisive. The Azores as a base would have allowed England to intercept the treasure flotas. But Elizabeth had been persuaded by Dom Antonio’s fantasies, and Drake had allowed himself to be carried along. “He had always reached for the stars, realized ambitions that some might have considered chimerical, and probably it was only a matter of time before he overreached himself. That time had finally come.” ^[source: sir_francis_drake_raw.txt]
Ch 21: Last Years Ashore (lines 16107–17153) — Plymouth; Parliament; Rehabilitation, 1589–1595
Contrary to the common picture of disgrace and idleness, Sugden argues that these were among Drake’s busiest years: Member of Parliament (Plymouth), acting Deputy Lord Lieutenant for Devon, military engineer (Plymouth’s defences), entrepreneur, prize commissioner, and civic leader. His most lasting legacy from this period may be the Plymouth water supply — the leat he engineered to bring fresh water from Dartmoor to Plymouth, sixteen miles of open channel, completed in 1591.
The broader war continued at low intensity: privateering fleets (the Lanzarote expedition, Cumberland’s Atlantic raids), Hawkins’s proposed blockade of the Azores trade routes that was never fully implemented. Drake’s name retained its terror value — Spanish coastal towns would panic at any rumour of his approach. Philip was reviving his navy and planning further armadas; England’s strategic position remained precarious. ^[source: sir_francis_drake_raw.txt]
Ch 22: ‘Into a Waste and Desert Wilderness’ (lines 17154–17835) — The Final Caribbean Expedition; Death, January 1596
The last voyage was compromised from the start by divided command: Drake and Sir John Hawkins received joint commissions with equal authority. Sugden quotes Thomas Maynarde’s portrait of the two old admirals as they embarked: Drake still full of spirit and fit “to conduct forces and discreetly to govern,” but “self-willed and peremptory”; Hawkins “old and wary, entering into matters with so leaden a foot that the other’s meat would be eaten before his spit could come to the fire.” The two commanders maintained effectively separate squadrons.
Puerto Rico was the first objective. Drake failed: the Spanish had been alerted by the capture of a straggler that carried the fleet’s plans, and San Juan was now fortified. Hawkins died at Puerto Rico on 12 November 1595. Drake pressed south to the Main, took Río de la Hacha, sacked Santa Marta, took Nombre de Dios — and then sent an army under Baskerville across the isthmus to attack Panama. The army was turned back by a Spanish force, the first time Drake’s Panama strategy had failed. Drake’s health collapsed: dysentery, possibly compounded by despair. He died aboard the Defiance off Buena Ventura (Panama) on 28 January 1596, and was buried at sea in a lead coffin west of Puerto Bello. ^[source: sir_francis_drake_raw.txt]
Ch 23: Afterword (lines 17836–18500) — Drake’s Legacy and Philip’s Death
Baskerville brought the fleet home. FitzGeffrey wrote a full-length epic. English seamen followed Drake’s wake — Puerto Rico, Puerto de Caballos, Puerto Bello — for decades. Captain William Parker, taking Puerto Bello in 1601, anchored east of the castle of Saint Philip “under the rock where Sir Francis Drake, his coffin, was thrown overboard,” in deliberate salute.
Philip II’s response to the news of Drake’s death: “It is good news, and now I will get well.” Lope de Vega wrote La Dragontea (1597) celebrating Drake’s death as a defeat of the Devil. A Spanish soldier who had fought against Drake, Don Alonso de Sotomayor, gave him this epitaph: “one of the most famous men of his profession that have existed in the world, very courteous and honourable with those who surrendered, of great humanity and gentleness, virtues which must be praised even in an enemy.”
Philip himself died in September 1598, his empire intact but his war unresolved. The conflict wound up by the Treaty of London in 1604. Sugden’s final judgement: the profits of privateering, in experience and treasure, constituted England’s principal legacy from the later war years — not decisive naval victory but the accumulation of maritime skill that would eventually generate genuine sea power. ^[source: sir_francis_drake_raw.txt]

sources/stationers-registers-arber-vol1.title: Arber — Transcript of the Registers of the Stationers' Company, Vol. I
sources/stationers-registers-arber-vol1.content:
Edward Arber (ed.), A Transcript of the Registers of the Company of Stationers of London, 1554–1640 A.D. Volume I — Text. Privately printed, London, 1 January 1875. Reprinted New York: Peter Smith, 1950. ~33,873 lines extracted from a zip of 648 OCR’d page files. University of Illinois Library copy.
This is the first of five volumes of Arber’s Transcript. Volume I contains the earliest surviving Stationers’ Company records: Arber’s long introductory essay; the text of the Company’s Ordinances (earliest surviving printed copy, 1678–82); Arber’s notes on his editorial method; and then the full text of Register A — the Wardens’ Account Books covering 9 December 1554 through 22 July 1571 — followed by summary Cash Abstracts from 1571 through 2 August 1596. The Register A accounts are the founding primary source for the English book trade under Mary I and Elizabeth I: every apprentice presented, every freeman admitted, every book licensed, every fine levied, and every payment made by the Company is recorded year by year. Inserted into the register text, out of its chronological place, is Christopher Barker’s full 1582 Report to the Privy Council on the printing patents of 1558–1582 — the single most important document for understanding how the Elizabethan book trade actually worked. ^[source: stationers_registers_arber_vol1_raw.txt]
Quality Assessment
OCR from a 1950 lithographic reprint of the 1875 original (University of Illinois Library copy). The body text is generally very readable. The register entries themselves are in Elizabethan English — early modern spellings, Latin-numeral money amounts (iij iiijd = 3s 4d), and abbreviated feast-day dates (e.g. “the feaste of saynt John baptest [24 June]”) — but consistently legible. Arber’s editorial footnotes appear in square brackets inline, clearly distinguishable from the primary-source text.
Artifact types:

Running headers inline — master and warden names, account date ranges (e.g. “9 December 1554–18 July 1557,” “T. Dockwray,” “J. Cawood”) repeat at the top of every page and are captured inline with the body text
Page numbers inline — both the book’s roman-numeral preliminary pages and arabic body page numbers appear as isolated lines
Library stamps in opening pages — University of Illinois library date-stamps, shelf marks, and barcode text appear in the first ~100 lines
Blank page markers — “[This page is entirely blank in the Original.]” appears occasionally
Inserted documents out of sequence — Barker’s 1582 Report is interpolated into the 3rd account (1558–59) and runs across multiple page-breaks with the header “[CHRISTOPHER BARKER’S REPORT IN DECEMBER 1582, ON THE PRINTING PATENTS OF 1558–1582.]” repeating as a running head



















































SectionLine rangeQualityFront matter, library stamps, title pages1–700Readable (with library noise)Arber’s Introduction~701–2804ReadableOrdinances of the Stationers’ Company, 1678–82~2805–4119ReadableOn the Present Transcript (editorial method)~4120–4389ReadableRegister A — Wardens’ Accounts, 1554–1571~4390–25142Readable (Elizabethan English throughout)Summary Cash Abstracts, 1571–1596~25143–33500ReadableAddendum — The Controversy of 1643–5~33500–33760ReadableCorrigenda~33775–endReadable

Contents — Section by Section
Arber’s Introduction (lines ~701–2804)
A substantial essay — the preface to the entire five-volume project — in which Arber argues for the importance of the English printer and publisher as figures equal in historical significance to the poets, statesmen, and explorers of the Elizabethan age. He names John Cawood, John Day, Henry Denham, Henry Binneman, and Christopher Barker as the representative men of the printing business, and places them beside Sidney, Spenser, Shakespeare, Burghley, Walsingham, and Drake.
He describes the great folios of the period — More’s Workes (printed by Walley, Cawood, and Tottle 1557); Becon’s Workes (Day, 1560–4); Fox’s Acts and Monuments (four editions, Day, 1563–83); Holinshed’s Chronicles (Denham 1587); Field’s edition of North’s Plutarch (1595); Hakluyt’s Voyages (Bishop, Newberry, and Robert Barker, 1599–1600) — as comparable in difficulty of production to a modern Encyclopædia Britannica.
Arber traces the history of the Company from the 1403 Brotherhood through the 1556 Charter and Elizabeth’s confirmation. He describes the five-year gap in the registers (1571–1576) where the Clerk’s book is lost. He explains his editorial system: Company members’ names are set in Clarendon type; non-members in Roman capitals. He notes that some misattributions of membership are inevitable because sheets had to be annotated as they came from the press, so later discoveries could only look backward.
The Introduction closes with a meditation on England’s Elizabethan “Golden Age” as a providential outpouring analogous to those of Israel, Greece, Rome, and Italy — framing the register as the material record of that age’s mind-world. ^[source: stationers_registers_arber_vol1_raw.txt]

Ordinances of the Stationers’ Company, 1678–1682 (lines ~2805–4119)
The full text of the Company’s Ordinances as approved by the Lord Keeper and the Lords Chief Justices, 10 February 1682. Arber explains that all earlier manuscript Ordinances appear to have perished, and that this 1678–82 printed text — the earliest surviving — is “doubtless substantially the same” as those now lost. The Ordinances in force in 1875 were substantially the same as these.
The text covers: the constitution and powers of the Court of Assistants; election of Master and Wardens; duties of the Renter Wardens; apprenticeship and freedom rules; searches for unlicensed printing; penalties for printing contrary to Company orders; the oath of a Freeman; and the financial governance of the Hall. Approved copies signed by Richard Rainsford and Francis North. ^[source: stationers_registers_arber_vol1_raw.txt]

On the Present Transcript (lines ~4120–4389)
Arber’s account of the editorial method. He describes the five-year labour of producing the Transcript from 2,500 manuscript pages. Key methodological points:

Company members’ names in Clarendon type; non-members in Roman capitals; the distinction is a general rule only, not always carried out with accuracy since the text had to be annotated sheet by sheet as it came from the press
Some forty thousand names appear across the five volumes; Arber could not always determine membership status in time
Example cases of misattribution: John Charlewood (not identified as a Company member until his appearance in Vol. II at a point after his earlier entries were already in print); John Wolf (apprenticed to John Day but freed in the Fishmongers’ Company, retransferred to Stationers 1583); Humphrey Toy (served as Under Warden but later found to be a Merchant Tailor)
The intent was to provide an apparatus of footnote cross-references to make the text its own interpreter

^[source: stationers_registers_arber_vol1_raw.txt]

Register A — Wardens’ Accounts, 1554–1571 (lines ~4390–25142)
The primary-source core of the volume. The Wardens’ Account Book is the oldest record of the Stationers’ Company, beginning with the Master and Wardens named in the Charter and running through the 15th Annual Account ending 22 July 1571.
Structure of each annual account. Each year is headed by the names of the Master and two Wardens for that year. The account is divided into Receipts (subdivided into: Apprentices presented; Freemen and Brothers admitted; Book Entries licensed; Fines levied; Livery; Miscellaneous) and Payments (Hall dinners; setting forth men for civic shows; Gifts; Miscellaneous outgoings). Arber’s bracketed editorial notes appear throughout, identifying individuals, correcting dates, and cross-referencing other volumes.
The first account (9 December 1554 – 18 July 1557). Master: Thomas Dockwray. Wardens: John Cawood, Henry Cooke. This covers the founding years of the incorporated Company under Philip and Mary. The fee for making a freeman was 3s 4d (the Half-Noble). Early entries record Freemen being made, apprentices presented (6d per presentation), and small fines. The book entries in this first account are few — the Company was newly incorporated and the licensing system not yet fully developed. Inserted illustrative documents include: the Proclamation against Protestant books (13 June 1555); the Charter of the Company (27 September 1556); the Act of Common Council on apprentices; the Grant of Arms by Sir G. Dethick; the enrollment of the Charter in the Corporation Records (3 June 1557).
The book entry format. From the 2nd account (July 1557) onward, book entries read as follows: “To [printer’s name] to prynte [abbreviated title] and for his lycense he geveth to the howse [fee].” The typical fee was 4d for a ballad or small pamphlet, more for substantial works. Author names are given when known (often in small capitals). A single entry may cover multiple titles at a combined fee. From this point Arber’s footnotes routinely identify the work and cross-reference surviving copies.
Christopher Barker’s 1582 Report (lines ~8444–9912). Inserted out of chronological sequence into the 3rd account (10 July 1558–10 July 1559), this is the full text of Barker’s December 1582 report to the Privy Council, drawn from the Burghley papers in the British Museum. Arber calls it “hardly possible to exaggerate the importance and authority of this graphic History of English Printing during the twenty-four years which had then elapsed since Elizabeth’s accession.”
The Report surveys every printing patent granted by Elizabeth from 1558 through 1582, assessing each patent’s value, the identity of its holder or assignee, and the problems arising from the patent system. The key passage: the Marian Charter gave authority to print to all Stationers — bookbinders, booksellers, joiners, chandlers — without specifying Printers; “so that the Bookesellers being growen the greater and wealthier nomber haue nowe many of the best Copies and keepe no printing howse, neither beare any charge of letter, or other furniture but onlie paye for the workmanship.” Barker describes individual patents: Seres’s psalter and primer patent (assigned to Henry Denham); Day’s patent for the ABC and catechism; Jugge’s patent for Bibles and New Testaments; Tottle’s law-book patent; Barker’s own Queen’s Printer patent (granted 28 September 1577). He gives the practical arrangements, disputes, and sub-assignments that the formal patent grants conceal.
Elizabeth’s Injunctions of 1559 (inserted into the 4th account). Two clauses of the Injunctions are reproduced as “the first printed notice of the Company” — the founding royal acknowledgment of the Stationers’ licensing system. The Confirmation of the Charter (1 February 1560) and the Lord Mayor’s Precept creating the Company a Livery Company are inserted at the same point.
Progression of the accounts. The annual accounts run through the 15th year (22 July 1570 – 22 July 1571), with Wardens including William Seres, Richard Tottle, John Day, and Humphrey Toy at various points. The book entries grow substantially in volume from the mid-1560s onward, reflecting the expanding Elizabethan press. A note at line 25142 marks the close of the detailed annual accounts: “Here end the detailed annual Wardens’ Accounts of the Company contained in this Book.” ^[source: stationers_registers_arber_vol1_raw.txt]

The Gap: 1571–1576
A note at line 25142–25151 states: “There is now a gap between the 22nd July 1571 and the 20th July 1576; all our knowledge of which period will be found on the following pp. 451–474.” The Register B (kept by George Wapull the Clerk) that would have covered this period is now lost. The gap means there is no primary-source record of book entries for five years in the early 1570s — a significant lacuna covering the period of the Puritan press and early Elizabethan literary output. Register B, beginning 1576, is the subject of Volumes II and III. ^[source: stationers_registers_arber_vol1_raw.txt]

Summary Cash Abstracts, 1571–1596 (lines ~25143–33500)
After the detailed annual accounts end, Volume I continues with summarised Cash Abstracts — annual financial summaries only — from 1571 through 2 August 1596. These give the broad receipts and payments for each year but do not list individual book entries, apprentice presentations, or freemen’s names. The receipt lines include “RECEIVED FOR LYCENCED COPPIES as doth appeare by the Register in the Clarkes booke” but the titles themselves are not given here — they are in the separate Register B (Volumes II and III). The Abstracts confirm the Company’s financial health year by year and record major exceptional items (setting forth men for civic shows, building works at the Hall, etc.). ^[source: stationers_registers_arber_vol1_raw.txt]

Addendum — The Controversy of 1643–5 (lines ~33500–33760)
A substantial appendix reproducing documents from a mid-17th century dispute between the Court of Assistants and a reform committee of the Company over the election and bonding of new Assistants. Includes a detailed narrative of the committee’s proceedings, the text of a Common Hall ticket issued June 1645, and a Petition to the Lord Mayor and Aldermen signed by 29 Livery members and 164 Yeomanry members on 14 June 1645. The documents debate the Company’s governance, the reform of its printing the Bible, suppression of seditious books, the Scottish Bible patent, and the importation of foreign Bibles. Beyond the period of this collection but included by Arber as illustrating the Company’s 17th-century governance. ^[source: stationers_registers_arber_vol1_raw.txt]

sources/stationers-registers-arber-vol2.title: Arber — Transcript of the Registers of the Stationers' Company, Vol. II
sources/stationers-registers-arber-vol2.content:
Edward Arber (ed.), A Transcript of the Registers of the Company of Stationers of London, 1554–1640 A.D. Volume II — Text. Privately printed, London, 1 October 1875. Reprinted New York: Peter Smith, 1950. ~45,409 lines extracted from a zip of 906 OCR’d page files. University of Minnesota Wilson Library copy.
This is the second of five volumes of Arber’s Transcript. Volume II contains the core primary-source record of the Elizabethan book trade at its height: Register B, the Stationers’ Company’s day-by-day register from 1576 onward, organized into four distinct sections — Apprentices, Book Entries (copyright registrations), Freemen, and Fines. Book entries run from 20 July 1576 to 25 June 1595; apprentice, freeman, and fine records run to 2 July 1605. Woven throughout the register sections are major illustrative documents from state papers and Company archives: the early printing patents granted to Seres, Day, and Vautrollier; the 1582 Star Chamber case of John Day v. Roger Ward; the full John Wolf controversy documents (1582–83); the Star Chamber Decree of 23 June 1586 — described by Arber as “the greatest enactment concerning the press in the reigns of Elizabeth or James I” — and the secret 1589 report to Lord Burghley naming the authors and printers of the Marprelate tracts. ^[source: stationers_registers_arber_vol2_raw.txt]
Quality Assessment
OCR from a 1950 lithographic reprint of the 1875 original (University of Minnesota Wilson Library copy). The register text is consistently readable throughout. The book entries are in a more standardised Elizabethan English than Volume I — the fixed formula (“Entred for his copie vnder th[e] handes of [licenser(s)], [title], [fee]”) makes entries easy to parse despite spelling variation. Arber’s editorial footnotes appear in square brackets inline.
Artifact types:

Running headers inline — master/warden names and account date ranges repeat at the top of every original page and are captured inline; also the section header “[Entrances of Copies.]” or “[Enrollments of the Freemen.]” repeats as a running head
Page numbers inline — “II. [n]” page numbers appear as isolated lines throughout
Library stamps — University of Minnesota library marks appear in the first ~90 lines
Illustrative document headers — major inserted documents are headed “[CHRISTOPHER BARKER’S REPORT…]” or “[The great Star Chamber Decree regulating printing.]” etc. repeating as running heads across multiple pages














































SectionLine rangeQualityFront matter, contents, introduction~1–3879ReadableIllustrative docs — early patents (1559–1574)~3600–3880ReadableRegister B — Apprentices (pages 31–292)~3880–16007ReadableRegister B — Book Entries / Entrances of Copies (pages 293–672)~16008–34489ReadableRegister B — Freemen (pages 673–842)~34490–43350ReadableRegister B — Fines (pages 843–864)~43351–44404ReadableRegister B — Livery and Miscellaneous (pages 865+)~44405–45409Readable

Contents — Section by Section
Introduction (lines ~603–3879)
Arber opens with an essay on the history of the word “Stationer” — its Latin and continental origins in the 13th century (Toulouse, Paris, Castile), its definition in the 1440 Promptorium Parvulorum, and its establishment in English trade. He sets out the key regulatory documents whose full texts appear in this volume and describes the framework of State Papers, Star Chamber Bills, and Company archives from which the illustrative documents are drawn. The “vital and essential documents” he identifies as foundational to understanding the 1576–1595 period are: the first Star Chamber Decree (1566); Lambarde’s draft Act for the press (1580); Thomas Norton’s letter to George Goring about John Wolf (23 October 1582); Barker’s letter to Burghley (December 1582); the Company’s complaint against Wolf (March 1583); the report on printing-presses in London (1583); the Star Chamber Decree of 23 June 1586; and the Marprelate secret report (1589).
Before the register text begins, Arber inserts the full texts of the major early patents:

William Seres’s patent for psalters and primers (8 July 1559, lines ~3600): the Letters Patent granting Seres and his son the exclusive right to print all psalters, primers, and prayer books in English and Latin; the foundation of the longest-running and most contentious monopoly in the Elizabethan book trade
John Day’s 7-year licence (11 November 1559, lines ~3709): the Letters Patent granting Day a privilege for the Cosmographical Glass and all books he might produce for seven years at his own cost, subject to pre-publication allowance — an early prototype of the later licensing system
High Commission letter to the Stationers’ Company (25 May 1560, lines ~3757): the earliest evidence of surreptitious printing — the Commissioners report that “evill desposyd persons” have “secretly taken uppon them to prynte” Seres’s privileged psalters on “pryvye presses” and direct the Wardens to seize the books and punish the offenders
Archbishop Parker’s correspondence on the Bishops’ Bible (1566–68, lines ~3849): Bishop Cox’s recommendation of Bodleigh’s Geneva Bible (9 March 1566); Parker’s notice that the revision of the Bishops’ Bible has commenced (26 November 1566); Parker’s report of the revision’s conclusion (22 September 1568); his letter presenting the first copy to Queen Elizabeth (5 October 1568) — the documentary record of the authorised Bible project that would culminate in Barker’s editions of 1568–72
Vautrollier’s patent for certain books (19 June 1574): referenced in the contents table; the grant that established Vautrollier’s printing privileges before his flight to Edinburgh

^[source: stationers_registers_arber_vol2_raw.txt]

Register B — Apprentices (lines ~3880–16007)
The complete enrollment record of apprentices presented to the Stationers’ Company from 20 July 1576 (20th year of Elizabeth’s reign) through 2 July 1605. Pages 31–292 of the original volume.
Entry format. Each entry gives: the date (in Latin, by feast-day and regnal year); the master’s name (in Clarendon type if a Company member); the apprentice’s full name; his father’s name, occupation, and place of origin (including the county); the term of years; the start date (by feast day); and the fee. From 1578 onward the enrollment fee rises from 6d to 2s 6d as a note marks (line ~4736). The county-of-origin data makes these records a geographical index of where Elizabethan stationers came from — apprentices from Yorkshire, Warwickshire, Kent, Lincolnshire, and London appear in the earliest entries.
The masters named in the earliest 1576 entries include William Seres, Richard Greene, Richard Gonneld, Richard Watkins, and William Norton. As the years progress, masters such as George Bishop, Henry Denham, John Charlewood, Robert Waldegrave, Richard Field, and Humphrey Lownes appear.
This section is the primary source for the apprenticeship careers of every known Elizabethan stationer: when an individual is identified as having been apprenticed to a particular master, the entry here gives the exact date, term, and geographical origin. ^[source: stationers_registers_arber_vol2_raw.txt]

Register B — Book Entries / Entrances of Copies (lines ~16008–34489)
The copyright registration record — the central primary source for Elizabethan literary and print history. Every book, pamphlet, ballad, and broadside entered at Stationers’ Hall for which a fee was paid is recorded here, from 20 July 1576 to 25 June 1595. Pages 293–672 of the original volume.
Entry format. The standard form from 1576 onward: “[Printer’s or publisher’s name] Entred for his copie vnder th[e] handes of [warden(s)] and [licenser], [abbreviated title], [fee].” The licenser changes across the period: in the late 1570s entries are frequently under the wardens’ hands alone, or under “the bishop of [London’s]” hand; from 1586 the Star Chamber Decree requires the Archbishop of Canterbury’s representative or a bishop alongside the Wardens for most categories of work. Fees are typically 4d for a ballad, 6d for a pamphlet or small book, and higher for substantial works.
Coverage. The 20-year span 1576–1595 covers the peak of Elizabethan literary production. Entries in these pages include:

Sidney’s Arcadia — entered by William Ponsonby, 23 August [1590]: “Receaued of him for a booke of Sir PHILIP SIDNEYS makinge intitled Arcadia: aucthorised vnder the Archbishop of CANTERBURY [his] hand” (line ~25997)
Lodge’s Penelope’s Web — entered by Edward White, 26 June 1587: “Receaued of him for printinge a booke intituled PENELOPES Webbe Aucthorised vnder the bishop of LONDONS hand” (line ~24955)
Early play texts, verse collections, chronicles, devotional works, and the full range of Elizabethan print are present

The register also shows the mechanics of transfer, conditional entry, and disputed copies: entries note “PROVIDED that ye cumpanie shall haue them at his hands,” conditional licences, and the occasional notation that a book has been withdrawn or its entry cancelled.
Embedded within this section are the major illustrative documents relevant to book-trade disputes of the period:

The Star Chamber case John Day v. Roger Ward and William Holmes (7 February–10 July 1582, lines ~38336): Day’s bill of complaint against Ward and Holmes for printing his ABC and catechism contrary to his patent; the full Star Chamber proceedings including demurrers, examinations, and the decree. The case establishes that the 1566 Star Chamber Decree was the primary legal instrument against patent infringers, and that Ward’s defence — that the patent was contrary to common law — was rejected

^[source: stationers_registers_arber_vol2_raw.txt]

The John Wolf Controversy Documents (lines ~39330–39600)
The documentary record of the early 1580s crisis over unauthorized printing, centred on John Wolf (alias Wolfe), who had been apprenticed to John Day and who organized a group of journeymen printers and non-Company stationers to print patented and privileged copies in defiance of the Company’s authority.
Documents reproduced in full:

Thomas Norton’s letter to George Goring about John Wolf (23 October 1582): Norton — the barrister and government censor — reports on Wolf’s activities and the Company’s failure to contain them
The Wardens’ report to Lord Burghley that Roger Ward’s family refused to allow a search of his house (29 October 1582)
The appeal of householders using the trade of Stationers to Lord Burghley against Thomas Norton (October 1582): the journeymen printers’ side of the dispute
A similar appeal to Sir Francis Walsingham (undated, c. October 1582)
The supplication to the Privy Council of the Wardens of the Stationers on behalf of the ancients and patentees against John Wolf and his associates (c. March 1583): the Company’s formal complaint naming Wolf’s associates
The University of Cambridge’s appeal to Lord Burghley against the seizure of their printer Thomas Thomas (14 June 1583): the Cambridge press’s challenge to London Stationers’ jurisdiction outside the City
The final report of the augmented Commission from the Privy Council on the Stationers’ Company controversy (1583): the government’s resolution that settled the Wolf dispute — Wolf was eventually brought into the Company and given his own printing rights

These documents collectively show how the Elizabethan book-trade regulatory system was tested and renegotiated in the early 1580s. ^[source: stationers_registers_arber_vol2_raw.txt]

The Star Chamber Decree of 23 June 1586 (lines ~41291–41400)
The full text of what Arber calls “the greatest enactment concerning the press in the reigns of Elizabeth or James I.” Written on vellum, this Decree — issued 23 June 1586, 28th year of Elizabeth’s reign — superseded all earlier orders and became the foundational press law for the next half-century.
Its key provisions: no person may print any book “against the fourme and meanyng” of any ordinance or statute; no press may be set up or kept except in London (plus the university towns of Oxford and Cambridge, by an earlier order); the number of presses in any printing house to be regulated by the Archbishop of Canterbury and the Bishop of London; no book to be printed until it has been “seen and perused” and allowed by the Archbishop or Bishop of London (or their nominees); a master printer who has been debarred may not exercise any branch of the trade even as a journeyman; any unlicensed books may be seized by any person whatsoever. The Act runs only for the life of the Queen.
The Decree is the direct legislative response to the Wolf controversy and to the perceived failure of the 1566 Star Chamber Decree to suppress unlicensed printing. It is the instrument that made the Archbishop of Canterbury’s imprimatur structurally necessary for all publishing — the requirement that appears in the book entries from 1586 onward. ^[source: stationers_registers_arber_vol2_raw.txt]

The Marprelate Secret Report (lines ~41811–41870)
The full text of the secret report to Lord Burghley, dated 21 September 1589 in Burghley’s own hand, identifying the authors and printers of the Martin Marprelate tracts. Arber calls this “most valuable.”
The report identifies Robert Waldegrave as printer of the first three Marprelate books (printed in “a Dutch letter [type]” at Sir Richard Knightley’s house in Northamptonshire); names Henry Sharpe and John Hodgkins as printers of the last two books (in “a litle Romaine and Italian letter [type]”). It traces how Waldegrave’s press was searched at Easter 1588, how he saved his type “in a boxe vnder his Cloke,” brought the type to Mistress Crane’s house in London, and then to sites outside the City. It identifies the paper supply route through “a Spurrier [a maker of spurs] dwellinge about Pie Corner neere West Smythfeild.” The report also names Sir Richard Knightley and Mr Wiston as the gentlemen who harboured the press — both were later fined by the Star Chamber, though Archbishop Whitgift obtained remission of the fines. ^[source: stationers_registers_arber_vol2_raw.txt]

Register B — Freemen (lines ~34490–43350)
The enrollment of freemen of the Company from April 1577 to July 1605. Pages 673–842 of the original volume. Each entry gives: date, freeman’s name, fee (initially 3s 4d + dinner paid), and master’s name. The fee rises progressively across the period. This section is the primary record of when each stationer took up his freedom — the moment he was legally entitled to publish (though not necessarily to print, absent a place in one of the twenty-two printing houses). ^[source: stationers_registers_arber_vol2_raw.txt]

Register B — Fines (lines ~43351–44404)
The record of fines levied by the Court of Assistants from 1576 to 1604. Pages 843–864 of the original volume. Entries record: date, the name of the person fined, the offence (printing without licence, breaking orders, working at an unlicensed press, etc.), and the amount. The fines section is a supplementary record to the book entries — where a book entry notes an infringement, the corresponding fine often appears here. ^[source: stationers_registers_arber_vol2_raw.txt]

Useful For

sources/stationers-registers-arber-vol3.title: Arber — Transcript of the Registers of the Stationers' Company, Vol. III
sources/stationers-registers-arber-vol3.content:
Edward Arber (ed.), A Transcript of the Registers of the Company of Stationers of London, 1554–1640 A.D. Volume III — Text. Privately printed, London, 1 July 1876. Reprinted New York: Peter Smith, 1950. ~40,530 lines extracted from a zip of 716 OCR’d page files. Pennsylvania State College Library copy.
This is the third of five volumes of Arber’s Transcript. Volume III contains Register C — the book entry (copyright registration) record from July 1595 to 11 July 1620, covering the last eight years of Elizabeth’s reign and the first seventeen years of James I. It also contains the Freeman list from 1605 to 31 December 1640 and the Succession of Master Printers in London 1586–1636. This is the volume most directly relevant to Elizabethan and Jacobean literary history: it contains the registration entries for Hamlet, Shakespeare’s Sonnets, Troilus and Cressida, the 1599 Bishops’ Order burning satirical books at Stationers’ Hall, the James I grant to the Company (1603), the 9 May 1615 list of Master Printers and their press allowances, and the full genealogy of London printing houses 1586–1635 tracing the succession of each of the twenty-two recognised presses. ^[source: stationers_registers_arber_vol3_raw.txt]
Quality Assessment
OCR from a 1950 lithographic reprint of the 1876 original (Pennsylvania State College Library copy). The book entry text is consistently readable — the standard entry formula (“Entred for his copie vnder th[e h]andes of [licenser(s)], [abbreviated title], [fee]”) makes entries identifiable despite spelling variation. The supplementary sections (Freemen list, Master Printers succession) are more table-like in layout and the OCR renders them as broken columns — readable with care, but not clean prose.
Artifact types:

Running headers inline — warden names, year-period dates, and section headers (“[Entrances of Copies.]”, “[Illustrative Documents.]”) repeat on every page and appear inline
Page numbers inline — “III. [n]” page numbers appear as isolated lines throughout
Library stamps in opening pages — Pennsylvania State College library marks in first ~15 lines
Table-format OCR noise — the Freemen list and Master Printers succession are printed in multi-column tabular format; the OCR captures these as broken fragments, readable but not clean text









































SectionLine rangeQualityFront matter, contents, introduction~1–2393ReadableRegister C — court notes and misc (1596)~2394–2984ReadableRegister C — Book Entries, 1595–1620~2985–35959Readable1599 Bishops’ Order and book burning~35900–36010ReadableFreemen, 1605–1640~36813–39604Readable (table-column layout)Succession of Master Printers, 1586–1636~39605–40530Readable (table-column layout)

Contents — Section by Section
Introduction (lines ~410–2393)
Arber opens with his most provocative claim across the five volumes: that “the Press in England in the reign of Queen ELIZABETH was probably the freest in Europe; as free indeed as the political situation at that time would admit of.” He attributes this to the long administration of Lord Burghley, “who was ever on the side of light and moderation, welcomed rather than feared all honest discussion of grievances or exposure of abuses in print.” The case of John Stubbs — who had his right hand cut off in 1579 for the fervently loyal protest against the Anjou marriage — is cited as an exception to the general spirit of Elizabeth’s government.
He quotes Bacon’s praise of Elizabethan Protestant theological writing (Of the Proficience and Advancement of Learning, 1605) and Wilkins’s judgment that English sermons and treatises were “most elaborate and useful” among all European languages — arguing that the press served this achievement. He identifies the true censors as “the lording hierarchy, the Archbishops and Bishops” rather than the general clergy, and describes Laud’s imposition of Arminian theology as the product of this episcopal oligarchy.
He then turns to the practical structure: how many printing houses existed in the age of Shakespeare and Jonson? The number of acknowledged London printing houses did not materially increase in the 86 years from 1554 to 1640. The 1615 list shows 19 Master Printers; the 1634 list shows 22; the 1635 and 1636 lists show 22 and 21 respectively. The pp. 699–704 lists are described as showing this continuity. ^[source: stationers_registers_arber_vol3_raw.txt]

Register C — Book Entries, July 1595 – July 1620 (lines ~2985–35959)
The copyright registration record for 25 years of English printing — the last eight years of Elizabeth’s reign (40th–45th years, 1595–1603) and the first seventeen years of James I (46th–64th years, 1603–1620). Pages 33–676 of the original volume.
Entry format. The standard form continues from Volume II: “[Stationer’s name] Entred for his copie vnder th[e h]andes of [licenser(s)], [abbreviated title], [fee].” The licenser named is now routinely an official appointed under the Archbishop of Canterbury — named individuals such as master Pasfield, master Murgetrod, master Harsnet, master Wilson, or master Barcham — alongside the warden. The fee remains 6d for most entries. Multiple titles entered on a single day by a single stationer are common, at 4d–6d each.
Key entries — Shakespeare and the Elizabethan stage:

Hamlet (26 July 1602, line ~10790): “Entred for his Copie vnder the handes of master PASFEILD and master waterson warden A booke called the Revenge of HAMLETT Prince [of] Denmarke as yt was latelie Acted by the Lord Chamberleyne his servantes vjd” — registered by James Roberts
Troilus and Cressida (28 January 1603, line ~19855): entered under Sir George Bucke and warden Lownes, “a booke called the history of TROYLUS and CRESSIDA vjd”
Shakespeare’s Sonnets (20 May 1609, line ~20355): “Entred for his copie vnder th[e h]andes of master WILSON and master Lownes Warden a Booke called SHAKESPEARES Sonnettes vjd” — registered by Thomas Thorpe
Merry Wives of Windsor: Arber’s footnote notes it was printed by J. Busby before the registration date; entered only when assigned to A. Johnson
King Lear: similar note at page 289 — entered by assignment rather than original registration

Key embedded documents:
List of printers who had set up contrary to the 1586 Star Chamber Decree (c. 7 July 1598, page 43): a list of names presented by the printers themselves of those who had, up to this date, established presses in violation of the Decree. A snapshot of the underground or irregular press on the eve of the 1599 book-burning.
The 1599 Bishops’ Order — books ordered burned or suppressed (1 June 1599 and 4 June 1599, lines ~35900–36010): The full text of the order signed by Archbishop Whitgift (JOHN WHITGIFT CANTUAR) and Bishop Bancroft (RICHARD BANCROFT LONDON), delivered to master Newbery, master Binge, and master Ponsonby (Wardens) at Croydon on 1 June. The Order: bans all verse satires and epigrams; directs that no plays be printed without the allowance of the Master of the Revels; bans all books of the nature of the Arcadian prose (ungodly love matters); bans all Nashe’s books and all Doctor Harvey’s books; and stipulates that no book shall be printed even with archiepiscopal signature until the Wardens have confirmed it is genuine.
Published at Stationers’ Hall on 4 June 1599 to the fourteen unprivileged printers then in business (named: John Wyndett, Gabriell Simpson, Richard Braddocke, Ffelixe Kingston, William Whyte, Raphe Blower, Thomas Judson, Peeter Shorte, Adam Islipe, Richard Ffeild, Edmond Bollifante, Thomas Creed, Edward Aldee, Valentyne Symes).
Books burnt in the hall that day:

Pygmalion (Marston)
The Scourge of Villainy (Marston)
The Shadow of Truth
Snarlinge Satires
Davies’s Epigrams
Marriage and Wyvinge
15 Foyes of Marriage

Books stayed (not burnt but called in):

Caltha Poetarum
Hall’s Satires
Willobie’s Aviso

Grant of James I to the Stationers’ Company (29 October 1603): Grant of primers, psalters, almanacks, and prognostications to the Company in perpetuity — subsequently surrendered and enlarged 8 March 1616.
Enlarged Grant of James I (8 March 1616, pages 679–682): The extended grant covering all manner of almanacks and prognostications, primers, psalters, and psalms in metre or prose, to the Company and their successors for ever. The full Latin and English text reproduced.
Gervase Markham’s promise (July 1617, page 679): Markham’s written undertaking not to write any more books on cattle, horses, or husbandry — an unusual document showing the Company enforcing a form of copyright management by requiring an author to limit his own output.
9 May 1615 list of Master Printers and their press allowances (page 699): A numbered list of 19 Master Printers, each allocated a specified number of presses. Includes Thomas Purfoot, Nicholas Oakes, Ralph Blower, George Purslow — with the number of presses each is permitted to operate. ^[source: stationers_registers_arber_vol3_raw.txt]

Freemen, 1605–1640 (lines ~36813–39604)
A complete list of all stationers who took up their freedom of the Company from 1605 to 31 December 1640. Pages 683–688 of the original volume. The list is tabular — names, dates (month and day), and year. This section extends the Freeman record begun in Volume II (which runs to 1605) through the full Stuart period to 1640.
For any stationer active in the Jacobean or Caroline press, this is the primary record of when they were admitted as a Freeman — the formal qualification to publish in their own right. ^[source: stationers_registers_arber_vol3_raw.txt]

Succession of Master Printers in London, 1586–1636 (lines ~39605–40530)
A series of documents tracing who held each of the twenty-two recognised London printing houses from the 1586 Star Chamber Decree through the mid-Caroline period. This is the primary source for the physical continuity of London printing capacity across fifty years.
Archbishop Abbot’s licences (pages 689): The petitions and licences by which new Master Printers were formally admitted with archiepiscopal sanction — specifically John Dawson (23 January 1621) and Miles Flesher (16 November 1624). Each petition shows the mechanism: the candidate had either served an apprenticeship and then a co-partnership with a deceased master, or had agreed for the deceased master’s “moitie” (half-share). Admission required the Archbishop’s written consent alongside the Company’s election.
Sir John Lambe’s notes on the former practice of licensing books (1636, lines ~39612): A 1636 survey by Sir John Lambe of the history of licensing, drawing on the Stationers’ Hall clerks’ books. Key findings: from the 19th year of Elizabeth (1576–77, the first year of Register B) until the 1586 Star Chamber Decree, many books were licensed by the Master and Wardens alone, some by the Master alone, some by the Archbishop and more by the Bishop of London. Lambe notes that the missing register for 1571–1576 was already lost when he made his enquiry (confirming the gap noted in Vol. I). He traces the root authority back to Elizabeth’s 51st Injunction (1559): “none shall print any booke &c. except it be licensed by ye Queenes maiestie’s writing or by [her commissioners]” — confirming this Injunction as the foundation of all Protestant press licensing. Master Kingston (then Master of the Company) testified that before the 1586 Decree “the master and wardens licensed all, And that when they had any Divinity booke of muche importance they would take the advise of some 2 or 3 ministers of this towne.”
8 October 1634 list of Master Printers — licensed and unlicensed (page 700, lines ~40057): A survey of 22 Master Printers then living, distinguishing those who had received formal archiepiscopal admission from those who had not. The unlicensed include: Adam Islip (who bought his printing house, letter, and implements from John Wolf and succeeded him — “an ancient Erection”); Felix Kingston (succeeded his father — “an ancient Erection”); Widow Aldee (succeeded her husband who was a master before the 1586 Decree); William Stansby (succeeded master Windet — “an ancient Erection”); William Jones (who farms his printing house from Widow Blore — “an ancient Erection”). The document shows that a significant number of the 22 recognised houses were “ancient Erections” — presses that predated the Decree and transmitted their legitimacy through widow succession or purchase, without formal archiepiscopal admission.
Genealogy of London printing houses, 1586–1635 (pp. 702–703, lines ~40282): A tabular genealogy tracing each of the 22 printing houses through its successive occupants from the 1586 Decree to 1635. Notable details: Robert Raworth was suppressed in 1635 for printing Venus and Adonis (a copy belonging to another stationer), but resumed printing two years later; Humphrey Lownes succeeded Short by marrying Short’s widow; Robert Young was admitted partner with Lownes in 1631 and after Lownes’s death held the house without formal admission. The document shows the 22 presses as essentially a fixed set of slots — when one master died or was suppressed, the slot was filled by succession (widow, son, partner) or by petition. ^[source: stationers_registers_arber_vol3_raw.txt]

Useful For
